teile.einleitung: The red squirrel is a nimble rodent with a bushy tail. It climbs skilfully around in the trees and lives in forests, parks and gardens. In autumn it eagerly gathers supplies for the winter.
wichtigste: The squirrel's nest is called a drey.
Squirrels mainly eat nuts, acorns and seeds.
In autumn they hide supplies in many places.
They do not hibernate but have a winter rest.
New trees can grow from forgotten nuts.
Their most dangerous enemy in the trees is the pine marten.

abschnitte.text: The red squirrel is called **Sciurus vulgaris** in science. Its fur on the back is **reddish-brown to blackish-brown**. The **belly**, however, is always pale to **white**. The long, bushy tail helps it keep its balance when jumping. In winter many squirrels have tufts of hair on their ears, called **ear tufts**.

The squirrel's round nest is called a **drey**. It is built from twigs and lined inside with **moss** and other soft material. The drey sits high up in a tree crown. A squirrel often has several dreys in its territory.

Squirrels mainly eat **nuts, acorns and seeds** from fir cones. Sometimes they also eat buds or mushrooms. In autumn they **bury** nuts and seeds in many places. Many hiding places are never found again. In spring the seeds sprout, and **new trees** grow. In this way the squirrel helps to spread the forest.

Squirrels do **not hibernate**. They have a **winter rest**: they sleep a lot in the warm drey but wake up again and again. Then they look for their supplies and eat some of them. On mild winter days you therefore often see them outside.

The most dangerous enemy is the **pine marten**. It climbs very skilfully and can chase squirrels right up into the tree crowns. Birds of prey such as the goshawk also hunt squirrels. With quick leaps and dodges they often escape.

gewusst: Many trees in the forest have grown from nuts that a squirrel forgot.
In winter, squirrels often grow long brushes of hair on their ears.

teile.einleitung: Cytokinins are plant hormones. They act like messengers and control how a plant grows. They are especially important for cell division, hence their name.
wichtigste: Cytokinins are formed mainly in the root tips.
They promote cell division, cytokinesis.
The natural cytokinin zeatin was obtained from unripe maize kernels.
Chemically, cytokinins are derived from the nucleobase adenine.
Leaves treated with cytokinin stay green longer.
Cytokinins stimulate dormant side buds to sprout.

abschnitte.text: The name **cytokinin** comes from **cytokinesis**, the technical word for cell division. Cytokinins stimulate cells to divide. In this way the plant can grow and form new tissue. They are made mainly in the **root tips**. From there they travel with the water stream upwards into shoot and leaves.

The first cytokinin that researchers discovered in the 1950s was **kinetin**, a substance that arises when genetic material is broken down. Later a natural cytokinin was found in **unripe maize kernels** and named **zeatin** after maize (Zea mays). Chemically, natural cytokinins are derived from the nucleobase **adenine**. Adenine is also a building block of the genetic material DNA.

Cytokinins often act as opponents of the hormone **auxin**. Auxin from the shoot tip keeps the side buds dormant. Cytokinins, by contrast, **stimulate dormant side buds** to **sprout**, and the plant becomes bushier. They also delay ageing: a **cut leaf** treated with cytokinin **stays green longer**. That is why people also speak of a rejuvenating effect.

In **tissue culture**, a **callus**, a heap of unordered cells, is grown from small pieces of plant. Depending on the ratio of the hormones, something different arises from it. With **a lot of cytokinin and little auxin**, the callus forms **shoots**. With a lot of auxin and little cytokinin, it forms roots instead. In this way, for example, orchids or healthy potato plants are multiplied in the lab.

The bacterium **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** causes **crown galls** on plants, that is, growths. It transfers its own genes into the plant cells. These genes make the plant itself produce a lot of auxin and cytokinin. The cells then divide without control. Researchers today use this trick to build genes into plants in a targeted way.

gewusst: Some bacteria and fungi also make cytokinins.
Coconut milk contains cytokinins and was therefore used in the past in tissue culture.

teile.einleitung: The umbellifers are a large plant family. Their small flowers grow in umbels that look like open umbrellas. The family includes many vegetables and kitchen herbs, but also some very poisonous plants.
wichtigste: Umbellifers carry their flowers in umbrella-shaped umbels.
Parsley, dill and lovage are kitchen herbs from this family.
Carrot, celery and fennel are umbellifers.
Caraway is a spice that comes from an umbellifer.
Many umbellifers have a hollow, grooved stem.
Hemlock is very poisonous.

abschnitte.text: In the **umbellifers**, many flower stalks grow out from a single point, like the spokes of an umbrella. This kind of flower cluster is called an **umbel**. Often many small umbels sit together in one large compound umbel. The stem is typical too: in many species it is **hollow and grooved**. Many umbellifers have a strong scent because they contain essential oils.

A surprising number of vegetables belong to this family. The **carrot** is an umbellifer, and we eat its root. Of **celery**, depending on the variety, people eat the thick **bulb** or the long **sticks**. **Fennel** has a thick bulb made of leaf bases and tastes of **aniseed**. The parsnip also belongs to this family.

**Parsley** is one of the best-known kitchen herbs and is an umbellifer. Dill, chervil and coriander belong to the family too. **Lovage** is also called **Maggi herb** because of its taste, which reminds people of the well-known seasoning. **Caraway** is often found in bread and sauerkraut. Aniseed is another spice from this family.

Some umbellifers are very poisonous. **Hemlock** has a stem with red spots and smells unpleasant. In ancient **Athens**, hemlock poison was used for executions, and the case of the philosopher Socrates is well known. Giant hogweed is dangerous too: its sap makes the skin sensitive to sunlight and can cause severe skin damage. Because many umbellifers look alike, you should never pick and eat wild species yourself.

gewusst: The wild form of the carrot has a thin white root; the orange colour is the result of breeding.
In the middle of the umbel of wild carrot there is often a single dark flower.

teile.einleitung: St John's wort is a yellow-flowering plant that you find in summer at the edges of paths and in dry meadows. It is a well-known medicinal plant and has some astonishing properties.
wichtigste: St John's wort flowers from around the end of June.
Its name recalls St John's Day on 24 June.
The flowers are bright yellow and have five petals.
Held up to the light, the leaves show many pale dots.
Oil with flowers steeped in it turns red.
St John's wort can weaken the effect of other medicines.

abschnitte.text: St John's wort carries **bright yellow flowers** with five petals. It grows at the edges of paths, in dry meadows and at the edges of woods. The **stem** is typical: it is round but has **two fine ridges along its length**. This is how you can tell it apart from similar species of St John's wort.
The plant flowers from around the end of June. Its name recalls **St John's Day on 24 June**. This is the feast day of **John the Baptist**. The scientific name is **Hypericum perforatum**.

If you hold a leaf up to the light, you see **many pale, translucent dots**. They are tiny **oil glands** that look like small holes. That is why the species is called “perforatum” in Latin, meaning “perforated”. If you steep the flowers in oil, the pigment **hypericin** turns the oil deep red. This **red oil** is traditionally used for skin care.

Preparations made from St John's wort are mainly used for **mildly low moods**. Studies show that they can help with mild to moderate low moods. The effect only sets in after a few weeks. You should only take them after talking to a doctor or at a pharmacy.

St John's wort can make the skin **more sensitive to sunlight**. Anyone who takes it should avoid strong sun. It also speeds up the breakdown of many other medicines in the **liver**. They then work less well. So you should not simply take it together with other medicines.

gewusst: The see-through dots in the leaves are tiny oil glands.
Yellow flowers turn oil red: this is because of the pigment hypericin.

teile.einleitung: An endemic species is an animal or plant species that occurs only in one particular, limited area. This can be an island, a lake or a mountain range. Many endemic species are rare and especially worth protecting.
wichtigste: Endemic species occur only in a narrowly limited area.
The opposite are cosmopolitans, which are spread almost worldwide.
Neoendemics are young species, palaeoendemics are old species in a remaining area.
On remote islands there are especially many endemic species.
The Baikal seal lives only in Lake Baikal in Siberia.
In Swiss lakes, many endemic whitefish species arose.

abschnitte.text: An **endemic species** lives only in a particular area. The opposite is a **cosmopolitan**, a species spread almost worldwide, such as the housefly or bracken. Two kinds of endemic species are distinguished. **Neoendemics** arose only recently and have not yet been able to spread. **Palaeoendemics** are old species that used to be more widespread and have survived only in a **refuge**.

abschnitte.titel: Islands as a workshop of evolution
abschnitte.text: On remote **islands** there are especially many endemic species. A few species that arrived there carry on developing without exchange with the mainland. This **isolation** produces new species that exist only there. Well-known examples are **Darwin's finches** on the Galápagos Islands. In **New Zealand** lives the **kakapo**, a flightless, nocturnal parrot.

Old, large lakes are also like islands. The **Baikal seal** lives only in **Lake Baikal** in Siberia. It is one of the few seals in fresh water. In the Swiss pre-Alpine lakes, numerous **whitefish species** arose after the last ice age, often living in only a single lake. Because of the over-fertilisation of the lakes in the 20th century, some of them have disappeared.

Endemic species are often under serious threat of **extinction**. Their range is small. A single event, such as an **introduced predator**, can wipe out the whole population. In the kakapo, introduced rats and stoats brought the species to the brink of extinction. That is why endemic species are often a special focus in nature conservation.

gewusst: Some whitefish species exist in the whole world only in a single Swiss lake.
The kakapo is a parrot that cannot fly.

teile.einleitung: Botanists want to record the structure of a blossom briefly and precisely. There are two aids for this: the **floral diagram**, a drawing, and the **floral formula**, a notation with letters and numbers. Both show at a glance how a blossom is built.
wichtigste: A floral diagram is a schematic plan of the blossom from above.
It shows the number and position of calyx, corolla, stamens and carpels.
The floral formula summarises the structure of a blossom in one line, for example “K5 C5 A10 G1”.
K stands for sepals, C for petals, A for stamens, G for carpels.
P stands for a uniform perianth, the perigon.
An asterisk means radially symmetrical, very many parts are written with ∞.

abschnitte.text: A **floral diagram** shows the blossom as if you cut it across from above. The individual parts are arranged as simple symbols in circles. On the outside lie the **sepals**, then the **petals**, inside the **stamens** and in the middle the **carpels**. This way you can see exactly how many parts there are and where they lie.

The **floral formula** is a shorthand. **K** stands for the sepals. **C** comes from the Latin word **corolla**, meaning crown, and stands for the petals. **A** stands for the **androecium**, all the stamens together. **G** stands for the **gynoecium**, that is, the carpels. The number after each letter says how many of these parts are present.

If sepals and petals look the same, as in the **tulip**, you write **P** for **perigon**, a uniform perianth. If parts are too numerous to count, the sign **∞** stands for infinite. This is so, for example, with the many stamens of the **rose**. At the start of the formula a sign shows the symmetry of the blossom.

An asterisk “*” at the start means that the blossom is **radially symmetrical**, that is, built like a star. You can divide it into equal halves by several planes, like a buttercup. **Bilaterally symmetrical** or **zygomorphic** blossoms, by contrast, have **exactly one** plane of symmetry. An example is the **papilionaceous flower** of pea and clover.

gewusst: With floral formulas you can recognise whole plant families, because related plants often have very similar formulas.
In the rose family you often find five sepals and five petals.

teile.einleitung: Bt maize is a genetically modified maize that itself makes a substance against certain pests. It is grown in some countries, but is controversial.
wichtigste: Bt stands for the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis.
The bacterium supplies the gene for an insect-killing Cry protein.
In Europe Bt maize was developed mainly against the European corn borer.
The protein acts only in the alkaline gut of certain insect larvae.
MON810 is the only genetically modified plant approved for cultivation in the EU (as of 2025).
Refuges are meant to prevent pests from becoming resistant.

abschnitte.text: **Bt** stands for **Bacillus thuringiensis**, a bacterium from the soil. It forms **Cry proteins** that are poisonous to certain insect larvae. The name comes from the English crystal, because the bacterium stores them as crystals. In **Bt maize** such a gene was built into the maize plant. This way the maize makes the protein itself.

In Europe Bt maize was developed mainly against the **European corn borer**. This is a moth whose caterpillars bore into the maize stalks and weaken the plant. Caterpillars in the stalk are hard to reach with sprays. Because the plant makes the toxin itself, you can often do without **insecticide sprays**.

abschnitte.titel: Why it affects only certain insects
abschnitte.text: The Bt protein is split and activated in the **alkaline** gut of the larvae. After that it binds to special **receptors** of the gut wall. Mammals and humans have neither this environment nor these receptors. That is why the protein is regarded as harmless to them. Different Cry proteins act against different groups of insects.

The maize line **MON810** is the only genetically modified plant that may be grown in the EU (as of 2025). It is grown mainly in Spain. Many EU countries have banned cultivation nationally. In **Switzerland**, since a popular vote in 2005, a **moratorium**, that is, a temporary ban, has applied to growing genetically modified plants in agriculture. It has been extended several times since.

Next to Bt maize fields, **refuges** are laid out, areas with maize without the Bt gene. There susceptible insects survive. They mate with the few resistant animals and so slow the spread of **resistance**. Supporters stress the lower use of sprays. Critics worry about consequences for other insects and about dependence on seed companies. Interesting is: preparations of Bacillus thuringiensis are also allowed as sprays in **organic farming**.

gewusst: Bacillus thuringiensis was named after the German region Thuringia.
Bt sprays have been used for decades against caterpillars in vegetable and fruit growing.

teile.einleitung: A diversity index is a number that describes how diverse a community of living things is. It takes into account not only how many species there are, but also how evenly the individuals are distributed among the species.
wichtigste: A diversity index measures the number of species and the distribution of individuals among the species.
The pure number of species is called species richness.
Evenness describes how evenly the individuals are distributed.
The Simpson index Σ p² states how likely it is that two random individuals belong to the same species.
Alpha diversity is the diversity within a habitat, beta diversity the difference between habitats.
Biodiversity has three levels: genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity.

abschnitte.text: The simplest way to measure diversity is to count the species. This number is called **species richness**. But imagine two meadows with three species each. On the first there are equally many plants of each species. On the second, almost all the plants are dandelion, and the other species occur only sparsely. The first meadow seems more diverse. How **evenly** the individuals are distributed among the species is called **evenness**. A **diversity index** combines both.

A well-known index is the **Simpson index**. For each species you determine its share p of all individuals. Then you square the shares and add them up: **D = Σ p²**. D states the **probability** that **two randomly drawn individuals** belong to the **same species**. The larger D is, the less diverse the community. That is why the **Simpson diversity** is often used: 1 minus Σ p².

A meadow has three species with the shares 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. The squares are 0.25, 0.0625 and 0.0625. Together this gives 0.375. The Simpson diversity is therefore 1 minus 0.375, which is **0.625**. Another well-known index is the **Shannon index**. It is calculated with logarithms and reacts more strongly to rare species.

The ecologist **Robert Whittaker** distinguished diversity at different spatial levels. **Alpha diversity** is the diversity **within a single habitat**, for example a meadow. **Beta diversity** describes the **difference in species composition** between habitats, for example between meadow and forest. **Gamma diversity** is the diversity of a whole landscape.

Biodiversity is more than the number of species. Usually three levels are distinguished: **genetic diversity** within a species, **species diversity** and **ecosystem diversity**, that is, the diversity of habitats. In Switzerland, **Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland** has for many years been observing, on behalf of the Confederation, how diversity is changing.

gewusst: The Simpson index is named after the British statistician Edward Simpson, who presented it in 1949.
The Shannon index originally comes from information theory and was developed to measure messages.

teile.einleitung: CAM plants are true water savers. They open their stomata mainly in the cool night and store the carbon dioxide as acid. During the day the pores stay closed, and photosynthesis runs on the stored supply.
wichtigste: CAM stands for Crassulacean Acid Metabolism.
The name comes from the stonecrop family.
CAM plants open their stomata mainly at night.
They store the CO2 as malic acid in the vacuole.
During the day the Calvin cycle gets its CO2 from the stored acid.
The biggest advantage: they save a great deal of water.
Pineapple and houseleek are CAM plants.

abschnitte.text: **CAM** is English and stands for **Crassulacean Acid Metabolism**. It is named after the **stonecrop family** (Crassulaceae), in which it was first studied precisely. This family includes the **houseleek**, which also grows on rocks and walls in the Swiss Alps. Its thick leaves store water.

Plants take in CO2 through tiny pores, the **stomata**. But water evaporates through them too. CAM plants open their stomata mainly **at night**, when it is cooler and damper. They bind the CO2 to a molecule and store it as **malic acid** in the **vacuole**, the large storage space of the cell. In the morning some CAM plants therefore taste slightly sour.

During the day the stomata stay closed. Now the stored acid is broken down again, and the CO2 is released. With it the **Calvin cycle** works with the help of sunlight and makes sugar. The difference from C4 plants: these separate the steps **in space** into two layers of cells. CAM plants separate them **in time**, into night and day.

The most important advantage is that CAM plants **save a great deal of water**. That is why many of them live in dry places. Examples are **cacti**, **agaves** and many stonecrop plants. The **pineapple** is a well-known crop with CAM metabolism. Some orchids that grow on trees also use this pathway. The disadvantage: CAM plants usually grow rather slowly.

gewusst: Some plants can switch between normal photosynthesis and CAM depending on the weather.
The houseleek is called Sempervivum in Latin, which means “always living”.

teile.einleitung: The chalet is the typical wooden house of the Swiss mountains. With its wide roof, wooden shutters and flowers in front of the windows, it has become an image of Switzerland worldwide.
wichtigste: A typical chalet is built mainly of wood.
It has a shallow, wide gabled roof.
In front of the windows there are often wooden shutters and flower boxes.
Especially many chalets stand in the mountains.
The word “chalet” comes from French.
A simple hut on the alp is called an alpine hut.

abschnitte.text: A typical **chalet** is built **mainly of wood**. Often it stands on a stone base that protects against damp. The walls often consist of beams laid on top of one another that interlock at the corners. This way of building is called **log construction**, in Switzerland also **Strickbau**. There was enough wood in the mountain forests, and it keeps warm well in winter.

The roof of a chalet is a **shallow, wide gabled roof**. It projects far beyond the walls. In this way it protects the wooden walls from rain and snow. On the shallow roof the snow stays lying in winter and acts like a blanket of warmth. In the past the roofs were often covered with wooden shingles or stone slabs.

In front of the windows, a chalet often has **wooden shutters** and **flower boxes**, for example with red geraniums. On old wooden houses in the **Bernese Oberland** there are often **inscriptions** on the beams. This can be a **saying**, a blessing, the names of the builders or the **year of construction**. Some houses are also decorated with carvings. In this way an old house tells something about its history.

The wood of old chalets turns **dark brown**, almost black, on the sunny side. This comes from **sun and weather**, which change the wood over many years. The word **“chalet”** comes from the **French** of western Switzerland. Originally it meant a simple hut on the alp. Such an **alpine hut** is still the place where herders live in summer and often make cheese.

gewusst: In the 19th century, chalets became so popular as “Swiss houses” that they were copied in other countries too.
In the Ballenberg open-air museum in the Bernese Oberland you can visit old farmhouses from all over Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Christian Körner is a plant ecologist who researched and taught at the University of Basel for a long time. He is among the best-known experts on plant life in the high mountains and on the question of how plants react to more CO2.
wichtigste: Christian Körner originally comes from Austria.
He taught for a long time as a professor at the University of Basel.
The standard work “Alpine Plant Life” is by him.
For almost 15 years he led the network Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment.
At Hofstetten near Basel his group used a crane to study CO2 enrichment in tree crowns.
He defines the alpine zone as the area above the natural treeline.

abschnitte.text: Christian Körner originally comes from **Austria**. He became a plant ecologist, that is, a researcher who studies how plants live together with their environment. For a long time he taught as **professor at the University of Basel**. There he led a research group at the Botanical Institute. He wrote many scientific articles and books that are read worldwide.

His standard work on the ecology of high-mountain plants is called **“Alpine Plant Life”**. Körner defines the **alpine zone** uniformly worldwide as the area **above the natural treeline**. In this way mountains all over the world can be compared. He stresses that the **air pressure** changes with height according to a law everywhere on Earth. Other factors such as precipitation, by contrast, are very different from one mountain range to another.

At **Hofstetten near Basel**, a large **crane** stood in the middle of the forest. With it, Körner’s group fed additional **CO2 into the crowns** of old trees. They wanted to find out whether trees grow faster with more CO2 in the air. The trees hardly grew faster. According to Körner’s thesis, in the cold it is not photosynthesis that first limits growth, but the **formation of new cells**.

For almost **15 years** Körner led the **Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment**. This is an international network that studies the diversity of plants and animals in the mountains of the world. Researchers from many countries exchange their knowledge in it. Mountains are especially important because very many different habitats lie close together there.

gewusst: According to Körner’s research, the treeline lies worldwide roughly where the mean soil temperature in the growing season is about 6 to 7 degrees.

teile.einleitung: The gentian is one of the best-known Alpine flowers of Switzerland. Many species flower bright blue, while the great yellow gentian grows tall and has a very bitter root.
wichtigste: The trumpet gentian has large, deep blue flowers shaped like a bell or a funnel.
It grows on mountain meadows and pastures and flowers in early summer.
In cold, rain and low light, the gentian closes its flowers.
The great yellow gentian usually grows 50 to 140 centimetres tall.
Its thick root is very bitter and is used for medicine.
Bumblebees crawl deep into the flower bells and pollinate them.

abschnitte.text: The **trumpet gentian** has large, **deep blue** flowers. They sit almost directly on the ground, because the stem is very short. The flowers are shaped like a **bell or a funnel** and can grow up to 5 centimetres long. It grows on **mountain meadows and pastures** and flowers there in early summer. A strong, deep blue is also called **gentian blue** after its flowers.

The **spring gentian** is much smaller. Its bright blue flowers have five lobes that stand open like a **star**. It flowers early in the year on meadows in the mountains and in the Jura. Like the other gentians, it opens in the sun.

When it gets **cold** or **rains**, the gentian closes its flowers. This keeps the pollen and nectar protected. When the sun shines again, they open. **Bumblebees** in particular often visit gentian flowers. They are strong enough to crawl deep into the bell. There they collect nectar and **pollinate** the flower as they do so.

The **great yellow gentian** looks quite different. It is a strong **perennial** and usually grows 50 to 140 centimetres tall, so often more than a metre. Its yellow flowers sit in tiers on the stem. It has a thick, long **root** that is dug up. It contains **bitter substances** and is among the bitterest plant substances known. From it, remedies meant to help the stomach are made, and also gentian schnapps.

gewusst: Many gentian species are protected in Switzerland and must not be picked.
The root of the great yellow gentian can become very old and as thick as an arm.

teile.einleitung: The edelweiss is a small white flower from the mountains. It is regarded as a symbol of the Alps and of Switzerland. Its white star is as soft as felt.
wichtigste: The edelweiss has a white, felty star.
Fine hairs protect it from sun, cold and drying out.
It grows on rocks and stony grassland high in the mountains.
In Switzerland the edelweiss is protected.
It flowers from about July to September.
Its scientific name means lion's foot.

abschnitte.text: What looks like one big white flower is really made of **white, felty bracts**. They form a star. In the middle sit small **yellowish flower heads**. The edelweiss usually grows only **5 to 20 centimetres** tall, about a hand's width. It flowers **from about July to September**.

The whole plant is thickly covered with fine **white hairs**. That is why it feels **soft and felty**. High in the mountains the sun is strong and the nights are cold. The coat of hairs protects the plant from **sun and cold** and helps against drying out.

The edelweiss grows on **stony grassland** and on **rocks**, often on **limestone**. It is usually found high up in the mountains. The scientific name **Leontopodium** comes from Greek: “leon” means lion and “podion” means little foot. The felty flowers are reminiscent of a small **paw**.

The edelweiss is **protected** in Switzerland. In the past, many people picked it as a souvenir, and it became rare. Today you should look at it and photograph it, but leave it standing. In gardens, cultivated edelweiss grows, and you can buy it.

The edelweiss is a well-known **symbol of the Alps**. Many **Swiss wrestlers** and Alpine herdsmen wear the blue **edelweiss shirt** with white flowers. You also often see it on souvenirs, badges and logos.

gewusst: The white star of the edelweiss is made not of petals but of felty bracts.
Leontopodium means “lion's foot” when translated.

teile.einleitung: Citizen science means science by citizens. Ordinary people without a specialist degree help to collect data for research. In this way everyone, including children, can contribute to science.
wichtigste: In citizen science, laypeople collect data and experts evaluate it.
Plant finds in Switzerland can be reported to Info Flora.
At a BioBlitz you look for as many species as possible in a short time.
A good record contains place, date and a photo.
Experts check the reports so that the data stay reliable.
In phenology you observe when plants sprout and bloom.
Many volunteers supply data from large areas and over many years.

abschnitte.text: In **citizen science**, researchers and interested laypeople work together. The volunteers observe, count, photograph and report what they discover. The experts collect these reports and evaluate them. The biggest advantage: researchers alone could never be in so many places at the same time. Thanks to many helpers, data arise from **large areas** and over many years.

**Info Flora** is the national data and information centre for the flora of Switzerland. There, experts and laypeople report where they have found which plants. From many reports, maps arise that show where a species grows and whether it is rare or threatened. A report with **location**, **date** and a **photo** is especially valuable. With place and date, the find can be placed on a map and in a time series, and the photo allows a check.

A **BioBlitz** is a short event in which experts and laypeople together look for as many animal and plant species as possible in an area. Often it lasts 24 hours. At the end there is a snapshot of the **biodiversity** at this place. Such events are also a good opportunity to learn from experts how to recognise species.

**Phenology** records when in the year certain events happen in nature. For example: when does the hazel bloom? When does the beech get its leaves? Laypeople too can write down such observations each year in the same place. Long series of observations show how the **climate** affects plants, for instance when blossoms appear earlier over the decades.

Many people today use **identification apps**. The app compares features such as flower shape and leaf margin with many reference pictures. **Sharp close-ups** of flower and leaf are therefore best. Even so, laypeople and apps sometimes confuse similar species. That is why **experts check** the reports and spot wrong identifications, so that the data stay reliable for research.

gewusst: At a BioBlitz, hundreds of different species are often found in just one day.
In ornithology too, many volunteers in Switzerland have been collecting observations for research for decades.

teile.einleitung: Double fertilisation is a special feature of the angiosperms, that is, flowering plants with an ovary. In it, the embryo and a nutritive tissue for the seed form at the same time. It was discovered more than 100 years ago.
wichtigste: Double fertilisation occurs in the angiosperms.
A pollen tube brings two sperm cells to the ovule.
It takes place in the embryo sac inside the ovule.
The most common type of embryo sac has seven cells.
The sperm cell and the central cell produce the endosperm, a nutritive tissue.
Sergei Nawaschin was the first to describe the process, in 1898.

abschnitte.text: After **pollination**, a pollen grain lies on the stigma of a flower. A fine **pollen tube** grows down through the style to the **ovule** in the ovary. **Two sperm cells** travel along inside the pollen tube. The **embryo sac** lies inside the ovule. That is where **double fertilisation** takes place.

The most common type of embryo sac consists of **seven cells**. These include the **egg cell**, two **synergids** next to it, three antipodal cells on the opposite side and a large **central cell** in the middle. The **synergids** give off attractant substances and so **lure** the **pollen tube**. It opens at one of the synergids and releases the two sperm cells.

Now it happens twice: the **first sperm cell** fuses with the egg cell. This produces the **zygote**, which has a **diploid**, that is, double, set of chromosomes. The embryo grows from it. The **second sperm cell** fuses with the **central cell**. This produces the **endosperm**, a **nutritive tissue** for the embryo. Because the central cell already brings two nuclei with it, the endosperm usually has three sets of chromosomes.

The Russian botanist **Sergei Nawaschin** was the first to describe double fertilisation, in **1898**, while studying lilies. It occurs only in the **angiosperms**. The endosperm is very important for us humans: the flour from wheat, rice and maize consists mostly of it. The white flesh and the water of the coconut are endosperm too.

gewusst: A large part of humanity's food comes from the endosperm of cereal grains.
At almost the same time as Nawaschin, the Frenchman Léon Guignard also described double fertilisation.

teile.einleitung: Thorns are sharp, hard parts of a plant. Many plants use them to protect themselves from animals that want to eat them. In botany, a distinction is made between thorns and prickles.
wichtigste: Many plants have thorns or prickles to protect them from animals.
Thorns are modified plant parts such as leaves or shoots.
The spines of a cactus are modified leaves.
The hawthorn has the word thorn right in its name.
The blackthorn is also called sloe and bears blue fruits.

abschnitte.text: Many plants have **thorns or prickles** to **protect themselves from animals**. Deer, goats and cows like to eat leaves and young shoots. Sharp thorns put them off. That is why birds find a safe place for their nests in hedges with thorny bushes.

In everyday speech, people often call everything that pricks a thorn. In botany, though, there is a difference. A **thorn** is a modified plant part, for example a leaf, a shoot or a stipule. That is why it is firmly joined to the inside of the plant. The **spines of a cactus** are **modified leaves**. A **prickle**, on the other hand, is only an outgrowth of the surface and breaks off easily. Strictly speaking, the rose therefore has prickles and not thorns.

The **hawthorn** has the word thorn right in its name. In spring it blooms **white** and later has red fruits. The **blackthorn**, also called **sloe**, gets its name from its dark bark. It blooms white very early in the year and bears **blue fruits** in autumn, which taste very sour. Both bushes often grow in hedges and at the edges of woods.

gewusst: Sloes taste milder after they have been touched by frost.
In a cactus, the green stem takes over the work of the leaves and carries out photosynthesis.

teile.einleitung: Chitin is a natural substance that is both firm and flexible. It forms the exoskeleton of insects, spiders and crustaceans and is found in the cell wall of fungi. After cellulose, chitin is one of the most common biopolymers on Earth.
wichtigste: Chitin is built from the building block N-acetylglucosamine.
In arthropods it forms the main component of the exoskeleton.
The cell wall of true fungi consists mainly of chitin and glucans.
Cellulose is even more common in nature than chitin.
Chitosan is formed by splitting off acetyl groups.
Many plants make chitinase to defend against fungi.

abschnitte.text: Chitin is a **polysaccharide**, that is, a multiple sugar made of long chains. Its building block is called **N-acetylglucosamine**. This is a sugar molecule that additionally carries a group containing nitrogen. The building blocks are linked in a similar way to **cellulose**. That is why chitin is also very firm. The word **“chitin”** comes from the Greek word for **garment or covering**.

The **arthropods** include insects, spiders, millipedes and crustaceans. Their **exoskeleton** consists mainly of chitin, combined with proteins. In crustaceans, lime is added, which makes the armour especially hard. Because the skeleton cannot grow along, these animals have to **moult** as they grow. After that the new covering is soft at first and hardens only slowly.

The **cell wall of true fungi** also consists mainly of **chitin and glucans**. This clearly distinguishes fungi from plants, whose cell walls are made of cellulose. As a storage substance, fungi do not make starch but **glycogen**, like animals. So fungi are a group of living things all of their own. Many **plants** make the enzyme **chitinase**, which breaks down chitin. With it they defend themselves against fungi that want to attack them.

Chitin occurs in huge amounts. Only **cellulose** is even more common as a biopolymer. From chitin you can make **chitosan**. In this process, **acetyl groups are split off**. Chitosan dissolves in weak acids and is used, for example, in water treatment, in wound dressings or in agriculture. The shells of crabs and prawns are often used as the raw material.

gewusst: The shimmering colours of some beetles arise from fine layers in the chitin armour, not from pigments.
An insect can moult several times in its life until it is fully grown.

teile.einleitung: Soils do not look the same everywhere. Experts group soils with a similar development into soil types, for example podzol, brown earth or black earth.
wichtigste: The soil texture describes the grain sizes, the soil type the sequence of horizons.
Floodplain soils arise in river valleys from deposits during floods.
The podzol has a pale, leached bleached horizon.
The chernozem or black earth is especially fertile.
In the luvisol, clay is moved downwards.
Internationally, soils are named with the World Reference Base.

abschnitte.text: The **soil texture** depends on the size of the grains, that is, on the proportion of sand, silt and clay. The **soil type**, by contrast, groups soils that have developed similarly and show a similar sequence of **horizons**. Internationally the **World Reference Base** (WRB) is used, which is supported by the FAO. Besides this, many countries have their own systems.

**Floodplain soils** lie in river valleys. In floods they are flooded and receive fresh sediments, so they are often layered. Also young are shallow **A-C soils**, in which the topsoil lies directly on the rock. On limestone such a soil is called a **rendzina**, on lime-free silicate rock such as granite a **ranker**. The ranker is usually acid.

Under coniferous forests and heaths the **podzol** often forms. Acid seepage water moves iron, aluminium and humus downwards. What remains is an ash-grey **bleached horizon**, below it a rust-brown accumulation horizon. In the **luvisol**, fine clay is washed out of the topsoil and accumulates in the subsoil. This process is called **lessivage**.

abschnitte.titel: Black earth and red tropical soils
abschnitte.text: The **chernozem** or black earth arises under steppe grass on loess, for example in Ukraine. Its dark humus horizon can be very thick and makes it extremely fertile. In the humid tropics many substances are washed out. What remains are **iron and aluminium oxides**. Especially the iron oxides colour soils such as the **ferralsols** red.

In bogs, soil arises from **peat**, that is, from hardly decomposed plant remains. In the **Grosses Moos** in the Seeland region such soils were drained for agriculture. Since then oxygen gets into the peat. Microorganisms break it down, and the soil surface sinks lower year after year. In Switzerland, brown earths are also very common.

gewusst: Chernozem comes from Russian and means “black earth”.
The bleached horizon of a podzol can be so pale that it looks like ash.

teile.einleitung: The field maple is the smallest of the three common maples in Switzerland. It likes to grow at sunny woodland edges and in hedges, and in autumn it glows bright yellow.
wichtigste: The field maple usually grows 10 to 15 metres tall.
Its leaves are small and have three to five rounded lobes.
In autumn they turn bright yellow.
White milky sap flows in the leaf stalks.
On young twigs it often forms corky ridges.
It tolerates cutting well and is often planted in hedges.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are three common maples: **sycamore**, **Norway maple** and **field maple**. The sycamore and the Norway maple grow 20 to 30 metres tall or more. The **field maple** stays smaller. It usually grows **10 to 15 metres** tall, and often it is only a **shrub**. It is a medium-sized, roundish tree.

The leaves of the field maple are only about **as big as the palm of a hand**. They have **three to five rounded lobes**. If you break off a leaf stalk, **white milky sap** comes out. This makes it easy to recognise. On young twigs it often forms **corky ridges**. The twigs then look as if they had wings. In **autumn** the field maple turns **bright yellow**, sometimes a little orange as well.

abschnitte.titel: At home at the edge of the field
abschnitte.text: The field maple likes **sunny woodland edges** and **field copses**. That is where its name comes from. It tolerates **cutting** well and sprouts anew again and again afterwards. That is why it is often planted in **hedges**. There it forms dense bushes in which birds nest and insects find food. Like all maples, it has fruits with wings that spin in the wind.

gewusst: In Switzerland the field maple is often part of species-rich hedges between fields.
The winged fruits of all maples spin like little propellers as they fall.

teile.einleitung: The dahlia is a popular garden flower with large, colourful blooms. It comes from Mexico and blooms here in summer and autumn. It exists in a great many shapes and colours.
wichtigste: The dahlia comes from Mexico.
It is also called Georgine in German.
Dahlias grow anew from tubers every year.
They bloom mainly in summer and autumn.
Some flowers grow as big as a plate.
There are no truly blue dahlias.

abschnitte.text: The dahlia comes from **Mexico**. There it is even the national flower. It came to Europe over 200 years ago. It got its name from the Swedish botanist Anders **Dahl**. Another name is **Georgine**, after the researcher Johann Gottlieb Georgi. The dahlia belongs to the **daisy family**, like the sunflower.

Dahlias grow anew from **tubers** every year. These tubers store nutrients underground. Because dahlias cannot tolerate frost, the tubers are dug up in autumn and stored cool and dry in the cellar over winter. In spring they are planted in the garden again, when frost no longer threatens.

There are thousands of **varieties**. Some flowers are small, others grow **as big as a plate**. **Pompon dahlias** look like **small balls**. Others have pointed petals or are quite flat. Dahlias come in white, yellow, orange, pink, red, violet and almost black. Only one colour is missing: **true blue**.

Dahlias bloom mainly in **summer and autumn**, often until the first frost. They like a sunny spot and enough water. Tall varieties are tied to a stake so that they do not snap. In spring you have to take care: **slugs** like to eat young dahlias very much. If you cut off faded flowers, the plant forms new ones.

gewusst: In Mexico the Aztecs used to eat the tubers of the dahlia.
Dahlias are important fodder plants for bees and bumblebees, especially varieties with open, single flowers.

teile.einleitung: When green leaves turn yellow although it is not autumn, chlorosis may be behind it. The plant then lacks chlorophyll, usually because a nutrient is missing. Where and how the leaves turn yellow often reveals which nutrient is missing.
wichtigste: Chlorosis is a yellowing of the leaves through lack of chlorophyll.
With iron deficiency, young leaves turn yellow between green veins.
On limy soils, iron is poorly soluble.
With magnesium deficiency, older leaves turn yellow between the veins.
Nitrogen deficiency shows as an even yellowing of the oldest leaves.
Sulphur deficiency makes young leaves turn evenly yellow.

abschnitte.text: The word **chlorosis** comes from the Greek **chlōros**, which means yellowish green. In chlorosis the leaves turn yellow because they make **too little chlorophyll**. Without enough chlorophyll the plant can do less photosynthesis and grows worse. The most common reason is a **nutrient deficiency**. Cold, waterlogging or diseases can also trigger chlorosis.

An important clue is **which leaves** turn yellow first. Some nutrients the plant can move from old leaves to young ones. If they are lacking, the **older leaves** suffer first. This is so with **nitrogen** and **magnesium**. Other nutrients such as **iron** and **sulphur** stay where they were built in. If they are lacking, the damage shows first on the **young leaves**.

With **iron deficiency**, young leaves turn yellow **between the leaf veins**, while the veins themselves stay green. With **magnesium deficiency** you see a similar pattern, but on the **older leaves**. **Nitrogen deficiency** shows as an **even yellowing** that begins with the oldest leaves. With **sulphur deficiency**, the young leaves turn evenly yellow. You often see this in **oilseed rape**, which needs a lot of sulphur.

**Iron deficiency chlorosis** often occurs on **limy soils**, although enough iron is present there. But at a high **pH** iron is **poorly soluble**, and the roots can hardly take it up. The **rhododendron** is especially sensitive. It needs acid soil and easily gets yellow leaves on soil containing lime. Gardeners therefore often plant it in special acid soil. Lime in the watering water can also make the problem worse.

gewusst: The alpenrose is a wild rhododendron of the Swiss mountains: the rusty-leaved alpenrose grows on acid soils, while the hairy alpenrose tolerates lime.
Some plants with yellow-spotted leaves are healthy, because they were bred that way.

teile.einleitung: The Casparian strip is a fine, sealing layer in the cell walls of the root. It acts like a checkpoint: water and dissolved substances must pass through living cells before they reach the plant’s conducting pathways.
wichtigste: The Casparian strip lies in the endodermis of the root.
It is named after the botanist Robert Caspary.
It is located in the radial and transverse cell walls.
It forces water and ions to pass through living cells.
In this way it prevents ions from flowing back out of the central cylinder.
Many plants also have such a strip in the exodermis.

abschnitte.text: In the cross section of a root you see the **cortex** on the outside and the **central cylinder** with the **conducting tissues** on the inside. Between them lies a single layer of cells, the **endodermis**. It surrounds the central cylinder like a ring. In the cell walls of the endodermis lies the **Casparian strip**. It is named after the German botanist **Robert Caspary**, who described it in the 19th century.

The strip is located in the **radial and transverse walls** of the endodermis cells, that is, where the cells meet. These parts of the wall are impregnated with water-repellent substances such as **suberin** and lignin. As a result, water can no longer simply seep between the cells. The route through the cell walls, the **apoplast**, is blocked at this point.

Water and **ions** must now go **through living cells**. In doing so they pass through the **cell membrane**, which controls precisely what may enter. In this way the plant can choose which nutrients it takes up and hold back harmful substances. In addition, the strip prevents ions from **flowing back** out of the central cylinder. As a result, ions collect there, water flows in after them, and **root pressure** arises.

In older roots, the endodermis cells are often thickly reinforced all round. But some cells stay **thin-walled**, usually opposite the xylem poles. They are called **passage cells**, because water gets through more easily here. Many plants additionally have an outer layer of the cortex with a Casparian strip. This layer is called the **exodermis**.

gewusst: The Casparian strip is so narrow that you can see it well only with a microscope and special stains.
You can sometimes see root pressure in the morning, when drops of water hang on the leaf edges of small plants.

teile.einleitung: Annual fleabane looks like a small ox-eye daisy. But this pretty plant comes from North America and is spreading strongly in Switzerland. That is why it is controlled in many places.
wichtigste: Annual fleabane comes from North America.
It was first grown in Europe as an ornamental plant.
Its flowers look like small daisies.
It forms seeds even without pollination.
Despite its name, it can also be biennial.
It is best pulled up with its root before it flowers.

abschnitte.text: Annual fleabane is called **Erigeron annuus** in science. It is native to **North America**. In Europe it was first grown as an **ornamental plant** and then escaped into the wild. Today it is regarded in Switzerland as an **invasive neophyte**, that is, an introduced plant that spreads strongly and causes problems.

The plant has **white ray flowers** around a **yellow centre**. That is why it is often mistaken for the **ox-eye daisy**. Its flower heads are much smaller, though, and one plant carries many of them. It loves **open, sunny places**. It is found in meadows, at the edges of paths, on embankments and on wasteland.

Fleabane can form **seeds even without pollination**. That is why even a single plant produces very many seeds that can germinate. Despite its name, it is not always an annual. It often survives the winter as a **leaf rosette** and only flowers in its second year. So it is **annual or biennial**.

**Mowing** alone does little: the plant sends up new stems from the base and soon flowers again, often lower down. It is better to **pull it up with its root before it flowers**. The roots are shallow, so this works well. That way the plant can neither grow back nor form seeds.

The German word **“berufen”** used to mean something like **to bewitch**. People believed that plants of this genus protected against magic. That is probably where the German name Berufkraut comes from.

gewusst: A single plant can form seeds without a bee visiting it.
After mowing, fleabane simply flowers again a little lower down.

teile.einleitung: In a green façade, plants grow on the wall of a house. They look beautiful, cool things down on hot days and offer animals food and shelter.
wichtigste: In wall-mounted systems, the plants grow in modules directly on the wall.
Ivy holds on with adhesive roots.
Virginia creeper, also called Boston ivy, climbs with adhesive discs.
Wisteria is a twiner and needs a trellis.
Green façades cool through shade and evaporation.
The leaves can trap fine dust.

abschnitte.text: Many climbing plants grow up the wall from the ground. **Ivy** forms short **adhesive roots** that cling into the smallest unevenness in the wall. It needs no climbing aid. The **Boston ivy**, also called **Virginia creeper**, has tendrils with small **adhesive discs**. With them it sticks even to smooth walls. In autumn its foliage turns bright red. **Wisteria**, on the other hand, is a **twiner**: it winds its shoots around supports and needs a sturdy **trellis**.

There are also green walls with no contact with the ground. In **wall-mounted systems**, the plants sit in **containers or felt modules** directly on the façade. Because they have no soil, they need **watering**. This way even tall walls can be greened right to the top.

On hot days, a green façade cools the wall of the house. The foliage gives **shade**, and the plants **evaporate** water. Both lower the temperature at the wall and in the rooms behind it. **Deciduous** plants are particularly useful on south-facing façades: in summer they give shade, and in winter they let the sun through. In addition, **fine dust** sticks to the leaves and is later washed off by the rain.

Green walls are valuable for animals. **Ivy** flowers late in the year, in **autumn**, when hardly any other plants offer nectar. Many bees, hoverflies and butterflies use this food. Birds find hiding places in the dense greenery. A famous example of green buildings is the **Bosco Verticale** in **Milan**. The “vertical forest” consists of two high-rise buildings on whose balconies hundreds of trees grow.

gewusst: Ivy can grow up to the roofs of tall houses without any climbing aid.
Green façades help cities to heat up less strongly in summer.

teile.einleitung: The soil is not dead dirt, but a huge home. Countless living things live in it, from tiny bacteria to the mole.
wichtigste: All the living things in the soil together are called the edaphon.
Bacteria are the most numerous soil organisms.
In a handful of soil live more living things than there are people on Earth.
Earthworms eat soil and loosen the ground with their tunnels.
Fungi form a partnership with roots, the mycorrhiza.
Soil organisms break down plant remains into humus.

abschnitte.text: The totality of all living things in the soil is called the **edaphon**. Most numerous are the **bacteria**. They are so small that you can see them only under the microscope. In a single gram of soil live millions to billions of them. In a handful of healthy soil there are more living things than there are people on the whole Earth.

The **earthworm** is one of the most important helpers in the soil. It eats soil and plant remains and excretes crumbly, nutrient-rich soil again. Its tunnels let air and water into the soil. This way plant roots can grow better, and rain drains away more easily. Earthworms also pull leaves down into their tunnels.

Many **fungi** live in the soil and break down dead wood and leaves. Some form a partnership with plant roots, the **mycorrhiza**. Fine fungal threads wrap around the roots. The fungus supplies the plant with water and nutrients, and the plant gives it sugar. Both benefit.

In the leaf layer there are swarms of small animals. **Millipedes** have a long body with very many pairs of legs and eat dead plant parts. The **springtail** is only a few millimetres in size. With a jumping fork on its abdomen it can spring far away. There are also mites, woodlice, beetles and insect larvae. Together they break up the litter until it becomes **humus**.

The **mole** is a mammal that lives almost only underground. With its broad front paws, the digging shovels, it builds long tunnels. In them it hunts mainly earthworms and insect larvae. The molehills on meadows show where it has been digging. It does not hibernate and is active all year round.

gewusst: Under one square metre of meadow, hundreds of earthworms can live.
The fungal threads in the soil can together be many kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Powdery mildew is a plant disease caused by fungi. You can recognise it by a white, powdery coating on the leaves. It attacks roses, cucumbers, cereals and also the grapevine.
wichtigste: Powdery mildew forms a white coating that can be wiped off, mostly on the upper side of the leaf.
The fungi that cause it belong to the sac fungi.
It does not need wet leaves and is therefore called a “fair-weather fungus”.
With haustoria it takes nutrients from the plant cells.
In winegrowing, sulphur has long been used against it.
Most species are specialised on particular host plants.

abschnitte.text: On affected leaves there is a **white coating**, as if someone had sprinkled flour over them. It usually sits on the **upper side of the leaf** and can be wiped off. The coating consists of a network of fungal threads with many **spores**. The leaves it affects gradually turn yellow and wither.

The powdery mildew fungi form the order **Erysiphales** and belong to the **sac fungi**. The network of fungal threads lies on the surface of the leaf. It sends small sucking organs, the **haustoria**, into the outermost cells of the plant. The plant cells stay alive. The similarly named **downy mildew** is caused by completely different organisms and tends to grow on the underside of the leaf.

The spores of powdery mildew also sprout on the leaf **without drops of water**. High humidity is often enough. That is why it spreads in warm, dry weather too. It is therefore called the **“fair-weather fungus”**.

On the grapevine, powdery mildew is also called **oidium**. The fungus that causes it is now named **Erysiphe necator**. **Sulphur** has long helped against it, including in organic farming. On cereals such as wheat and barley, the fungus is called **Blumeria graminis**.

Most powdery mildew fungi are specialised on **particular host plants**. Mildew from a rose does not usually pass to cucumbers. Blumeria graminis occurs in different forms, each of which attacks only one kind of cereal. For gardeners this means that a sick rose bush does not immediately infect the whole vegetable bed.

gewusst: Powdery mildew likes dry, warm weather, even though it is a fungus.
Sulphur has been used against mildew in winegrowing for a very long time.

teile.einleitung: The blossom is the part of a plant that takes care of reproduction. With colours, scent and sweet nectar it attracts bees and other animals. After a blossom has been pollinated, a fruit with seeds arises from it.
wichtigste: The blossom serves the plant for reproduction.
Many blossoms contain nectar, a sweet juice.
The fine yellow dust in many blossoms is called flower dust or pollen.
Bees fly from blossom to blossom and make honey from the nectar.
After pollination, a fruit arises from the blossom.
A typical blossom has sepals, petals, stamens and a pistil.
Some blossoms are pollinated by the wind and are therefore small and inconspicuous.

abschnitte.text: On the outside there are usually green **sepals**, which protect the bud. Above them follow the coloured **petals**, which attract animals. In the middle stand the stamens with the pollen and the **pistil** with stigma, style and ovary. In the ovary lie the ovules, from which seeds later arise.

Many blossoms produce sweet **nectar** to attract insects. The bee sucks up the nectar with its tongue and brings it to the beehive. There the bees make **honey** from it. On the visit, pollen sticks to their furry body, which they carry to the next blossom.

The fine yellow **flower dust**, also called pollen, arises in the stamens. If it reaches the stigma of a blossom of the same species, this is called **pollination**. Besides bees, bumblebees, butterflies and flies also help, and in other countries even birds and bats. Grasses, hazel and birch simply let their pollen be carried by the wind, which triggers hay fever in some people.

After pollination a pollen tube grows to the ovule, and **fertilisation** takes place. The petals wilt and fall off. The ovary now grows into a **fruit** in which the seeds lie. This is how an apple blossom in spring becomes an apple by autumn, and a cherry blossom a cherry.

Blossoms come in almost all colours and sizes. Bees also see **ultraviolet light**, which is why many blossoms have patterns visible only to insects. Some plants have many small blossoms together, for example the daisy, which is really a whole flower head. The largest single flower in the world is that of the Rafflesia from South-East Asia, about one metre across.

In Switzerland the **flowering season** begins in late winter with snowdrops and hazel shrubs. In April and May the fruit trees bloom, especially beautifully for example in Thurgau and the Zug region. In summer the flower meadows in the Alps shine. Anyone who wants to help bees plants flowers that bloom one after another from spring to autumn.

begriffe.erklaerung: The coloured leaves of a blossom that attract animals.
The parts of the blossom in which the pollen is made.
The female part in the middle of the blossom with stigma, style and ovary.
Another word for flower dust.
When pollen and ovule join so that a seed arises.

gewusst: Bees see ultraviolet light and recognise patterns on blossoms that are invisible to us.
A daisy is not one blossom, but a head of many tiny blossoms.
The Rafflesia has the largest single flower in the world and smells of rotting meat.

teile.einleitung: How many lizards live on a slope? Hardly anyone can count them. With the mark-recapture method, though, the size of a population can still be estimated well.
wichtigste: Animals are caught, marked and released, and caught again later.
The Lincoln-Petersen formula is N = M times C divided by R.
The population must be closed between the catches.
Lost marks lead to an overestimate.
Trap-happy animals lead to an underestimate.
The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach coordinates the ringing of birds in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: First a number of animals are caught, **marked** and released again. Their number is called **M**. Later, animals are caught again. **C** is the number of all animals in the second catch, **R** the number of marked ones among them. The idea: the share of marked animals in the second catch matches the share in the whole population. This gives the **Lincoln-Petersen formula**: **N = M times C divided by R**.

40 lizards are marked. Later 50 are caught, of which 10 are marked. Then N = 40 times 50 divided by 10 = **200** animals. A second example: 60 beetles are marked, and in the second catch 12 out of 80 are marked. N = 60 times 80 divided by 12 = **400**. As a check: 12 out of 80 is 15 per cent, and 60 out of 400 is also 15 per cent. With very few recaptures, the simple formula overestimates the population. The **Chapman correction** therefore adds 1 to each of the catch numbers and subtracts 1 at the end.

The population must be **closed** between the catches. So there must be no births, deaths, immigration or emigration. The **mark** must not affect survival. A conspicuous colour could make animals more visible to enemies. If many animals lose their mark, R becomes too small and the population is **overestimated**. If marked animals like to go back to the trap, R becomes too large and the population is **underestimated**.

In Switzerland, the **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** coordinates the scientific **ringing** of birds. Recoveries of ringed birds provide data on migration routes, age and numbers. Fish or amphibians are often marked with a **PIT tag**. This is a tiny **passive transponder** with no battery of its own, which is placed under the skin. A reading device can then recognise each animal unambiguously.

gewusst: A PIT tag is often hardly bigger than a grain of rice.
Thanks to ringed birds, we know that many Swiss migratory birds fly all the way to Africa.

teile.einleitung: Himalayan balsam is a tall plant with pink flowers that you often see by streams and rivers. It comes from the Himalayas and is spreading so strongly here that it is pushing out native plants.
wichtigste: Himalayan balsam comes from the Himalayas.
It came to Europe as an ornamental plant in the 19th century.
The plant is an annual, yet it grows up to about 2 metres tall.
The flowers are mostly pink to purple-red, rarely white.
Ripe seed pods burst open and fling the seeds away.
The best way to control it is to pull it up before the seeds ripen.

abschnitte.text: Himalayan balsam is native to the **Himalayas**. In the 19th century it was brought to Europe as a pretty **ornamental plant**. Soon it was growing outside gardens too. Plants that people have brought into new areas are called **neophytes**. Because balsam spreads strongly and does damage, it is considered **invasive**.

The plant has a thick, often reddish stem and grows up to about **2 metres** tall. This makes it one of the tallest annual plants here. The large flowers hang on long stalks and are mostly **pink to purple-red**. Small **glands** on the leaf stalks give off a sugary liquid. The plant gets its name “glandular” from them.

Balsam is an **annual**: it sprouts in spring, flowers in summer and dies in autumn. It survives the winter only as **seeds**. When the pods are ripe, they burst open at a touch and fling the seeds several metres. That is where the German name Springkraut, meaning jumping plant, comes from. Streams and rivers carry the seeds even further.

Balsam grows thickly and shades smaller plants. Its flowers produce a great deal of **nectar** and attract bumblebees and bees. As a result, native flowers nearby are visited less often. On riverbanks where only dead balsam plants stand in winter, the soil can be washed away more easily.

The roots are small and shallow. That is why the plant is easy to **pull up**. It is important to do this **before the seeds ripen**, otherwise the pods burst open. In Switzerland, many volunteers, school classes and nature conservation groups help with pulling it up every summer.

gewusst: The seed pods burst open at even a light touch.
Although the plant grows from a new seed every year, it gets taller than many people.

teile.einleitung: Soil science studies the thin layer beneath our feet. It asks how soils arise, what they consist of and how to protect them.
wichtigste: Soil science is also called pedology, from the Greek “pedon” for soil.
The Russian Vasily Dokuchaev is regarded as its founder.
Soils arise from parent rock, climate, relief, organisms and time.
By grain size, sand, silt and clay are distinguished.
A soil profile is divided into horizons with letters such as A, B and C.
The soil layer of the Earth is called the pedosphere.

abschnitte.text: **Soil science** or **pedology** is the science of the soil. Do not confuse it: petrology is the study of rocks, pomology the study of fruit growing. The Russian **Vasily Dokuchaev** is regarded as the founder of modern soil science. In the 19th century he studied the fertile black earths of Russia. In doing so he recognised that soils arise from the interplay of several factors.

Soil forms in the **pedosphere**. This is the name for the zone where the rock shell, the air shell, the water shell and living things overlap. The classic **soil-forming factors** are parent rock, climate, relief (that is, the shape of the terrain), organisms and time. Air pressure is not one of them. Because these factors work together differently everywhere, there are very many different soils.

The soil type depends on the size of the grains. Particles smaller than 0.002 millimetres are called **clay**, somewhat coarser ones **silt**, still coarser ones **sand**. A mixture with roughly balanced proportions is called **loam**. In the field you estimate the soil type with the **finger test**: you rub moist soil between your fingers. Sand feels rough, silt floury, clay sticky and can be rolled out well.

If you dig a hole, you see layers, the **horizons**. At the top there is often an organic litter layer (O), below it the humus-rich topsoil (A), then the subsoil (B) and at the bottom the hardly weathered parent rock (C). Experts determine the colour of a horizon with the **Munsell colour charts**. They arrange colours by hue, lightness and saturation, so that soils are described the same way worldwide.

Soil is full of small cavities, the **pores**. After rain, part of the water drains downwards as seepage water. What is held against gravity in the medium and fine pores is called **field capacity**. Plants cannot use all of it, because in the finest pores the water is too tightly bound. Such knowledge helps in agriculture, in building and in protecting groundwater.

gewusst: Before one centimetre of soil forms, it can take centuries depending on the place.
With the Munsell colour charts, researchers in Switzerland and in Brazil can name the same soil colour the same way.

teile.einleitung: Remote sensing means collecting information about the Earth without touching it. Satellites, aircraft and drones measure light and other radiation from a distance.
wichtigste: Remote sensing records data without direct contact, for example by satellite.
Spatial resolution tells you how big a pixel is on the ground.
Radar also works through clouds and at night.
LiDAR sends out laser pulses and so measures, for example, the height of trees.
The Sentinel satellites belong to the European programme Copernicus.
Landsat has been supplying images of the land surface since the 1970s.
Field data, called ground truth, check the analysis.

abschnitte.text: In **remote sensing**, data is collected without touching the object directly. Sensors on **satellites**, aircraft or drones measure the light that is reflected from the Earth. This shows, for example, how healthy forests are, where glaciers are shrinking or how cities are spreading. Large areas can be watched regularly and quickly this way.

A satellite image is made up of many **pixels**. The **spatial resolution** describes how big a pixel is on the ground. A **multispectral sensor** measures a few broad colour bands, including some that our eyes cannot see. A **hyperspectral sensor** measures very many narrow wavelength bands. With it you can tell plant species or rocks apart more precisely, for example.

Some sensors send out radiation themselves. **Radar** sends microwaves down to the Earth and therefore also works **through clouds and at night**. **LiDAR** sends out laser pulses and measures how long they take to come back. This produces accurate height models, and you can work out the **height of trees**. In Switzerland there are such height models for the whole country.

The US satellite series **Landsat** has been supplying images of the land surface continuously since the **1970s**. This makes it possible to compare changes over decades. Europe runs the Earth observation programme **Copernicus** with the **Sentinel satellites**. Much of their data is freely available, including to schools and researchers in Switzerland.

For small areas, **drones** are handy. They fly low and reach a very high spatial resolution. Despite all the technology, measurements on the spot are still needed, the so-called **ground truth**. They are used to check and calibrate the analysis of the images. Only then do you know whether a shade of colour in the image really shows a particular wood or meadow.

gewusst: The first Landsat satellite was launched in 1972.
With radar satellites you can measure whether a mountain slope is moving by a few millimetres.

teile.einleitung: At 4,634 metres above sea level, the Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland. It belongs to the mighty Monte Rosa massif in the canton of Valais, right on the border with Italy. It is named after General Guillaume-Henri Dufour, who produced the first accurate map of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland.
It is 4,634 metres high.
The summit lies in the Monte Rosa massif in the canton of Valais.
The border between Switzerland and Italy runs very close by.
The mountain was first climbed in 1855.
Since 1863 it has carried the name of General Guillaume-Henri Dufour.

abschnitte.text: The Dufourspitze lies in the south of the canton of **Valais**, east of Zermatt. It is the highest peak of the **Monte Rosa massif**, a huge mountain block with many peaks over 4,000 metres. The summit itself lies entirely on Swiss soil, only about 160 metres from the border with Italy. After Mont Blanc, Monte Rosa is the second highest mountain massif in the Alps.

Around the Dufourspitze there is nothing but rock, snow and ice. At its foot flows the **Gorner Glacier**, one of the largest glaciers in the Alps. At this height the air is thin, and it is usually freezing cold even in summer. Almost no plants grow up there any more. In fine weather you can see from the summit far into Italy.

In the past, the peak was simply called the “Highest Peak”. In 1863 the Federal Council named it after General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour**. Dufour led the work on the first accurate map of Switzerland, the Dufour Map. It was only during the survey that people realised this peak was the highest in the country.

On 1 August 1855, a rope team of English climbers and Swiss mountain guides reached the summit for the first time. This was in the middle of the so-called **Golden Age of Alpinism**, when many Alpine peaks were climbed for the first time. Today the climb is a demanding high-mountain tour over glacier and rock. Most climbers spend the night beforehand in the **Monte Rosa Hut** of the Swiss Alpine Club.

The Dufourspitze is not only the highest point in Switzerland but also the second highest mountain in the whole of the Alps, after Mont Blanc. It even towers above the famous Matterhorn, which is 4,478 metres high. Very close by, on the Italian border, stands the Signalkuppe with the **Capanna Margherita**. This hut is considered the highest building in Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of mountains that belong together.
A mountain that is more than 4,000 metres high.
Climbers who climb together tied to one rope.
A large stream of ice that flows slowly down a valley.

gewusst: The first ascent took place, of all days, on 1 August, today's Swiss national day.
The new Monte Rosa Hut of 2009 looks like a glittering rock crystal and produces a large part of its energy itself.

teile.einleitung: Einkorn is one of the oldest cereals in the world. The first farmers in the New Stone Age already grew it. Today it is only rarely grown, but it is in demand again because of its yellow flour.
wichtigste: Einkorn is called Triticum monococcum in science.
It is diploid and has 14 chromosomes.
It was probably domesticated in the Karacadağ mountains in south-eastern Turkey.
Its wild form is called Triticum boeoticum.
Einkorn is a hulled cereal.
Remains of einkorn were found in Ötzi's stomach.

abschnitte.text: Einkorn is a **type of wheat**. Its scientific name **Triticum monococcum** means roughly “single-grained”. It is **diploid**, so it has two sets of chromosomes with **14 chromosomes** in all. This makes it the genetically simplest of the cultivated wheats. Bread wheat, by contrast, has six sets of chromosomes.

The wild form is called **Triticum boeoticum**. It still grows today in the Near East and in south-eastern Europe. Genetic comparisons showed that cultivated einkorn is closest to the wild forms from the **Karacadağ mountains** in south-eastern Turkey. People probably first bred it there as a crop.

**Ötzi**, the Iceman, was found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps. The glacier mummy is around **5,300 years** old. In his stomach, researchers found, among other things, remains of **einkorn** and wild meat. Ötzi lived in the late **New Stone Age**, when einkorn was an important cereal.

Einkorn is a **hulled cereal**. When it is threshed, the grains stay firmly inside their coverings, the **husks**. They have to be **dehusked** in an additional step. Einkorn contains a lot of **lutein**, a yellow pigment from the group of carotenoids. That is why flour and pasta made from einkorn are noticeably **yellow**.

gewusst: Ötzi had eaten einkorn more than 5,000 years ago.
Einkorn flour is naturally yellow, with no eggs at all.

teile.einleitung: At harvest, farmers bring in what has grown in fields, meadows and on trees. Depending on the plant, this happens at a different time of year, from early summer into autumn.
wichtigste: Strawberries are harvested in Switzerland mainly in early summer.
Cereals such as wheat are ripe in July and August.
The combine harvester cuts the cereal and separates the grains from the straw.
Most apples are picked in autumn.
The grape harvest is called Wümmet in German-speaking Switzerland.
At the harvest festival, many people give thanks for the harvest.

abschnitte.text: Harvesting begins as early as **early summer** with the **strawberries**, in May, June and July. In summer, farmers mow the meadows and dry the grass. Dried grass is called **hay**. They use it to feed their cows in winter, when nothing grows outside. In **July and August** the cereal is ripe. Then the ears of wheat are golden yellow and dry.

Cereal is harvested with a large machine, the **combine harvester**. It **cuts** the cereal and **threshes** it straight away. Threshing means separating the grains from the straw. That is where the machine gets its name. The grains end up in a tank, while the straw stays lying on the field and is later pressed into bales.

**Autumn** is the main harvest time. Apples need the whole summer to ripen, and most varieties are picked in September and October. **Pumpkins** are ripe then too. At Halloween some are hollowed out. The grape harvest is called **Wümmet** in German-speaking Switzerland. On the south side of the Alps, for example in **Ticino**, **chestnuts** are gathered. Roasted, they are called **Marroni**.

In autumn many people celebrate the **harvest festival**. People give thanks that enough has grown. Often fruit, vegetables and bread are brought to church and used to decorate the altar. In many villages there are also parades or festivals for the grape harvest.

gewusst: A modern combine harvester can bring in the crop of many fields in a single day.
In winter, hot Marroni are also bought at small stalls in many German-Swiss towns.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Office for the Environment, FOEN for short (in German BAFU), is the federal specialist authority for the environment. It looks after forests, water, air, noise, biodiversity and natural hazards.
wichtigste: The FOEN belongs to the department DETEC (German UVEK).
It was created in 2006 from the BUWAL and parts of the Federal Office for Water and Geology.
The first environmental protection article entered the Federal Constitution in 1971.
The Environmental Protection Act dates from 1983.
Important principles are the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
Medicines are not approved by the FOEN, but by Swissmedic.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)** belongs to the **DETEC**, the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications. The offices for transport, energy and spatial development are also housed there. The FOEN deals with **forests**, **water**, **biodiversity**, **natural hazards**, **air** and **noise**. It works closely with the cantons, which carry out many environmental laws on the spot.

On 6 June **1971**, the people and the cantons adopted the first constitutional article on the protection of humans and their natural environment, by a large majority.
