In the same year the **Federal Office for Environmental Protection** (BUS) was created. In 1989 it was merged with the Federal Office for Forestry and Landscape Protection to form the **BUWAL**, the Federal Office for the Environment, Forests and Landscape. In **2006** the **FOEN** arose from it together with parts of the Federal Office for Water and Geology. Since then it has also looked after flood protection.

The central basis is the **Environmental Protection Act** (EPA) of 7 October **1983**. It came into force in 1985. Among other things it regulates air pollution control, noise protection, waste and **contaminated sites**, that is, polluted soils from earlier times. In addition there are further laws, for example on water protection, on forests and on nature and cultural heritage protection.

The **precautionary principle** demands that burdens that could become harmful or annoying are limited early. So one does not wait until damage has been proven. The **polluter pays principle** says: whoever causes an environmental burden bears the costs. A well-known example is the **refuse bag with a fee**, where you pay according to the amount of waste.

abschnitte.titel: What the FOEN does not do
abschnitte.text: Not everything that has to do with health and nature is a matter for the FOEN. Medicines, for example, are approved in Switzerland by **Swissmedic**. Another federal office is responsible for food safety. The FOEN concentrates on protecting the environment and landscape and on protecting the population from natural hazards.

gewusst: The FOEN has its headquarters in Ittigen near Bern.
The vote on the environmental protection article in 1971 was accepted with over 90 per cent yes votes.

teile.einleitung: Soil is not just soil. Depending on how big its grains are, it behaves quite differently. This property is called **soil type**.
wichtigste: The soil type depends on the proportions of sand, silt and clay.
Sand has the largest grains, about 0.05 to 2 millimetres.
Clay has the smallest particles, smaller than two thousandths of a millimetre.
Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay.
Sandy soil lets water drain away quickly, clay soil holds a lot of water.
With the finger test you can easily determine the soil type.

abschnitte.text: The fine parts of the soil are classified by their **grain size**. **Sand** has the largest grains, about **0.05 to 2 millimetres**. The lower limit is at 0.05 or 0.063 millimetres depending on the classification. Larger grains count as **gravel**. Smaller than sand is **silt**. The smallest particles belong to **clay**, and they measure less than two thousandths of a millimetre.

Between the large grains of sand there are **large pores**. Water therefore **drains away** quickly, and the soil **dries out** fast. **Nutrients** are also easily washed out. In return, sandy soils are easy to work and warm up quickly in spring. They are also called light soils.

Clay soil has many **fine pores** and **holds water** strongly. Wet it is **sticky**, dry it becomes **hard** and **cracked**. That is why it is hard to work. It is called a heavy soil. Clay can, however, store many nutrients. **Loam** contains sand, silt and clay in similar proportions. Loam soils combine good properties and are often **very fertile**.

With the **finger test** you can determine the soil type without instruments. You take some **moist soil** and rub it between your fingers. **Sand** crunches and feels rough. **Silt** feels floury, like flour on the skin. **Clay** is smooth and sticky and can be shaped well. This way you quickly notice what is in the soil.

gewusst: From clay, bricks, pots and tableware are fired.
Rock finely ground by the glacier is called glacial milk and makes many mountain streams in Switzerland cloudy.

teile.einleitung: Epiphytes are plants that grow on other plants, usually high up in trees. They use the tree only as a support and take nothing from it.
wichtigste: Epiphytes are also called air plants or perching plants in German (Aufsitzerpflanzen).
They get their water from rain, mist and damp air.
High up in the trees they receive more light.
Many orchids and bromeliads are epiphytes.
Mistletoe is not a true epiphyte, because it taps water from the tree.
In Switzerland, mosses and lichens grow as epiphytes on tree bark.

abschnitte.text: An **epiphyte** grows on another plant without tapping it. It is also called a **perching plant**. The host tree serves only as a support. Epiphytes grow high up because there is little light on the dark **forest floor**. On the branches they get enough sun for **photosynthesis** without having to form a trunk themselves. Especially many epiphytes are found in tropical rainforests.

Epiphytes have no contact with the ground. They catch **rainwater** and take up moisture from **air and mist**. Many **orchids** have **aerial roots** for this, with a silvery, sponge-like covering. This covering is called **velamen** and soaks up water like a sponge. Many house orchids that are popular here, such as the moth orchid, are originally epiphytes.

The leaves of many **bromeliads** form a **funnel**, a kind of small cistern. Rainwater and fallen leaves collect in it. The plant takes up water and nutrients from it. In these mini ponds, animals live too. Some **poison dart frogs** carry their tadpoles into them. There they are protected from many enemies.

**Mistletoe** also grows on trees, but is not a true epiphyte. It is a **hemiparasite**: it carries out photosynthesis itself, but takes water and minerals from the wood of the host tree. An epiphyte, on the other hand, takes nothing from its host. There are epiphytes in Switzerland too: **mosses and lichens** often cover trunks and branches. They live on rainwater and dust.

gewusst: Hundreds of plants of other species can grow on a single rainforest tree.
In the water funnels of bromeliads, whole small communities of living things, including insect larvae, sometimes live.

teile.einleitung: Ferns have large, finely divided leaves called fronds. In spring the young fronds slowly unroll, which looks like a snail shell opening.
wichtigste: The large leaves of a fern are called fronds.
Young fronds are curled up like a snail shell.
The curled tip is also called a crozier.
Most fronds are feathered like a feather.
The brown dots on the underside are clusters of spores.
The fronds grow from a rootstock in the ground.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of ferns are called **fronds**. Most are **feathered**, that is, divided into many small parts. This makes them look like a big green **feather**. Ferns have a **rootstock** in the ground. From it the fronds grow upwards every year. Ferns like shady, damp places, for example in the forest.

In **spring** it gets warmer and lighter. Then the ferns sprout. At the start, the young fronds are **curled up** like a snail shell. Slowly they unroll. The curled tip looks like the curved staff of a bishop. That is why it is also called a **crozier** (in German, “bishop's staff”).

On the underside of some fronds you can see **brown dots**. They are not a disease. They are **clusters of spores**. Ferns form no flowers and no seeds. They reproduce with tiny **spores**. When the spores are ripe, they come away easily. If you stroke the underside, it feels **slightly dusty**, and often brown dust is left on your fingers.

gewusst: Ferns existed long before the dinosaurs.
A single fern frond can produce millions of tiny spores.

t1hkdayy.t: Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments

teile.einleitung: The Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments, BLN for short, is a list of the most beautiful and valuable landscapes in Switzerland. These areas are to be preserved as intact as possible.
wichtigste: BLN stands for Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance.
The Federal Council put it into force in 1977.
It comprises 162 objects (as of 2025).
BLN areas cover just under 20 per cent of the country’s area.
The Federal Office for the Environment is responsible for it.
The Rhine Falls are an example of a BLN object.

abschnitte.text: **BLN** is the abbreviation of the **Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance**. An inventory is a register, that is, a list. The **Federal Council** put the BLN into force in **1977**. Since then it has been supplemented and revised several times. The basis is the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage.

The BLN comprises **162** landscapes and natural monuments (as of 2025). Together they cover **just under 20 per cent**, so about a fifth, of the area of Switzerland. There are large areas such as whole mountain landscapes and small ones such as single gorges. The **Federal Office for the Environment** (FOEN) is responsible. It keeps the inventory and advises the authorities on projects in these areas.

A **natural monument** is a special, striking feature of nature. It can be a large **erratic boulder**, that is, a block of rock transported by a glacier. A **waterfall** or a special rock formation can also be a natural monument. A well-known example in the BLN is the **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen. Buildings such as castles or bridges, by contrast, do not belong in this inventory.

When the Confederation carries out a task in a BLN area, for example building a road or granting a permit, the landscape is to be **preserved undiminished** or at least **spared as much as possible**. But a BLN area is not a reserve where everything is forbidden. Farming, housing and tourism continue to exist there. The inventory ensures that projects are weighed up especially carefully.

gewusst: Besides the BLN there are further federal inventories, for example for moors, floodplains and townscapes worth protecting.
Every BLN object has its own description that explains why it is so valuable.

teile.einleitung: Endemism means that an animal or plant species occurs naturally only in one particular, limited area and nowhere else in the world. Such species are called endemic. Especially many of them are found on remote islands such as Madagascar or the Galápagos Islands.
wichtigste: An endemic species occurs naturally only in one particular, limited area.
The area can be an island, a mountain range, a lake or a whole continent.
Islands have especially many endemic species because they were separated from other areas for a long time.
The koala, for example, is endemic to Australia.
Endemic species are often highly endangered because they live in only one place.
In Switzerland there are only a few endemic species, because ice age glaciers covered large parts of the country.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek “endemos”, which means something like “native”. A species is **endemic** if it lives naturally only in a clearly limited area. The area can be very small, for example a single lake or a mountain. But it can also be a whole continent. The opposite are **cosmopolitans**, that is, species that occur almost everywhere in the world.

On islands, animals and plants often develop separately from the mainland for a long time. Over many generations they change and become new species that exist only there. This process is called **evolution**. On the **Galápagos Islands**, for example, live giant tortoises and marine iguanas that exist nowhere else. Charles Darwin observed Darwin's finches there and developed important ideas for his theory of evolution from them.

On **Madagascar** the vast majority of animal and plant species are endemic, including all lemurs such as the ring-tailed lemur. In Australia, koalas, kangaroos and the platypus live only there. The kiwi is an endemic bird of New Zealand. On Hawaii and the Canary Islands, too, there are many plants that grow only there.

During the **ice ages**, most of Switzerland was covered by glaciers. Many species had to retreat and returned only later, which is why there are only few endemic species here. Interesting examples are some of the **whitefish** (Felchen), fish that each live in only one particular Swiss lake. In the Alps there are also plants and insects that occur only in the Alpine region.

Endemic species are particularly vulnerable because they cannot simply move to another area. If their habitat is destroyed, they often disappear from the Earth for ever. Introduced animals such as rats, cats or goats can also wipe out island species. A well-known example is the **dodo** on Mauritius, which died out as early as the 17th century. That is why areas with many endemic species are now given special protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: Occurring naturally only in one particular area.
A species that is spread almost all over the world.
The slow development and change of living things over many generations.
The place where an animal or plant species lives.

gewusst: The dodo on Mauritius was an endemic bird that had no enemies and so could not fly.
On the island of Socotra in Yemen grows the umbrella-shaped dragon's blood tree, which occurs naturally only there.

teile.einleitung: Plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. If the CO2 content of the air rises, they can often grow better. This effect is called the CO2 fertilisation effect. But it has limits and does not simply make up for the consequences of climate change.
wichtigste: The CO2 fertilisation effect means stronger plant growth through more CO2 in the air.
C3 plants such as wheat benefit more than C4 plants.
More CO2 reduces photorespiration in C3 plants.
Water use efficiency often rises, because the stomata are less wide open.
Nutrient shortage limits the effect in the long term.
Wheat and rice often contain less protein, zinc and iron under more CO2.

abschnitte.text: For **photosynthesis**, plants take in **carbon dioxide** from the air. Humans have greatly raised the CO2 content of the air, mainly by burning coal, oil and gas. Many plants therefore grow faster. This effect is called the **CO2 fertilisation effect**. In greenhouses, CO2 is even added deliberately so that tomatoes or cucumbers thrive better.

**C3 plants** such as wheat, rice and most trees benefit especially strongly. In them, the enzyme Rubisco often binds oxygen instead of CO2. This loss process is called **photorespiration**. More CO2 in the air reduces it. **C4 plants** such as maize already enrich CO2 themselves and therefore benefit less.

With more CO2, plants often open their **stomata** less wide. They still get enough CO2, but lose less water. So the **water use efficiency** rises. This is studied in **FACE experiments** (Free-Air CO2 Enrichment). In them, plant stands in the open are supplied with additional CO2. In Switzerland, at Hofstetten near Basel, CO2 was fed with a crane into the crowns of old trees.

Satellite data show that many land areas of the Earth have become **greener** in recent decades. A part of this **global greening** is attributed to the CO2 fertilisation effect. Other reasons are, for example, agriculture, afforestation and a warmer climate in the far north. How large the share of CO2 is exactly is still being researched.

In many ecosystems, **nutrients** such as **nitrogen and phosphorus** are lacking in the long term. Then plants can hardly use the additional CO2. Studies also show that **wheat and rice** under more CO2 often contain **less protein, zinc and iron**. This can be important for nutrition. In addition, **heat and drought** can slow growth more strongly than additional CO2 promotes it. That is why the effect does not simply make up for the consequences of climate change.

gewusst: In some greenhouses the air is enriched to a multiple of the normal CO2 content.
In the Basel crane experiment, the old trees hardly grew faster despite more CO2, probably because of lacking nutrients.

teile.einleitung: Ferns are ancient plants without flowers or seeds, which reproduce with tiny spores. You recognise them by their feathery leaves, the fronds, which unroll in spring like a snail. Long before the dinosaurs, their ancestors grew in huge forests.
wichtigste: Ferns form their spores in little clusters on the underside of the leaf.
Unlike mosses, ferns have vascular bundles and true roots.
Young fern fronds unroll in spring like a snail.
When a spore sprouts, a small, flat prothallus forms first.
About 300 million years ago, large parts of hard coal formed from tree-sized fern plants.
Ferns love damp, shady places such as woods and gorges.
In the tropics there are tree ferns that grow many metres tall.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of ferns are called **fronds** and are often finely feathered. In spring the young fronds are curled up like a snail shell or the head of a violin. Slowly they then unroll to full size. Ferns have **vascular bundles** that carry water, and true roots. This sets them apart from the mosses, which have neither.

Ferns have no flowers and no seeds. On the underside of their leaves sit small brown clusters, the **sori**, in which thousands of tiny **spores** ripen. The spores are blown away by the wind. When a spore sprouts, a small, flat, often heart-shaped **prothallus** forms first. On it, in wet conditions, sperm cells swim to the egg cells, and a new fern grows from them.

Worldwide there are over 10,000 species of fern, most of them in damp tropical forests. **Tree ferns** with a trunk also grow there, reaching over ten metres tall. In Switzerland, ferns are found mainly in shady, damp woods and gorges. Common ones are the **male fern** and the bracken, which can cover large areas. On damp rocks grows the hart's-tongue fern with undivided, tongue-shaped leaves.

Fern plants have existed for over 350 million years. In the **Carboniferous**, tree-sized fern plants together with clubmosses and horsetails formed huge swamp forests. A large part of the **hard coal** was formed from their remains about 300 million years ago. In coal and rock, imprints of fern leaves are often found as fossils.

Many ferns are popular ornamental plants for gardens and homes, for example the sword fern. In some countries, young, curled-up fern tips are eaten as a vegetable. Many ferns, for example bracken, are however **poisonous** when raw. In the past, dried fern fronds were used as bedding for livestock.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large, often feathered leaf of a fern.
A tiny reproductive grain that can sprout without fertilisation.
A small, flat little plant that grows from a fern spore.
Fine tubes in the plant that carry water and nutrients.

gewusst: A single fern frond can produce millions of spores.
In the past, people believed in magical fern seeds, although ferns have no seeds at all.

teile.einleitung: Eawag is a Swiss research institute devoted entirely to water. It studies lakes, rivers, drinking water and wastewater, and looks for solutions for clean water in Switzerland and all over the world.
wichtigste: Eawag is the water research institute of the ETH Domain.
Its headquarters are in Dübendorf in the canton of Zurich.
A second site is in Kastanienbaum on Lake Lucerne.
Its predecessor was founded in 1936 as an advisory office of the ETH.
Eawag promoted SODIS, a way of disinfecting water with sunlight.
The Forum Chriesbach building is considered a model for sustainable building.

abschnitte.text: Eawag researches water in all its aspects, from lakes to wastewater. It belongs to the **ETH Domain**, like ETH Zurich, EPFL, Empa, PSI and the WSL. The name was originally an abbreviation of **“Eidgenössische Anstalt für Wasserversorgung, Abwasserreinigung und Gewässerschutz”**, the Swiss Federal Institute for Water Supply, Wastewater Treatment and Water Protection. Today only the short form Eawag is used.

The **headquarters** are in **Dübendorf** in the canton of Zurich. In **Kastanienbaum** near Lucerne, right on **Lake Lucerne**, Eawag runs its centre for lake and fish research. There, lakes and their animals can be studied right on the doorstep.

Eawag was founded in **1936** as an advisory office of the ETH for wastewater treatment and drinking water supply. At that time many Swiss lakes and rivers were heavily polluted. Later it became an independent research institute. Its work helped to get sewage treatment plants built and the waters cleaner again.

With **SODIS**, you fill clear water into transparent **PET bottles** and leave them in the sun for a few hours. The **UV radiation** and the heat kill disease-causing germs. The method is simple and cheap. Eawag made it known in countries without safe drinking water.

The **Forum Chriesbach** in Dübendorf was occupied in 2006 and manages without a conventional heating system. Eawag also researches **urine separation**: urine is collected separately because it contains many nutrients. **Fertiliser** can be obtained from it.

gewusst: A PET bottle and sunlight are enough to make water drinkable with the SODIS method.
Fertiliser for plants can be made from separately collected urine.

teile.einleitung: The champignon, or button mushroom, is the mushroom you buy most often in the shop. It is cultivated in white or brown, but also grows wild in meadows. When collecting, however, you must be very careful.
wichtigste: The champignon is the most commonly sold mushroom.
Cultivated champignons grow in halls on compost.
In the shop they are available white or brown.
Young champignons have pink gills, old ones dark brown.
The field mushroom grows on pastures with cows and horses.
Young champignons can be confused with the deadly poisonous death cap.

abschnitte.text: The French word **“champignon”** simply means **mushroom**. In German the champignon is also called **Egerling**. It is the mushroom that is **sold most often in shops**. You eat it raw in salad, fried, in sauces or on pizza. There are **white** and **brown** cultivated champignons. The brown ones often taste a little stronger.

Cultivated champignons grow **in halls on compost**. This compost is often made from straw and horse manure. In it grows the fine mushroom network, the **mycelium**. With a covering layer of soil or peat and the right moisture, the fruiting bodies that we eat form from it. Because the halls are dark and cool, you can harvest all year round. There are champignon farms in Switzerland too.

Under the cap a champignon has thin blades, the **gills**. In young champignons they are **pink**. The older the mushroom gets, the darker they become, until they are **dark brown**. This comes from the many dark **spores** with which the mushroom reproduces. Old champignons can usually still be eaten, but they are less firm.

The **field mushroom** grows wild on **pastures with cows and horses**, mainly in late summer. But young champignons can be confused with the **death cap**, which is **deadly poisonous**. It always has **white gills** and a bulb at the base of the stem. Anyone who collects mushrooms should always have them checked by an expert. In Switzerland, many communes have a **mushroom inspection** for this.

gewusst: Champignons are among the first mushrooms that humans deliberately cultivated, over 300 years ago in France.
What we eat as a mushroom is only the fruiting body, while the actual mushroom grows as a fine network in the soil.

teile.einleitung: An exoplanet is a planet outside our solar system that circles another star. For a long time nobody knew whether such worlds existed at all. Today astronomers know thousands of them, and the first discovery around a sun-like star was made by two Swiss researchers.
wichtigste: An exoplanet is a planet outside our solar system.
The first exoplanet around a sun-like star was discovered in 1995.
It was discovered by the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz.
For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
By 2025, over 6,000 exoplanets had been confirmed.
Most exoplanets are not found directly, but through their influence on their star.
Researchers search especially for planets where liquid water could exist.

abschnitte.text: Our solar system has eight planets that circle the sun. But the sun is only one of billions of stars in our Milky Way. Many of these stars also have planets, which are called **exoplanets** or extrasolar planets. The prefix “exo” means “outside”. Exoplanets are so far away that they usually cannot even be seen directly with the largest telescopes.

In 1995, **Michel Mayor** and **Didier Queloz** of the University of Geneva discovered a planet around the star 51 Pegasi. It is called 51 Pegasi b and is about 50 light years away from us. The planet is a huge gas planet that goes round its star in just over four days. For this discovery the two received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in 2019. Planets around a special dead star, a pulsar, had already been found in 1992.

With the **transit method**, you watch whether a star regularly becomes a tiny bit darker. This happens when a planet passes in front of it. With the **radial velocity method**, you measure how the star wobbles slightly back and forth because of the pull of the planet. Mayor and Queloz found their planet with this method. Only rarely does a direct photograph of an exoplanet succeed.

NASA's **Kepler** space telescope discovered thousands of exoplanets between 2009 and 2018. Since 2018, the TESS telescope has been scanning the whole sky. The **CHEOPS** satellite, built under the leadership of the University of Bern, has been studying known exoplanets more closely since 2019. The James Webb Space Telescope can even find out which gases occur in the atmospheres of some exoplanets.

Exoplanets are very varied: there are hot gas giants, ice worlds and rocky planets. Planets in the **habitable zone** of their star are especially exciting. There it is neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water. The nearest known exoplanet, Proxima Centauri b, lies in such a zone and is about 4.2 light years away. Whether life exists there, nobody yet knows.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet that circles a star other than the sun.
The distance that light travels in a year, almost 10 trillion kilometres.
When a planet, seen from us, passes in front of its star.
The region around a star in which liquid water can exist.

gewusst: Around the star TRAPPIST-1 circle seven planets of roughly the size of the Earth.
With a spacecraft of today, the journey to the nearest exoplanet would take tens of thousands of years.
Some exoplanets circle two suns at the same time.

teile.einleitung: A soil profile is like a look into the inside of the soil. In it you see the layers from the surface down to the rock.
wichtigste: A soil profile is a vertical cut through the soil.
You look at it on the wall of a dug pit.
A profile consists of layers lying one above another.
At the very bottom lies the parent rock.
Dark layers usually contain a lot of humus.
With a soil auger you can look at a profile without a pit.

abschnitte.text: A **soil profile** is a vertical section of the soil from the surface to the rock. To see it, you dig a **profile pit** with a straight, vertical wall. On this wall you recognise the different layers one above another. Sometimes you also see a profile at a building site or a stream bank.

In technical language the layers are called **horizons**. They differ in colour, texture and humus content. In the forest, at the very top lies the **litter layer** of leaves, needles and twigs. Below it follows the dark **topsoil** with a lot of humus and many roots. Then comes the paler **subsoil**, and at the very bottom lies the **parent rock** from which the soil arose through weathering.

**Humus** colours the soil dark brown to black. The darker a layer, the more humus it usually contains. Brown or reddish colours often come from iron. Grey or mottled layers show that water often stands there. This way you can read from the colours how a soil works.

You do not always want to dig a pit. Then a **soil auger** helps, a metal rod with a groove. You drive it into the ground and pull it out again. In the groove you see a narrow strip of the profile. This way samples can be taken quickly in many places.

Soil profiles look different in different places. This depends on the parent rock, the climate, the plants, the living things and time. A soil on limestone in the Jura looks different from one on granite in the Alps. The science that studies this is called **soil science** or pedology.

gewusst: A soil profile can be only a few centimetres or several metres deep.
Experts name the horizons with letters, for example A for the topsoil and C for the rock.

teile.einleitung: Direct payments are contributions that the Confederation pays to Swiss farms. With them it rewards services for which there is no price on the market, for example looking after the landscape or especially animal-friendly keeping.
wichtigste: The direct payments are paid by the Confederation.
The Federal Office for Agriculture (FOAG) is responsible.
Support for agriculture is written in the Federal Constitution.
In 2024 the Confederation paid out about 2.8 billion francs.
Farmers receive money, for example, for looking after the landscape.
BTS and RAUS are programmes for more animal welfare.

abschnitte.text: The direct payments are paid by the **Confederation**. The **Federal Office for Agriculture** (FOAG) is responsible. The **Federal Constitution** says that agriculture fulfils important tasks: it is to supply the population with food, preserve the natural foundations of life, **look after the landscape** and help ensure that remote areas stay inhabited. For these services the farms receive money.

In **2024** the Confederation paid out **about 2.8 billion francs** as direct payments. The money is spread over many thousands of farms. Anyone who wants direct payments must keep to rules, the so-called **proof of ecological performance**. This includes, for example, a balanced use of fertiliser, areas for biodiversity and animal-friendly keeping.

A part of the money is for the **cultural landscape**. Anyone who mows **steep meadows** receives additional contributions, **because work on a slope is much more laborious**. Without care, many mountain meadows would become overgrown with scrub and turn into forest. There are also contributions for alpine pastures in summer, species-rich meadows, hedges and standard fruit trees. In this way the typical Swiss landscape is preserved.

abschnitte.titel: More animal welfare: BTS and RAUS
abschnitte.text: With two programmes the Confederation promotes **animal welfare**. **BTS** stands for **especially animal-friendly housing systems**. The animals live in groups, free to move, with lying areas and daylight. **RAUS** stands for **regular outdoor access**. The animals are regularly allowed out onto the pasture or into a run. Taking part is voluntary, but is rewarded with additional contributions.

gewusst: For many Swiss farms, direct payments make up a large part of the income.
Since the 1990s, Switzerland has gradually switched its agricultural policy from price supports to direct payments.

teile.einleitung: The Calvin cycle is the part of photosynthesis in which sugar is made from carbon dioxide. It takes place in the stroma of the chloroplasts and uses the energy that was previously gained from light. It is named after the chemist Melvin Calvin.
wichtigste: The Calvin cycle has three phases: fixation, reduction and regeneration.
Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate takes up the CO2, and 3-phosphoglycerate is formed from it.
Per CO2, 3 ATP and 2 NADPH are consumed.
For one molecule of glucose, 6 CO2 must be fixed.
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is branched off for glucose and sucrose.
Melvin Calvin received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1961.

abschnitte.text: The Calvin cycle is a **cycle** of many chemical steps. It is divided into three phases: **fixation**, **reduction** and **regeneration**. At the end there is again the molecule with which everything began. This allows the cycle to start again from the beginning, over and over. It takes place in the **stroma**, the basic fluid of the chloroplasts.

In **fixation**, the molecule **ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate** takes up one CO2. The enzyme for this is called **Rubisco**. This produces two molecules of **3-phosphoglycerate**. In **reduction**, they are converted using energy from **ATP** and **NADPH**. This produces the sugar **glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate** with three carbon atoms. A part of it is branched off to make **glucose** or **sucrose** from it.

In **regeneration**, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate is formed again from the remaining sugar. For each fixed CO2, the Calvin cycle consumes **3 ATP and 2 NADPH**. One molecule of glucose (C6H12O6) has six carbon atoms. So **6 CO2** must be fixed for one glucose to be made. For this, a total of 18 ATP and 12 NADPH is needed.

abschnitte.titel: Light independent, but not in the dark
abschnitte.text: The Calvin cycle is often called **light independent**, because it does **not directly** use light. But the substances it needs, ATP and NADPH, come from the **light reactions**. That is why it runs mainly during the day. Several of its enzymes are switched on in light via the **ferredoxin-thioredoxin system**. In this way the cycle works only when enough energy is available.

The American chemist **Melvin Calvin** and his colleagues, including Andrew Benson and James Bassham, researched the path of carbon. They gave **green algae** CO2 with radioactive **carbon-14**. Then they stopped the algae after a few seconds and looked for which substances contained the labelled carbon. In this way they found the cycle step by step. In **1961** Calvin received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for it.

gewusst: The enzyme Rubisco is regarded as the most abundant protein on Earth.
In honour of its discoverers, the cycle is also called the Calvin-Benson cycle.

teile.einleitung: Quinine is a bitter substance from the bark of the cinchona tree. For centuries it was the most important remedy against malaria. Today many people know the taste mainly from tonic water.
wichtigste: Quinine comes from the bark of the cinchona tree.
For centuries it was the most important remedy against malaria.
In Europe in the 17th century the bark was called Jesuits’ bark.
Pelletier and Caventou isolated quinine in 1820.
The Netherlands set up large plantations on Java.
Quinine makes tonic water bitter, and under UV light it glows bluish.

abschnitte.text: The **cinchona tree** comes from the **Andes** in South America. In its bark is the bitter substance **quinine**. In the 17th century, members of religious orders brought the bark to Europe. Because mainly the **Jesuits** spread it, it was called **Jesuits’ bark**. The powder from the bark helped against fever, especially against intermittent fever, **malaria**.

**Malaria** is a dangerous disease that is transmitted by certain mosquitoes. It occurs mainly in warm countries. Quinine was **for centuries the most important remedy** against it. Following its model, artificial malaria drugs such as **chloroquine** were developed later. Today there are also many other drugs, but quinine is still used in some cases.

In **1820** the two French pharmacists **Pelletier and Caventou** succeeded in obtaining the pure active substance quinine from cinchona bark. This made it possible to dose it more precisely. Because the demand was huge, in the 19th century the **Netherlands** set up large **plantations** of cinchona trees on the island of **Java**. For a long time most of the world’s quinine came from there.

Quinine gives **tonic water** its bitter taste. If you shine **UV light** on tonic water, **it glows bluish**. This phenomenon is called **fluorescence**. Too much quinine, however, is harmful. With too high a dose, ringing in the ears, visual disturbances and nausea can occur. This group of side effects is called **cinchonism**, after the Latin name of the tree, Cinchona.

gewusst: Tonic water contains only very little quinine, much less than a medicine.
The cinchona tree is shown on the coat of arms of Peru.

teile.einleitung: Denitrification is a process in which bacteria convert nitrate into nitrogen gas. It is an important part of the nitrogen cycle. In sewage works it is used deliberately, in arable soils it can cost fertiliser.
wichtigste: At the end of complete denitrification, molecular nitrogen (N₂) is formed.
It takes place mainly when oxygen is lacking.
The bacteria use nitrate as an electron acceptor instead of oxygen.
The order is: nitrate, nitrite, NO, N₂O, N₂.
The intermediate product nitrous oxide (N₂O) is a strong greenhouse gas.
Many denitrifiers belong to the genus Pseudomonas.

abschnitte.text: Nitrogen is an important building block of all living things. It travels in a cycle between air, soil, water and living things. In the air it exists as **molecular nitrogen (N₂)**. In the soil it occurs, among other forms, as **nitrate**, which plants take up. In **denitrification**, bacteria convert nitrate back into N₂. In this way the nitrogen returns to the air, and the cycle closes.

Most living things need oxygen to gain energy. Experts say: oxygen serves as the **electron acceptor**. If oxygen is lacking, certain bacteria can use **nitrate** instead. That is why denitrification takes place mainly when **oxygen is lacking**, for example in wet soil or in mud. Many well-known denitrifiers belong to the genus **Pseudomonas**.

The conversion takes place in several steps: **nitrate** (NO₃⁻) becomes **nitrite** (NO₂⁻), then nitric oxide (**NO**), then **nitrous oxide** (**N₂O**) and finally **N₂**. If the process is not complete, part of it escapes as nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide is a **strong greenhouse gas** that warms much more strongly than carbon dioxide. It also harms the ozone layer.

A farmer fertilises his field so that the plants have enough nitrogen. But if the soil is **waterlogged**, that is, full of water, oxygen is lacking there. Then **bacteria convert the nitrate into gas**, and it escapes into the air. The fertiliser is lost in this way, and nitrous oxide can be produced. Good soil structure and adapted fertilising help to reduce such losses.

Wastewater contains a lot of nitrogen, for example from urine. If too much of it gets into rivers and lakes, algae grow too strongly. Modern **sewage works** therefore have a **denitrification stage**. There, bacteria live in a tank without oxygen supply and **remove the nitrogen from the wastewater as gas**. In Switzerland too, many larger sewage works are equipped in this way.

gewusst: The air we breathe consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen.
Nitrous oxide is also used as an anaesthetic and as a propellant for cream from a spray can.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is our home planet, on which we live. It is the third planet from the sun and the only one on which life has been found so far. From space it looks like a blue marble, because most of it is covered with water.
wichtigste: The Earth is our home planet and the third planet from the sun.
It is about 4.6 billion years old.
Around 71 per cent of its surface is covered with water.
Its diameter is about 12,700 kilometres.
The Earth has one natural companion, the Moon.
A shell of air, the atmosphere, protects life and supplies oxygen.
About 8.2 billion people live on Earth (as of 2025).

abschnitte.titel: A planet in the solar system
abschnitte.text: The Earth is one of eight planets that circle the sun. It is the third from the inside, after Mercury and Venus. Among the eight planets it is the fifth largest and the largest of the **rocky planets**. Its distance from the sun is just right for liquid water to exist. This region is called the **habitable zone**.

About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered by oceans, lakes and ice. The land is spread over seven continents, the largest of which is Asia. Around the Earth lies the **atmosphere**, a shell of air made up of about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen. It protects us from dangerous radiation from space and holds on to the warmth.

The Earth is built like an onion from several layers. On the very outside lies the thin, solid **Earth's crust**, on which we live. Below it follows the hot mantle of thick, viscous rock. In the middle lies the **core** of iron and nickel, which is about as hot as the surface of the sun. The movements inside make continents drift, mountains grow and volcanoes erupt.

The Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago from dust and rock that circled the young sun. The first simple living things probably existed in the sea more than 3.5 billion years ago. Much later, plants and animals came onto land, and dinosaurs lived from about 230 to 66 million years ago. Modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, have existed for only around 300,000 years.

The Earth turns once around itself in about 24 hours, which creates **day and night**. In about a year it goes round the sun. The **Moon** circles the Earth in just under a month and, together with the sun, causes the tides. It also stabilises the tilt of the Earth's axis and so provides a calmer climate.

The Earth is the only place where we know of life so far, with millions of animal and plant species. But humans are changing it greatly, for example through deforestation, waste and **climate change**. That is why many countries, Switzerland among them, work for environmental protection. Every year on 22 April, Earth Day is celebrated worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large heavenly body that circles a star.
The shell of air that surrounds a planet.
The outermost solid layer of rock of the Earth.
A very large connected mass of land, for example Europe or Africa.

gewusst: Once around the Earth at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres.
The Earth is not quite round but slightly flattened at the poles.
The famous “Blue Marble” photo of the whole Earth was taken by Apollo 17 astronauts in 1972.

teile.einleitung: Emmer is a very old type of wheat. Even in ancient Egypt, bread was baked from it. Emmer later gave rise to durum wheat, from which we make pasta today.
wichtigste: Emmer is called Triticum dicoccum in science.
It usually forms two grains per spikelet and is therefore also called two-grain wheat.
Emmer is tetraploid and has 28 chromosomes.
Durum wheat arose from emmer.
In ancient Egypt, emmer was the most important wheat cereal.
In 1906 Aaron Aaronsohn found wild emmer growing in Galilee.

abschnitte.text: Emmer usually forms **two grains per spikelet**. That is why it is also called **“two-grain wheat”**. Its scientific name **Triticum dicoccum** means roughly “two-grained”. It is one of the **oldest types of wheat**. Like einkorn, it is a hulled cereal.

Emmer is **tetraploid**: it has four sets of chromosomes with **28 chromosomes** in all. Wild emmer arose from a cross between the wild grass **Triticum urartu** and a **goat grass**. The sets of chromosomes of both parents were kept. Such an origin is called **allopolyploidy**.

abschnitte.titel: From emmer to durum wheat and bread wheat
abschnitte.text: Cultivated emmer gave rise to **durum wheat** (Triticum durum). It is also tetraploid, but can be threshed without husks. It is used mainly to make **pasta**. Later, tetraploid wheat crossed by chance with the goat grass **Aegilops tauschii**. This added a third set of chromosomes, and hexaploid **bread wheat** arose.

In **ancient Egypt**, emmer was the most important wheat cereal. **Bread** and **beer** were made from it. Finds from tombs prove its great importance. In Europe, too, the farmers of the New Stone Age already grew emmer.

abschnitte.titel: The discovery of the wild form
abschnitte.text: Wild emmer is called **Triticum dicoccoides**. For a long time it was known only from a few dried plants in collections. In **1906** the agronomist **Aaron Aaronsohn** found wild emmer growing near **Rosh Pina** in Galilee. This was very important for research into the origin of wheat.

gewusst: The ancient Egyptians even brewed beer from emmer.
Our modern bread wheat has genes from three different wild grasses.

teile.einleitung: Angel's trumpets are striking shrubs with huge, hanging flowers that look like trumpets. They are beautiful, but also very poisonous.
wichtigste: Angel's trumpets come from South America.
They belong to the nightshade family, like the potato and deadly nightshade.
Their large, funnel-shaped flowers hang downwards.
The flowers smell strongest in the evening and at night.
The plant contains the poisons scopolamine and atropine.
In the wild, all species are regarded as extinct.

abschnitte.text: Angel's trumpets grow as woody **shrubs or small trees**. In tubs they often grow more than two metres tall. Their **trumpet-shaped flowers** are very large and hang downwards. This is how you can tell them from the related **thorn apple**, whose flowers point upwards. There are varieties in white, yellow, orange and pink.

Angel's trumpets come from **South America**. They belong to the **nightshade family**. This family also includes the potato, the tomato and the poisonous deadly nightshade. Astonishingly, in the wild all species are regarded as **extinct**. They survive only because people plant them in gardens. In Switzerland they are popular **tub plants** on balconies and terraces.

The flowers give off a strong, sweet scent above all **in the evening and at night**. In their homeland this attracts **nocturnal pollinators**. Anyone with an angel's trumpet on their balcony notices this clearly on warm summer evenings.

All parts of the angel's trumpet are poisonous. It contains **scopolamine** and **atropine**, substances similar to those in deadly nightshade. These poisons confuse the senses and put a strain on the heart. Some people use the plant as an intoxicant, which is very dangerous. The **poison content** varies greatly from plant to plant and can hardly be estimated. Confusion, delusions and a racing heart can occur, which can end in death.

gewusst: A single flower of the angel's trumpet can be longer than a hand.
Although they bloom in many gardens, angel's trumpets no longer exist in the wild.

teile.einleitung: Deforestation means that forests disappear for good because people cut them down or burn them. The tropical rainforests are particularly affected, but Switzerland too had a big forest problem in the 19th century.
wichtigste: In the Amazon region, most of the cleared land becomes cattle pasture.
In Indonesia and Malaysia, a lot of rainforest was cleared for oil palms.
In slash-and-burn clearing, forest is burned down, producing a lot of CO2.
The UN programme REDD+ rewards countries that preserve their forests.
Since 1902 the rule in Switzerland has been that the forest area must not be reduced.
Researchers fear that parts of the Amazon could become a savanna.

abschnitte.text: In the **Amazon rainforest**, most cleared areas become **pasture for cattle**. Soy farming, mining and road building also play a role. In **Indonesia and Malaysia**, large rainforests and peat bogs were destroyed for **oil palm** plantations. The two countries are the largest producers of palm oil. This has consequences for animals such as the **orangutan**, whose habitat is shrinking.

In **slash-and-burn clearing**, forest is burned down to gain land for farming. The ash fertilises the soil only briefly. In the process a lot of stored carbon is released as **CO2**, which strengthens climate change. On tropical coasts, **mangrove forests** grow in the tidal zone. They protect against storm surges and are a nursery for many fish. Nevertheless they are often cut down for **prawn** farming ponds.

Trees evaporate large amounts of water. The water vapour travels on with the wind and brings rain to other parts of South America. These air currents are called **flying rivers**. The rainforest thus produces a large part of its own rain. If too much forest is removed, a **tipping point** could be crossed. Researchers fear that large parts would then dry out and turn into a **savanna-like landscape**.

In the 19th century, many forests in Switzerland were cut down. There were severe **floods** and landslides. The federal government responded with laws. Since the revision of the federal **Forest Police Law of 1902**, the principle has applied that the forest area must not be reduced. Anyone who is exceptionally allowed to clear forest must in principle **plant replacement forest**. Today the forest area of Switzerland is even growing.

gewusst: The plus in REDD+ stands for additional measures such as sustainable forest management.
In Switzerland, the forest protects many villages and roads from avalanches and rockfall.

teile.einleitung: The endosperm is the nutritive tissue in the seed of many plants. It supplies the embryo with energy until it has leaves of its own. We eat it every day, for example in white flour.
wichtigste: The endosperm is a nutritive tissue in the seed.
In most angiosperms it is triploid.
White flour consists mainly of the starchy endosperm.
Coconut water is liquid endosperm.
The aleurone layer forms amylase during germination.
Peas and beans store their nutrients in the seed leaves.

abschnitte.text: In the seed lies a tiny **embryo**. Until it has leaves of its own and carries out photosynthesis, it needs supplies. These are provided by the **endosperm**, a nutritive tissue full of **starch**, protein or oil. In most **angiosperms** the endosperm is **triploid**, so it has three sets of chromosomes. In **conifers**, by contrast, the nutritive tissue is **haploid** and forms in a different way.

A cereal grain consists of the **embryo**, the **bran** and the starch-rich **starchy endosperm**. When **white flour** is milled, the embryo and bran are removed. What is left is mainly the starchy endosperm. Wholemeal flour, by contrast, contains the whole grain.

During germination, the embryo releases the plant hormone **gibberellin**. It acts on the **aleurone layer**, the outer layer of the endosperm in the cereal grain. This then forms the enzyme **amylase**. The amylase breaks the starch down into sugar, which the embryo can use. When barley is malted for beer, exactly this process is used.

In the **coconut**, the endosperm is at first **liquid**: this is the **coconut water**. Later, the firm white flesh is deposited from it on the shell. Here, at first only the nuclei divide, without cell walls. This form is called **nuclear endosperm**.

Not all seeds keep their endosperm. In **peas and beans** it is almost entirely used up while the seed ripens. The supplies then lie in the thick **seed leaves**. That is why beans fall easily into two halves when peeled: these are the two seed leaves.

gewusst: Coconut water is really the liquid nutritive tissue of the seed.
The two halves of a bean are its two seed leaves.

teile.einleitung: Elias Landolt was a well-known Swiss botanist, that is, a plant researcher. He taught at ETH Zurich and wrote important books about the plants of Switzerland. His indicator values are still used today.
wichtigste: Elias Landolt was Professor of Geobotany at ETH Zurich.
He headed the Geobotanical Institute of the ETH.
In 1977 he published ecological indicator values for the Swiss flora.
In 2010 the expanded edition “Flora indicativa” appeared.
Internationally he was an expert on duckweeds.
His “Flora der Stadt Zürich” (Flora of the City of Zurich) appeared in 2001.

abschnitte.text: Elias Landolt was **Professor of Geobotany** at **ETH Zurich**. Geobotany studies where plants grow and why. Landolt was director of the ETH's **Geobotanical Institute**, which was also called the Rübel Foundation. There, the distribution of plants and plant communities was researched.

Many plants grow only where it suits them: rather damp or dry, rather acidic or rich in lime. **Indicator values** express this in numbers. The **moisture value**, for example, shows how damp the typical habitat of a species is. In **1977** Landolt published the “Ökologische Zeigerwerte zur Schweizer Flora” (Ecological indicator values for the Swiss flora). The German **Heinz Ellenberg** had published similar values for central Europe in 1974.

In **2010**, together with co-authors, the greatly expanded **“Flora indicativa”** appeared. It contains indicator values and biological features of the plants of Switzerland and the Alps. Experts in nature conservation and research use it to assess habitats. If many species with a high moisture value are found in one place, the soil there is probably wet.

abschnitte.titel: Duckweeds, the city and the mountains
abschnitte.text: Internationally, Landolt was an expert on **duckweeds**, tiny plants that float on ponds. His books about them are regarded as standard works. In **2001** his **“Flora der Stadt Zürich”** appeared, about the wild-growing plants of the city. For the Swiss Alpine Club he wrote the identification guide **“Unsere Alpenflora”** (Our Alpine Flora), which went through many editions.

gewusst: For decades Landolt researched duckweeds, which are among the smallest flowering plants in the world.
Even in the middle of a city like Zurich, very many wild plant species grow.

teile.einleitung: Dendrochronology is the science of tree rings. Because trees form one ring every year and the ring widths differ depending on the weather, timber can often be dated to the exact year with it.
wichtigste: The US astronomer Andrew Ellicott Douglass is regarded as the founder.
Ring patterns of different timbers are strung together overlapping, which is called cross-dating.
The waney edge is the last ring directly under the bark.
With an increment borer, samples are taken without felling the tree.
In Switzerland it is used to date prehistoric pile dwelling settlements to the exact year.
The central European chronology from oaks and pines goes back over 12,000 years.
Long ring series serve to calibrate C14 dates.

abschnitte.text: In our latitudes a tree grows in spring and summer and rests in winter. In this way one **tree ring** forms every year. In good years the ring becomes wide, in dry or cold years narrow. All trees of one area therefore show a similar **pattern** of wide and narrow rings. This pattern is like a barcode of time. The word **dendrochronology** comes from Greek: dendron means tree, chronos time.

The US astronomer **Andrew Ellicott Douglass** is regarded as the founder. At the start of the 20th century he wanted to find out whether solar activity influences the climate. To do so he studied tree rings of trees in Arizona. In doing so he recognised that timber can be dated with the ring patterns. In North America, the **bristlecone pines** supplied long ring series. Some of these trees are over 4,800 years old.

With an **increment borer** you pull a thin **core** out of a living tree without felling it. With old building timber you take cores or slices. The ring widths are measured and compared with known series. If the patterns fit together, you know the age. With **cross-dating** (synchronisation), the patterns of ever older timbers are strung together **overlapping**. If the **waney edge**, that is, the last ring directly under the bark, is preserved, you even know in which year the tree was felled.

In **Swiss archaeology**, dendrochronology is especially important. On many lakes, **pile dwelling settlements** stood in the Neolithic and Bronze Age. Their wooden piles were preserved in the damp ground. Thanks to the tree rings, it is often known **to the exact year** when the houses were built or repaired. The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been UNESCO World Heritage since 2011.

With the **radiocarbon method** (C14), the age of organic material is determined. But this method is not quite exact, because the C14 content of the air has changed over time. Long **tree-ring chronologies** help here: you measure the C14 content in rings of known age and so **calibrate** the method. The central European chronology from **oaks and pines** goes back over **12,000 years**.

gewusst: Musical instruments and paintings on wooden panels are also dated with tree rings.
Narrow tree rings can point to volcanic eruptions, after which it was cooler worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Bark beetles are tiny beetles that live under the bark of trees. Some species can multiply in huge numbers and kill whole spruce forests.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the European spruce bark beetle does the greatest damage.
The European spruce bark beetle attacks mainly spruces.
It makes its tunnels between bark and wood.
The tunnels interrupt the sap flow of the tree.
Healthy spruces defend themselves with resin.
Hot, dry summers favour a mass outbreak.

abschnitte.text: There are many species of bark beetle. In Switzerland the **European spruce bark beetle** does the greatest forest damage. It is only about half a centimetre long, but can multiply in huge numbers. It specialises in the **spruce**. Especially at risk are weakened spruces at lower altitudes.

The beetle bores through the bark. **Between bark and wood** the female makes tunnels and lays eggs there. From there the larvae eat side tunnels. This creates a typical **gallery pattern** that is reminiscent of letters or writing. That is where the German name Buchdrucker, “book printer”, comes from.

Directly under the bark lies a fine layer in which water, sugar and nutrients are transported. The tunnels destroy this layer and interrupt the **sap flow**. The crown is no longer supplied and dries out. From outside you often first recognise a fresh attack by brown **boring dust**, which looks like coffee powder and collects in bark crevices and at the base of the trunk. Later the crown changes colour.

A healthy spruce defends itself with **resin**. If a beetle bores in, sticky resin flows out that glues it fast or pushes it out. In **hot, dry summers**, however, the trees lack water and form less resin. At the same time the beetles develop faster in warmth and manage several generations a year. Storm-felled wood left lying in the forest also offers them plenty of food.

The most important measure is to **fell** infested trees **quickly** and take them out of the forest or debark them. Then the young beetles cannot fly out, and the spread is slowed. With **pheromone traps**, beetles are attracted with scent substances that they use to attract each other. These traps serve mainly to monitor the number of beetles. In the long term, mixed forests with different tree species help.

gewusst: Bark beetles belong to the natural forest and otherwise help to break down dead wood.
From a single infested tree, thousands of new beetles can fly out.

teile.einleitung: Chromoplasts are small pigment carriers in plant cells. They make tomatoes red, carrots orange and many flowers yellow. Their colours attract animals that spread seeds or visit flowers.
wichtigste: Chromoplasts contain mainly carotenoids.
Carotenoids belong to the substance class of the tetraterpenes.
Lycopene makes ripe tomatoes red.
β-carotene makes carrots orange.
When fruit ripens, chromoplasts often arise from chloroplasts.
From β-carotene, humans can make vitamin A.

abschnitte.text: Like chloroplasts, chromoplasts belong to the **plastids**. But they contain no leaf green, rather mainly **carotenoids**. These are yellow, orange and red pigments. Chemically, carotenoids belong to the **tetraterpenes**, molecules with 40 carbon atoms. Chromoplasts are found in fruits, flowers and some roots.

The pigment **lycopene** in the chromoplasts makes **ripe tomatoes red**. **β-carotene** makes **carrots orange**. During **fruit ripening**, chromoplasts often arise **from chloroplasts**. The chlorophyll is broken down, and new pigments are made. That is why a tomato changes from green to red as it ripens.

abschnitte.titel: Not all colours come from plastids
abschnitte.text: Not all plant colours are found in chromoplasts. The blue colour of the **cornflower** comes from **anthocyanins**. These pigments lie dissolved in the **cell sap of the vacuole**, the large storage space of the cell. Many red and violet flowers also owe their colour to anthocyanins. Yellow and orange tones, by contrast, often come from carotenoids in chromoplasts.

The bright colours have an **ecological function**. In fruits they **attract animals**, for example birds. These eat the fruits and excrete the seeds again in another place. In this way the colour helps with **seed dispersal**. In flowers, the colours attract insects that pollinate the flowers.

From **β-carotene**, humans can make **vitamin A**. Vitamin A is important, among other things, for seeing. That is why β-carotene is also called **provitamin A**. Because carotenoids are fat soluble, the body can take them up better if you eat a little oil or butter with them. The lycopene from tomatoes, too, is often taken up better when cooked than raw.

gewusst: The word carotene comes from the carrot, from which this pigment was first obtained.
The orange carrot is a breeding result, and in the past there were mainly violet and yellow varieties.

teile.einleitung: The wood anemone is one of the first flowers of spring. In March and April it covers the floor of many deciduous forests with a white carpet of blossoms, before the trees have their leaves.
wichtigste: The wood anemone usually blooms white, sometimes slightly pink on the outside.
It blooms in March and April.
The flower usually has about 6 petals.
The plant grows about 10 to 25 cm tall.
Underground it has a creeping rootstock.
The wood anemone is poisonous and must not be eaten.

abschnitte.text: The **wood anemone** is a small plant that grows about **10 to 25 cm** tall. Each stem usually bears a single flower with about **6 white petals**. On the outside they are sometimes tinged a delicate pink. Below the flower sit three leaves divided like a hand. In the middle of the flower, yellow stamens shine. The wood anemone belongs to the buttercup family.

abschnitte.titel: A carpet in the spring forest
abschnitte.text: The wood anemone grows mainly in **deciduous forests** and at forest edges, and is widespread in Switzerland too. It blooms in **March and April**, when the trees are still bare. Then a lot of light falls on the forest floor. The plant uses this time to grow and bloom. Later in spring, when the leaves of the trees cast shade, its leaves disappear again.

Underground the wood anemone has a **creeping rootstock**, also called a **rhizome**. In it, it stores nutrients for the next year. That is why it can sprout so quickly in spring. The rootstock grows sideways and branches. From it grow many new shoots. In this way, over time, the large **carpets of blossoms** arise that you see in the forest.

The wood anemone is **poisonous**, like many members of the buttercup family. The plant sap can irritate the skin. If you eat parts of it, you can get stomach ache and nausea. So you should never eat it. It is best anyway to leave the flowers standing in the forest. There, in spring, they are an important food source for the first insects.

gewusst: The German name comes from the fact that the delicate flowers move even in a little wind.
In rain and at night the wood anemone closes its flowers and lets them hang.

teile.einleitung: Emd is an old word from farming. It means the hay from the second cut of a meadow. In Switzerland the word is still in use today.
wichtigste: Emd is hay from the second cut.
It is finer and softer than the first hay.
Emd is made in summer after the first cut.
In many parts of Germany it is called Grummet.
The word Emd is mainly used in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In early summer, farmers mow their meadows for the first time and dry the grass. This is the **hay**, and in Switzerland the work is called **Heuet**. After that the grass grows back from below. If it is mown and dried a second time, it is called **Emd**. Mowing and bringing it in is accordingly called **Emden**.

In the second cut, the grass has **more leaves** and **fewer hard stalks**. That is why Emd is **finer and softer** than the first hay. In winter, when the animals cannot go out to pasture, cows, goats and sheep eat hay and Emd from the store.

abschnitte.titel: Many words for the second cut
abschnitte.text: The word **Emd** is used mainly in **Switzerland** and in the south of the German-speaking area. In many parts of Germany people say **Grummet**. Because good meadows grow back several times a year, there are often further cuts after the Emd.

gewusst: Emd is finer than hay because the regrown grass has more leaves.
The same feed is called Emd in Switzerland and Grummet in many parts of Germany.

teile.einleitung: Spelt is a very old cereal and closely related to wheat. Its grains are surrounded by firm husks. In Switzerland spelt is popular for bread, plaited loaf and pasta.
wichtigste: Spelt is closely related to wheat.
Another German name is Spelz.
Spelt is a very old cereal.
The firm husks protect the grain.
After threshing, the husks still have to be removed.
Spelt harvested unripe and dried is called Grünkern.

abschnitte.text: Spelt is a cereal and **closely related to wheat**. In German it is also called **Spelz**. Spelt is a **very old cereal**: people grew it in Europe thousands of years ago. The plants are often taller than modern wheat. Spelt copes well with cool weather and poor soils, which is why it used to be grown a lot on the Swiss Central Plateau too.

In spelt, each grain is surrounded by **firm husks**, the glumes. The husks **protect the grain** from pests and diseases. In wheat, the grains fall out easily during **threshing**. In spelt, the husks stay on. They then have to be **removed** in a mill in a separate step. This is called dehulling.

If you harvest spelt before it is fully ripe and dry the grains over a fire or in a kiln, **Grünkern**, green spelt, is made. It tastes savoury and slightly nutty. Grünkern is used for soups, patties and stuffings. This way of preserving spelt has existed for centuries.

From **spelt flour** you can bake **bread and plaited loaf**, but also biscuits, pasta and pizza. Spelt bread tastes a little nuttier than wheat bread. In Switzerland, spelt has found many fans again in recent decades. Important: like wheat, spelt contains **gluten**. It is therefore not suitable for people who cannot tolerate gluten.

gewusst: In Switzerland, old spelt not crossed with modern wheat is sold under the name “UrDinkel”.
The husks of spelt are sometimes used as a filling for cushions.

teile.einleitung: A dendrometer is a measuring device for trees. It measures the diameter or circumference of a tree trunk. In this way foresters and researchers can see how strongly a tree is growing and how much wood stands in a forest.
wichtigste: A dendrometer measures the diameter or circumference of a tree trunk.
A band dendrometer is a band with a scale stretched around the trunk.
The traditional measuring device of foresters is called a calliper.
Growth in thickness arises in the cambium.
During the day the trunk shrinks slightly, because water evaporates.
To get from circumference to diameter, you divide by pi, about 3.14.

abschnitte.text: The word **dendrometer** means tree measurer. There are several kinds. The traditional measuring device of foresters is the **calliper**, a large sliding gauge that is laid around the trunk. A **band dendrometer** is a **band with a scale stretched around the trunk**. It stays on the tree, and you read off regularly how much thicker the trunk has become. A **point dendrometer** measures with a fine sensor at one place on the bark, often automatically.

Trees grow not only in height, but also in thickness. Responsible for this is the **cambium**, a thin layer of cells able to divide between wood and bark. Inwards it makes new wood, outwards new bark. This **growth in thickness** is measured by dendrometers. Measurement is usually made at **breast height**, which is 1.3 metres above the ground.

A precise point dendrometer shows something astonishing: the trunk **shrinks a little during the day** and **swells again at night**. The reason is the **water content**. By day the leaves evaporate a lot of water, and the tree also draws water from the trunk. At night it refills its stores. In this way researchers recognise when trees suffer from drought.

If you know the **circumference**, you find the **diameter** by dividing by **pi** (about 3.14). A tree with a circumference of 157 cm therefore has a diameter of **about 50 cm**. The **basal area** is the area of the cross section of the trunk. It is calculated like a circle: pi times radius times radius. With a diameter of 40 cm, the radius is 0.2 m, so the area is **about 0.13 m²**. From such values, foresters estimate how much wood a forest has.

Dendrometers measure how a tree is growing **now**, over days, months or a few years. **Dendrochronology**, by contrast, studies the **sequence of ring widths** over **a long time**, often centuries. The two methods complement each other. Together they show how weather and climate influence the growth of trees.

gewusst: A tree trunk can measurably become thinner and thicker again in the course of a day.
In the Swiss National Forest Inventory, experts regularly measure tens of thousands of trees across the country.

teile.einleitung: Blackberries grow at forest edges, in hedges and along paths. In late summer you can pick the sweet, black berries, but beware of the thorns!
wichtigste: Ripe blackberries are glossy black.
Before ripening they are green and then red.
You pick them mainly in August and September.
A blackberry consists of many small beads.
The blackberry is closely related to the raspberry.
It grows with long, thorny canes.

abschnitte.text: The **blackberry** forms long, **thorny canes**. It grows fast and often forms a dense thicket at forest edges, in hedges and in clearings. In summer it flowers **white to pale pink**. Bees and other insects like to visit the blossoms. From the blossoms the berries later develop.

The berries are first **green**, then **red** and finally **glossy black**. Red blackberries are still sour, and only the black ones taste sweet. They ripen in late summer, mainly in **August and September**. Often you find them into autumn.

A blackberry is an **aggregate fruit**. It consists of many small beads, and in each there is a tiny seed. The blackberry is closely related to the **raspberry**, and both belong to the same plant genus. Unlike the raspberry, the blackberry comes away when picked together with the core in the middle.

From young, dried **blackberry leaves** you brew a mild tea. The leaves often stay green into winter. That is why they are important food for the **roe deer** in winter, when little else grows. In the dense thicket, birds and small animals also find shelter.

gewusst: In Europe there are hundreds of different blackberry species, which even experts find hard to tell apart.
Blackberry canes can take root at the tip and so form new plants.

teile.einleitung: The beech family includes beeches, oaks and sweet chestnuts. They shape many forests of Europe and supply wood, nuts and even cork.
wichtigste: Typical of the beech family is the cupule.
Beeches, oaks and sweet chestnuts belong to it.
The horse chestnut does not belong to it.
Wine barrels are traditionally made of oak wood.
The cork oak supplies cork.
In Ticino, chestnut groves shape the landscape.

abschnitte.text: A typical feature of the **beech family** is the **cupule**. In the oak it encloses the acorn only at the bottom, like a small cup. In the beech the cupule is woody, softly spiny and opens in autumn with four valves. Inside there are usually **two** three-edged beechnuts. In the sweet chestnut the husk is densely covered with sharp spines.

Beeches form a very **dense canopy**. In summer hardly any light reaches the ground, so few plants grow there. Many spring flowers therefore bloom before the beeches come into leaf. In **mast years** beeches and oaks bear huge numbers of fruits. In the past, pigs were driven into these forests to fatten. **Oak wood** is dense and durable. That is why wine has been stored for centuries in oak barrels, the **barriques**, which give the wine flavouring substances.

The **sweet chestnut** also belongs to the beech family. In **Ticino**, chestnut groves, the **selve**, have shaped the landscape for centuries. In southern Switzerland the fruits used to be a staple food. They were called the **“bread of the poor”**. Today they are eaten mainly as hot roast chestnuts in autumn.

The **cork oak** grows in the Mediterranean region. Its thick bark is stripped about every nine years without felling the tree. From it **cork** is made, for example for bottle stoppers, pinboards or floors. The tree then grows new bark.

The **horse chestnut** has similar fruits, but does not belong to the beech family. It is a member of the **soapberry family** and is not closely related to the sweet chestnut. Its fruits are not edible for humans. The hornbeam is not a true beech either, but a member of the birch family.

gewusst: A cork oak can be stripped many times during its life.
In Ticino, chestnuts used to be dried on racks over the fire so that they kept all winter.

teile.einleitung: Bokashi is a method from Japan for fermenting kitchen waste in a bucket. Instead of rotting, the waste turns sour like sauerkraut and later becomes valuable soil.
wichtigste: Bokashi is a Japanese word for fermented organic material.
In the bucket a lactic acid fermentation takes place without air.
Effective Microorganisms are often used.
The leachate is drained off through a tap and used diluted as fertiliser.
Successful bokashi smells sourish.
Only in the soil does the bokashi become humus.

abschnitte.text: The term **bokashi** comes from **Japan**. It refers to fermented organic material. In bokashi, kitchen waste is collected in an airtight bucket. Instead of rotting as in compost, it is **fermented** by bacteria. This works in a flat without a garden too.

In the bucket it is mainly **lactic acid bacteria** that work. They ferment the waste without air, so it is a **fermentation** and not rotting. The **lactic acid** produced lowers the pH. In the acid environment, putrefying bacteria can hardly grow, similar to sauerkraut or silage. That is why successful bokashi smells sourish. A putrid smell shows that something has gone wrong.

Often **Effective Microorganisms** are added, EM for short. This is a mixture mainly of lactic acid bacteria, yeasts and photosynthetic bacteria. You spray it over the waste or sprinkle inoculated bran on it. After every layer you press the waste down firmly so that as little air as possible stays in it.

During fermentation liquid comes out. For this the bokashi bucket has a **tap** at the bottom. The **leachate** must be drained off regularly, otherwise the waste can rot. It contains nutrients and microorganisms. Because it is acid, you pour it as liquid fertiliser only **strongly diluted**.

abschnitte.titel: From the bucket into the soil
abschnitte.text: After a few weeks the bokashi is fully fermented. It is pre-digested, but not yet decomposed, and you can still see the waste. So you must **bury it in soil** or put it on the compost. There soil organisms convert it into **humus** within a few weeks. This produces nutrient-rich soil for garden and balcony.

gewusst: Bokashi originally means roughly “graded” or “blurred”, and today it refers to fermented waste.
Freshly buried bokashi often attracts earthworms especially.

teile.einleitung: Digitoxin is an active substance from the foxglove. It strengthens the power of the heart and has been used as a heart medicine for a long time. At the same time it is very poisonous if you receive too much of it.
wichtigste: Digitoxin comes from plants of the foxglove genus.
It belongs to the cardiac glycosides.
It increases the force with which the heart contracts.
It inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase in the heart muscle cells.
The effective and the poisonous dose lie very close together.
A typical sign of poisoning is seeing yellow or green.

abschnitte.text: The **foxglove** (genus Digitalis) is a tall plant with bell-shaped flowers. The purple foxglove also grows wild in Switzerland, for example at forest edges. All parts of the plant are very poisonous. In the leaves there are active substances that act on the heart. One of them is **digitoxin**. The related active substance **digoxin** is obtained mainly from the **woolly foxglove**.

Digitoxin belongs to the group of active substances called **cardiac glycosides**. A glycoside consists of a sugar part and a part without sugar, the **aglycone**. In digitoxin, the aglycone is a steroid with a five-membered lactone ring. Such substances are called **cardenolides**. The sugar part influences how well the substance is taken up in the body and how long it acts.

abschnitte.titel: How it acts on the heart
abschnitte.text: In the heart muscle cells, digitoxin inhibits a transport protein, the **sodium-potassium ATPase**. As a result, more calcium collects in the cells. Calcium is important for muscle work. The heart **contracts more strongly** and pumps better. It also often beats more slowly. That is why digitoxin was used in heart failure and certain heart rhythm disorders.

With digitoxin, the **effective and the poisonous dose lie very close together**. Even a little too much can be dangerous. That is why doctors often check the level in the blood. Digitoxin is broken down mainly by the **liver** and stays in the body for a long time. **Digoxin**, by contrast, is excreted mainly by the **kidney**. Depending on the patient, the suitable active substance is chosen.

Poisoning with foxglove or an excess of the medicine shows itself through nausea, vomiting and heart rhythm disorders. A striking sign is a visual disturbance: those affected see their surroundings coloured **yellow or green**. Such poisoning is an emergency. Children should never touch foxglove in the garden or in the forest or put it in their mouths.

gewusst: The English doctor William Withering described the effect of foxglove on heart ailments in 1785.
The name Digitalis comes from the Latin word digitus for finger, because the flowers look like thimbles.

teile.einleitung: The C/N ratio states how much carbon a material contains compared with nitrogen. It is important for compost and soil, because microorganisms need both in a good mixture.
wichtigste: C stands for carbon, N for nitrogen.
For compost starting material, about 25 to 30 to 1 is favourable.
Mature compost has roughly 10 to 15 to 1.
Fresh lawn clippings supply a lot of nitrogen.
If the ratio is too narrow, ammonia escapes and there is a sharp smell.
If it is too wide, decomposition is slow.

abschnitte.text: For the **C/N ratio**, you divide the amount of **carbon** (C) by the amount of **nitrogen** (N). An example: a mixture contains 15 kg of carbon and 0.5 kg of nitrogen. Then you calculate 15 divided by 0.5 and get **30 to 1**. A **wide** ratio means a lot of carbon and little nitrogen, as in straw or wood. A **narrow** ratio means a lot of nitrogen, as in fresh grass.

In compost, **microorganisms** such as bacteria and fungi break down the waste. They use the carbon as an energy source. They need the nitrogen to build protein for their own bodies. For the starting material, a ratio of **about 25 to 30 to 1** is therefore favourable. During rotting, a lot of carbon is released as CO2. That is why **mature compost** has only about **10 to 15 to 1** left.

If the ratio is **too narrow**, there is more nitrogen than the microorganisms need. It then escapes as **ammonia**, and there is a sharp smell.
