This happens, for example, with a heap of almost only **fresh lawn clippings**. You improve it by mixing in **carbon-rich, coarse chopped material**. If the ratio is **too wide**, nitrogen is lacking, and decomposition is very slow.

For a mixture, you first add up all the amounts of carbon and all the amounts of nitrogen. An example: material with 30 kg C and 0.5 kg N is mixed with material with 10 kg C and 1 kg N. Together that makes 40 kg C and 1.5 kg N. 40 divided by 1.5 gives **about 27 to 1**. So you must not simply average the two ratios.

The C/N ratio also plays a role in the soil. **Straw** has a very wide ratio. If it is worked fresh into the soil, the microorganisms take **nitrogen from the soil** to break it down. This is then temporarily missing for the plants. This is called **nitrogen immobilisation**. Only when the straw has decomposed is the nitrogen released again.

gewusst: Sawdust can have a C/N ratio of several hundred to 1 and therefore rots very slowly.
Communes in Switzerland that compost green waste also pay attention to a good mixture of lawn clippings and chopped material.

teile.einleitung: A field notebook is a notebook that researchers use outdoors in nature. In it they write down what they see, hear and find right on the spot.
wichtigste: In a field notebook you note observations directly in the field.
Every observation starts with the date and place.
With coordinates, a find spot can be given very precisely.
It is best to write in pencil, because it does not run in the rain.
Small sketches record features such as leaf shapes accurately.
A collection number links notes to collected plants in the herbarium.

abschnitte.text: The word “field” here does not mean only a farmer's field, but any work outdoors in nature. A **field notebook** is a sturdy notebook that you take along on trips. Biologists, geologists or archaeologists write down in it what they observe. This way no information is lost before you are back home. Many field notebooks are small so that they fit in a jacket pocket.

It is best to write with a **pencil**. It does not run when wet and stays readable for many years. Ink, on the other hand, can smudge in the rain. Some field notebooks have special paper that repels water. A sharpener, a ruler and a magnifying glass are also handy.

Every observation begins with the **date and place**. Without these details you cannot place it later. A find spot is described especially precisely with **coordinates**, for example from a phone or from the national map. Then come details such as species, number, time, weather and habitat. You write everything down **straight away on the spot**, because memories quickly become inaccurate.

Often you draw small **sketches** of leaves, flowers or tracks. When you draw, you look more closely. A sketch can also show what stays unclear in a photo. Anyone who collects plants for a **herbarium** gives each specimen a **collection number**. The same number appears in the field notebook, so later you know which notes belong to which plant.

The naturalist **Charles Darwin** travelled around the world on the ship **HMS Beagle** from 1831 to 1836. On the way he filled many notebooks with observations of animals, plants and rocks. These records later formed the basis for important discoveries. Old field notebooks are valuable even today, because they show what nature used to look like.

gewusst: Darwin's notebooks are still kept today and read by researchers.
With old field notebooks you can find out whether a plant or animal has become rarer in a place.

teile.einleitung: The Bödmerenwald in the Muotatal in the canton of Schwyz is one of the largest primeval-like spruce forests of the Alps. It grows on fissured limestone, under which hides the huge cave system Hölloch.
wichtigste: The Bödmerenwald lies in the Muotatal in the canton of Schwyz.
The most important tree species is the spruce.
The forest grows on karst of limestone with many karren.
Under the forest lies the cave system Hölloch.
Because of the difficult terrain it was hardly ever used.
Young spruces often germinate on rotting tree trunks.

abschnitte.text: The **Bödmerenwald** lies high above the **Muotatal** in the canton of **Schwyz**. It is shaped mainly by the **spruce**. Many trees are very old, and dead trunks stay lying or standing. Such a forest, in which humans have hardly intervened, is called a **primeval forest**. In central Europe only a few such forests remain. Large parts of the Bödmerenwald are today protected as a reserve.

The ground consists of **karst**, that is, of **limestone** that is dissolved by water. Rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone. This creates channels and furrows called **karren**. Between them there are fissures, holes and small hollows. The water drains quickly into the depths. The soil is thin in many places, and very wet in others.

Under the Bödmerenwald lies the **Hölloch**, one of the longest cave systems in the world. The water that drains away in the forest flows through this labyrinth of passages. Over many decades, researchers have discovered and surveyed new parts there again and again. Forest and cave belong to the same karst landscape. What happens above therefore also influences the water in the depths.

abschnitte.titel: Why the forest stayed so wild
abschnitte.text: In the **fissured karst terrain** it was very difficult to carry wood away. That is why the Bödmerenwald was **hardly ever used economically**. Young spruces here germinate especially often **on rotting tree trunks**, because the ground is otherwise too thin or too wet. That is why some trees stand in a straight row where a trunk once lay. On old spruces hangs the rare, very long beard lichen **angel hair**. It grows only in clean air in old forests.

gewusst: Angel hair can hang down from the branches as a long, pale green thread, almost like tinsel.
Because the forest is so undisturbed, researchers there study how a mountain forest develops without human intervention.

teile.einleitung: Caspar Bauhin was a physician and botanist in Basel. He collected the plant knowledge of his time in a large catalogue and in doing so anticipated an idea that later made Carl Linnaeus famous.
wichtigste: Caspar Bauhin taught anatomy and botany at the University of Basel.
His family came to Basel as Reformed religious refugees.
His main work of 1623 is called “Pinax theatri botanici”.
In it he listed about 6000 plant species.
He already often used two-part plant names.
The Bauhin valve between the small and large intestine bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Caspar Bauhin was born in **Basel** in **1560**. His family came from France. Because it was **Reformed**, it was persecuted there and came to Basel as **religious refugees**. His father was a doctor. Caspar’s older brother **Johann Bauhin** also became an important botanist. The two brothers are regarded as important plant researchers of their time.

Caspar Bauhin studied medicine, among other places in Italy and France. After that he returned to Basel. At the **University of Basel** he taught **anatomy and botany**. Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body. As a doctor he examined the body very precisely. The **Bauhin valve** is named after him, a **valve between the small and large intestine** that prevents the contents of the gut from flowing back.

In Bauhin’s time, many plants had several names, depending on the book and the country. This made it hard to understand one another. Bauhin sorted these names in his main work **“Pinax theatri botanici”** of **1623**. In it he listed **about 6000 plant species**. For many years the book was an important reference work for botanists all over Europe.

Bauhin named many plants with **two-part names**: a genus name and an addition for the species. In doing so he anticipated an idea that **Carl Linnaeus** later fixed. Bauhin also already distinguished clearly between genus and species. In honour of the Bauhin brothers, a plant genus is called **Bauhinia**. Its leaves are **two-lobed**, like two halves grown together, fitting the two brothers.

gewusst: The name “Pinax” comes from Greek and means something like tablet or list.
In Basel, Bauhin built up a large collection of dried plants, a so-called herbarium.

teile.einleitung: Many blossoms smell sweet, spicy or sometimes even unpleasant. With their **flower scent** they attract insects. The scent tells them: here there is nectar or pollen.
wichtigste: Flower scent attracts insects that pollinate the blossom.
The scent shows insects that there is food.
Bees smell with their antennae.
Bees remember good blossoms by scent and colour.
Blossoms for moths often smell strongly only in the evening.
In warm weather you smell flower scent especially well.

abschnitte.text: Insects have no nose like ours. **Bees** smell with their **antennae**, on which many smell cells sit. With them they perceive flower scents very well. The scent tells them: here there is **nectar** or **pollen**. Bees learn quickly. They remember the **scent** and **colour** of blossoms that have a lot of nectar, and fly back to them deliberately.

Many blossoms that are visited by **moths** smell strongly only **in the evening**. That is when these moths are out and about. An example is the **honeysuckle**, a climbing plant with long, narrow flower tubes. Moths fetch the nectar deep out of the tubes with their long tongues.

Not all blossoms smell pleasant. Some smell of **rotting meat**. With this they attract **flies**, which otherwise feed on carrion. The flies carry pollen from blossom to blossom as they do so. A native example is the **lords-and-ladies**, which attracts insects with its smell.

**Bumblebees** leave a faint **scent trail** when visiting a blossom. Other bumblebees smell it and fly on, because this blossom is empty for the moment. This way they save time. For us humans a garden smells especially strong on **warm days**. Warmth lets the **scent substances** rise better into the air.

gewusst: Perfume is made from flower scent. For a little rose oil, huge amounts of rose blossoms are needed.
The titan arum from Sumatra has one of the largest flower clusters in the world and stinks strongly of carrion.

teile.einleitung: Strawberries are sweet, red fruits that grow on small plants close to the ground. In Switzerland, strawberry season begins in early summer.
wichtigste: Ripe strawberries are bright red, unripe ones are green or white.
The plants are small, and the fruits lie almost on the ground.
Strawberry flowers are white with a yellow centre.
Swiss strawberries are available mainly in May, June and July.
For plant scientists, the strawberry is not a true berry.
Strawberries hardly ripen any further after picking.

abschnitte.text: The strawberry plant is small and stays **close to the ground**. It has **white flowers** with a yellow centre. The fruits later develop from them. At first the strawberries are **green or white**, and when ripe they are **bright red**. The plant forms long runners on which new small plants grow.

Many gardeners lay **straw** under the strawberry plants. This way the fruits do not lie on damp soil, stay clean and **rot less**. **Slugs** are a problem. They creep to the strawberries at night and eat holes in them. That is why gardeners protect their plants. Strawberries **hardly ripen any further** after picking. They are picked only when they are completely red.

Strawberries from Switzerland are available outdoors mainly in **early summer**, that is, in May, June and July. That is strawberry season. On some fields you can pick the fruits yourself. At the edge of the woods, **wild strawberries** also grow. They are much smaller than garden strawberries but taste very aromatic.

Although it is called one, the strawberry is **not a true berry** for plant scientists. It is an **aggregate fruit**. The red flesh is the swollen flower base. The actual fruits are the many small yellow **nutlets** on the surface. Only in everyday language do we call the strawberry a berry.

gewusst: The little dots on a strawberry are really tiny fruits.
Our large garden strawberries arose from a cross between two American strawberry species.

teile.einleitung: Edaphon is the technical term for all the living things that live in the soil. It includes tiny bacteria just as much as earthworms and moles. Together they make the soil fertile.
wichtigste: Edaphon means the whole of the soil organisms.
The term goes back to the biologist Raoul Heinrich Francé.
A handful of soil contains more living things than there are people.
Soil animals are divided by size into micro-, meso-, macro- and megafauna.
Actinomycetes are responsible for the typical smell of fresh earth.
Earthworms form stable clay-humus complexes.

abschnitte.text: The **edaphon** includes all organisms in the soil: **bacteria, fungi, algae and soil animals**. The term goes back to the biologist **Raoul Heinrich Francé**. In a handful of fertile soil live **billions** of microorganisms. That is more living things than there are people on Earth.

Soil animals are divided up according to their size. The **microfauna** includes single-celled creatures such as ciliates and tiny roundworms. **Springtails and mites** are about 0.2 to 2 millimetres in size and belong to the **mesofauna**. Earthworms, woodlice and millipedes belong to the **macrofauna**. The largest soil dwellers, such as the **mole** and the vole, make up the **megafauna**.

**Litter decomposers** such as woodlice and millipedes eat dead plant parts and break them into small pieces. This makes the surface of the fallen leaves larger. After that, **fungi and bacteria** can break down what is left more quickly. In the end **humus** is formed, and the nutrients are available to the plants again.

abschnitte.titel: Earthworms and the smell of earth
abschnitte.text: Earthworms eat soil and plant remains and mix them in their gut. Their droppings contain stable **clay-humus complexes**. These give the soil a crumbly structure. The typical **smell of fresh earth**, especially after rain, comes from **actinomycetes**, also called ray fungi. They are bacteria that make the scent substance **geosmin**.

With a **Berlese funnel** you can make small soil animals visible. A lamp warms the soil sample from above. The animals flee from the warmth and light downwards and fall into a collecting container. That way you can count and identify them under a magnifying glass.

gewusst: The smell of rain comes partly from bacteria in the soil.
In a handful of soil live more living things than there are people on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Beechnuts are the small nuts of the beech. In autumn they lie by the thousand in the forest and are important food for many animals.
wichtigste: Beechnuts grow on the European beech.
They sit in a woody husk with soft spines.
Usually two beechnuts lie in one husk.
Many raw beechnuts can cause stomach ache.
In a mast year beeches bear especially many fruits.
In some winters brambling come to Switzerland by the million.

abschnitte.text: Beechnuts grow on the **European beech**, the most common broadleaved tree in Swiss forests. Its wood is slightly reddish, hence the German name Rotbuche. The **hornbeam**, despite its name, is not a true beech at all. Ripe beechnuts have a smooth, **glossy brown** shell with three edges. Inside is a pale kernel.

The beechnuts grow in a **woody husk** with soft spines. When it is ripe in autumn, it springs open with **four valves**. Usually **two beechnuts** lie in it. After that they fall to the ground, and the empty husks often stay lying for a long time.

Raw beechnuts contain substances that in larger amounts can cause **stomach ache** and nausea. A few are no problem, but you should not eat many raw. **Roasted** they are easier to digest and taste nutty. Because they contain a lot of fat, **cooking oil** used to be pressed from them, especially in times of need.

Beeches do not bear the same number of fruits every year. In a **mast year**, especially many beechnuts hang on the trees. Then squirrels, mice, wild boar and birds find plenty of food. In such winters **brambling** come from the north to Switzerland by the million. They spend the night together at large roosts, an impressive spectacle.

gewusst: At some roosts in Switzerland, several million brambling have been counted at the same time.
The name “mast year” comes from the fact that in the past pigs were driven into the forests to feed.

teile.einleitung: Downy mildew is one of the most dangerous diseases of the grapevine. It was introduced from North America in the 19th century and threatens the harvest especially in wet summers.
wichtigste: The organism that causes it is called Plasmopara viticola, and in winegrowing it is also called Peronospora.
It belongs to the oomycetes and is not a true fungus.
It came to Europe from North America in the 19th century.
Typical are yellowish “oil spots” on the upper side of the leaf.
Wet leaves are needed for an infection.
Bordeaux mixture was developed against it in the Bordeaux region.

abschnitte.text: Downy mildew of the vine is caused by **Plasmopara viticola**. In winegrowing the disease is also called **Peronospora**. It attacks all green parts of the grapevine. It belongs to the **oomycetes**, like Phytophthora. Oomycetes look like fungi but are not true fungi. That is why remedies against fungi often work poorly against it.

The organism comes from **North America**. In the 19th century it probably reached Europe with American vines. These had been imported to protect the vineyards against **phylloxera**. The European vines had no defence against the new organism. The disease therefore spread quickly.

The organism forms **zoospores**, which can swim with small flagella. They swim in a **film of water** to the **stomata** on the underside of the leaf and enter there. Without wet leaves this does not work. In **rainy summers** the danger is therefore particularly great. On the upper side of the leaf, an early infection can be recognised by yellowish **“oil spots”**. On the underside, a white carpet of spores forms in damp conditions.

If the grapes are infected late, the berries turn greyish-brown, become leathery and shrivel. Such **leather berries** are lost for wine. In the **Bordeaux** region in the 19th century, a mixture of **copper sulphate and lime** was developed. This **Bordeaux mixture** was one of the first effective plant protection products of all. It goes back to the botanist **Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet**.

gewusst: Bordeaux mixture often colours vine leaves slightly blue.
New grape varieties that are more resistant to fungal diseases are also grown in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Colchicine is a strong plant poison. It is found mainly in the autumn crocus, a pretty plant that blooms in autumn on damp meadows. In tiny amounts, however, colchicine is also a medicine.
wichtigste: Colchicine is the poison of the autumn crocus.
The genus Colchicum is named after the region of Colchis on the Black Sea.
Colchicine blocks cell division.
In a small dose it helps as a medicine against gout.
The symptoms of poisoning begin only after hours.
In hay the poison is preserved and is dangerous for cows too.

abschnitte.text: The **autumn crocus** blooms in autumn with pale violet flowers on meadows. No leaves are seen at that time. During flowering the **ovary** lies deep in the ground, well protected from the cold. Only in spring do the leaves and the seed capsule appear above the ground. The scientific name **Colchicum** recalls the ancient region of **Colchis** on the Black Sea. All parts of the plant are poisonous.

In cells, colchicine acts on fine protein threads that pull the chromosomes apart during cell division. Without these threads the cell cannot divide properly: colchicine **blocks cell division**. Tissues that renew themselves often are especially affected, for example the lining of the gut. That is why poisoning first causes stomach ache, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Typical of colchicine poisoning is that the symptoms begin **only after hours**. That is why it is often noticed late. Poisoning is very dangerous and must be treated in hospital at once. In spring, people sometimes confuse the leaves with **wild garlic**. Wild garlic smells strongly of garlic, the autumn crocus does not. In Switzerland, the emergency number 145 of Tox Info Suisse helps if poisoning is suspected.

In a very small, precisely measured dose, colchicine is used as a medicine, mainly against **gout**. In gout, crystals are deposited in the joints, and painful inflammation arises. Colchicine slows this inflammation. Because the effective amount and the poisonous amount lie close together, it may be taken only on a doctor’s instructions.

abschnitte.titel: Danger in hay and use in breeding
abschnitte.text: The poison is **preserved when dried**. If there is autumn crocus in hay, cows and horses can become ill. On the pasture, the animals usually avoid the fresh plant. **Plant breeders** use colchicine in the lab: because cell division stops but the chromosomes still double, plants with **more sets of chromosomes** arise. Such plants are often bigger and stronger.

gewusst: The autumn crocus blooms in autumn, but its seeds ripen only in the following spring and summer.
Tox Info Suisse in Zurich can be reached around the clock on the number 145.

teile.einleitung: The Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de la Ville de Genève are the botanical garden and botanical research institute of the City of Geneva. They are among the most important institutions of this kind in the world.
wichtigste: The institution was founded in 1817.
The founder was the Geneva botanist Augustin Pyramus de Candolle.
Since 1904 the garden has stood at its present site on Lake Geneva.
The garden is about 28 hectares in size.
The herbarium has over 6 million specimens.
The institution belongs to the City of Geneva.

abschnitte.text: The Geneva botanist **Augustin Pyramus de Candolle** founded the botanical garden in **1817**. De Candolle was one of the most important plant researchers of his time and worked on a great system for ordering all plants. The first garden lay in the middle of the city, in today’s Parc des Bastions. In **1904** the garden moved to its present site on the shore of **Lake Geneva**.

The name has two parts. The **Jardin** is the garden that everyone can visit. The **Conservatoire** is the part with the **herbarium**, the library and the research. A herbarium is a collection of pressed and dried plants. Each plant is glued onto a sheet and labelled with place of finding, date and name. Such a sheet is called a **herbarium specimen**.

The Geneva herbarium has **over 6 million** herbarium specimens and is among the largest in the world. Researchers from many countries use it to compare plant species and describe them anew. In addition there is a large botanical library. In this way the collection helps to understand how many plant species there are and where they grow.

The garden is about **28 hectares** in size, which is about 40 football pitches. There are greenhouses with tropical plants, a rock garden with mountain plants, an arboretum with trees and beds with useful and medicinal plants. Entry to the garden is free. The institution belongs to the **City of Geneva** and also looks after the protection of rare plants.

gewusst: De Candolle introduced the word “taxonomy” for the study of the ordering of living things.
The herbarium also holds very old specimens that researchers collected over 200 years ago.

teile.einleitung: Earth's rotation is the turning of the Earth around its own axis. In about 24 hours the Earth turns once around itself, and this creates day and night. Although we travel along very fast, we feel nothing of it.
wichtigste: The Earth turns once around itself in about 24 hours.
That is why there is day and night.
The Earth turns from west to east.
That is why the sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
At the equator the ground moves at about 1,670 kilometres per hour.
The rotation is very slowly braked by the tides.
The physicist Léon Foucault made the Earth's rotation visible with a pendulum in 1851.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns like a spinning top around an imaginary line, the **Earth's axis**. This axis runs through the North Pole and the South Pole. One full turn takes about 24 hours. Besides its orbit around the sun, Earth's rotation is the most important movement of our planet.

The sun can only ever light up half of the Earth. On the side facing the sun it is **day**, on the other side it is **night**. Because of the rotation, Switzerland moves once a day through the light and once through the shadow. Because the Earth turns from west to east, we see the sun rise in the east. In reality, then, it is not the sun that moves across the sky, but we who are turning.

abschnitte.titel: How fast does the Earth turn?
abschnitte.text: At the **equator**, a point covers around 40,000 kilometres in 24 hours. That is about 1,670 kilometres per hour, faster than an airliner. In Switzerland, which lies further north, it is still about 1,100 kilometres per hour. At the poles, by contrast, you simply turn on the spot. We feel nothing because the air, the houses and we ourselves all move along evenly.

A solar day lasts 24 hours, measured from noon to noon. Relative to the distant stars, however, the Earth turns once in about **23 hours and 56 minutes**. Because it is not noon everywhere at the same time, the world has been divided into **time zones**. When it is noon in Switzerland, it is only six o'clock in the morning in New York.

In 1851 the French physicist **Léon Foucault** hung up a long pendulum in Paris. Over the course of the hours, the direction of its swing seemed to turn slowly. In truth, the Earth was turning away beneath the pendulum. Such **Foucault pendulums** can be seen today in many museums. Because of Earth's rotation, hurricanes in the northern hemisphere also always turn anticlockwise.

The pull of the Moon creates ebb and flow and in doing so brakes the Earth very slightly. As a result, days are getting longer over time, by about two thousandths of a second per century. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day was therefore much shorter than today. For accurate clocks, a **leap second** is therefore added now and then.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole around which the Earth turns.
The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth.
An area of the Earth in which the same time applies.
A long pendulum that makes the rotation of the Earth visible.

gewusst: At the equator, Earth's rotation carries us along faster than a passenger aeroplane.
If the Earth did not rotate, a day on Earth would last half a year and a night just as long.

teile.einleitung: Renewable energies are sources of energy that renew themselves again and again and are not used up. Examples are solar power, wind power and hydropower. They help to protect the climate because they give off hardly any gases that harm the climate.
wichtigste: Renewable energy sources are, for example, solar or wind power.
They do not run out, because nature keeps supplying them.
Renewable energies also include hydropower, wood and geothermal heat.
In Switzerland, more than half of the electricity comes from hydropower.
Oil, natural gas and coal, by contrast, are not renewable.
Renewable energies give off hardly any carbon dioxide when in operation.
Solar panels on roofs are becoming more and more common in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Renewable energies come from sources that refill themselves by themselves in a short time. The sun shines anew every day, the wind blows again and again, and rain fills rivers and reservoirs. The opposite are **fossil fuels** such as oil, natural gas and coal. These were formed over millions of years and will run out at some point. When burned, they also release a lot of **carbon dioxide**, which strengthens climate change.

With **solar cells**, sunlight can be turned directly into electricity, which is called photovoltaics. Solar collectors on roofs, by contrast, heat water for showers and heating. **Wind turbines** have large rotor blades that are turned by the wind and drive a generator. So far there are only a few wind turbines in Switzerland, for example on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura.

Switzerland is a water tower with many mountains, rivers and glaciers. That is why **hydropower** is its most important source of electricity, supplying about six out of every ten kilowatt hours. In reservoirs in the Alps, water is collected and led through pipes to turbines. The dam of **Grande Dixence** in Valais is 285 metres high and is among the highest in the world.

**Wood** is also a renewable energy, as long as no more trees are felled than grow back. **Biogas** can be made from liquid manure, food scraps and green waste. With **heat pumps**, heat is taken from the ground, the groundwater or the air to heat houses. In Switzerland, heat pumps are being installed in many new houses.

Renewable energies protect the climate and make a country less dependent on oil and gas imports. However, the sun does not shine at night, and the wind does not always blow equally strongly. That is why **storage** is needed, for example batteries or pumped-storage power stations, which pump water up into a higher lake when there is surplus electricity. Landscape protection is also an issue, because wind turbines and dams change nature.

In 2017 the Swiss electorate approved the **Energy Strategy 2050**. It provides for using more renewable energy, saving energy and not building any new nuclear power stations. By 2050 Switzerland wants to emit no greenhouse gases on balance. Every family can help, for example with solar panels on the roof or by saving energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy from oil, natural gas or coal, which were formed millions of years ago.
Technology with which solar cells turn sunlight into electricity.
A wheel with blades that is turned by water, steam or wind.
A device that uses heat from air, ground or water for heating.

gewusst: In one hour the sun sends more energy to the Earth than all people together use in a year.
Hundreds of years ago, people were already using renewable energy, for example with water mills and windmills.

teile.einleitung: The acorn is the fruit of the oak. In autumn, many brown acorns with their small cups fall onto the forest floor. For animals they are an important food, and on Swiss Jass playing cards they are even a suit.
wichtigste: The acorn is the fruit of the oak and counts as a nut.
Ripe acorns are brown, young ones are green.
Raw acorns are very bitter because of tannins.
In the past, pigs were driven into the forest to fatten on acorns.
Acorns are a suit on German-Swiss Jass cards.
A young oak grows from a sprouting acorn.

abschnitte.text: In botany the acorn is a **nut**: it has a hard shell and a **seed** inside. At the bottom it sits in a small **cup**. Young acorns are **green**, and in autumn they turn **brown** and shiny. In the **sessile oak**, the acorns sit close to the twig almost without a stalk. In the pedunculate oak they hang on long stalks.

If an acorn falls on good soil, a small **seedling** can grow in spring. From it a young oak develops. Oaks grow slowly. An oak often bears its first acorns only after **40 years or more**. Animals such as jays and squirrels hide acorns. Forgotten acorns can sprout.

Acorns contain a lot of **tannins**. These taste very **bitter** and are bad for the stomach when raw. That is why we do not eat them raw. For many animals, though, they are valuable food. In the past, farmers drove their **pigs** into the oak wood in autumn. This was called **acorn mast**.

In hard times, when there was no real coffee, acorns were roasted. They were used to brew a **coffee substitute**. The **German-Swiss Jass cards** have the suits **acorns, bells, roses and shields**. French cards, by contrast, have hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades.

gewusst: An oak often has to be decades old before it bears its first acorn.
Botanically speaking, the acorn is a nut.

teile.einleitung: Ethylene is a plant hormone that makes fruit ripen. The special thing about it is that it is a gas and can therefore spread through the air from fruit to fruit.
wichtigste: Ethylene, also called ethene, has the formula C2H4 and is a gas at room temperature.
Ripe apples give off a lot of ethylene and make other fruits ripen faster.
Climacteric fruits such as bananas and tomatoes keep ripening after harvest.
Strawberries hardly ripen further after picking.
In plants, ethylene is made from the precursor ACC.
The substance 1-MCP blocks ethylene and keeps apples crisp for longer.

abschnitte.text: Almost all **plant hormones** are dissolved substances. **Ethylene** is different: it is a simple **gaseous hydrocarbon** with the formula C2H4. That is why it can spread through the air to other parts of plants and to fruits. In the plant it is made from the amino acid **methionine** in several steps. The direct precursor is called **1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid**, or **ACC** for short. The enzyme ACC oxidase releases ethylene from it.

Some fruits keep ripening after harvest. They are called **climacteric fruits**, for example **bananas, apples and tomatoes**. As they ripen, their respiration and ethylene production rise. That is why they can be harvested unripe and left to ripen later. A household trick: if you put hard **kiwis** in a bag with a ripe **apple**, they ripen faster. The apple gives off ethylene, which builds up in the bag. **Strawberries**, on the other hand, are not climacteric and do not become sweeter after picking.

Ethylene also affects growth. Pea seedlings that are exposed to ethylene in the dark show the **triple response**. They grow **shorter**, their shoot becomes **thicker**, and they grow **sideways** instead of straight up. This way a seedling can work its way around obstacles in the soil.

In fruit stores, **1-methylcyclopropene**, or 1-MCP for short, is used. It binds firmly to the ethylene receptors. The fruits no longer sense the ethylene, ripen more slowly and stay crisp for longer. The other way round, farming uses the substance **ethephon**. It breaks down in plant tissue and gives off ethylene as it does so. In this way you can achieve, for example, even ripening, or trigger flowering in **pineapples**.

In the 19th century, street lamps were run on **town gas**. It was observed that plants near leaking pipes stunted and lost their leaves early. The Russian botanist **Dimitri Neljubow** found out from pea seedlings that the ethylene in the town gas was the cause. He reported on this in 1901.

gewusst: A single overripe fruit in a fruit bowl can make the others ripen faster.
On plantations, pineapples are made to flower all at the same time with ethylene.

teile.einleitung: Ellenberg indicator values are numbers that show under which conditions a plant species likes to grow best. With them, you can read from the plants in a place how bright, damp or nutrient-rich it is. They go back to the German botanist Heinz Ellenberg.
wichtigste: Indicator values describe how plants behave in relation to habitat factors.
Most values range from 1 to 9, the moisture value from 1 to 12.
L stands for light, F for moisture, R for reaction and N for nitrogen.
The stinging nettle has the nitrogen value 9.
An “x” means that the species is indifferent.
For Switzerland, Elias Landolt drew up his own indicator values.

abschnitte.text: Every plant species has preferences. Indicator values show under which conditions a species has its **centre of gravity** in the field. They describe its behaviour **under competition**, that is, as it actually occurs in nature. **Heinz Ellenberg** published indicator values for the plants of central Europe in 1974.

The **light value L** ranges from 1 for deep-shade plants to 9 for full-light plants. There are further numbers for temperature, continentality, **moisture F**, **reaction R** (acidic or basic) and **nitrogen N**. Most of them range from **1 to 9**. For the moisture value there are also levels 10 to 12 for **plants of changing water levels and water plants**. An **“x”** means that the species is indifferent for this factor and does not indicate it.

The **stinging nettle** has the nitrogen value **9**. It grows lushly near manure heaps and on over-fertilised woodland edges. High N values point to **over-fertilisation**. The **bilberry** has a low reaction value. It grows on **acidic** soils poor in bases, for example under spruces. Many woodland floor plants have **low light values**.

The Swiss botanist **Elias Landolt** presented his own indicator values for the Swiss flora in **1977**. In **2010** the expanded **“Flora indicativa”** appeared. In Switzerland it is often used for nature conservation and research.

Often, the **mean** of the indicator values of all species is calculated for an area. This is **disputed** in terms of method, because indicator values are **ordinal**. They are ranks, and the gaps between the levels are not all the same size. In practice, though, means are still often used as an approximation.

gewusst: Where many stinging nettles grow, the soil is usually very rich in nitrogen.
For the moisture value there are extra levels for plants that live in water.

teile.einleitung: Percentage cover is a measure from plant science. It shows how much of an area a plant species covers. Experts use it to describe and compare meadows, forests and other habitats.
wichtigste: Percentage cover states what share of the area a species covers when seen vertically from above.
Because plants overlap in layers, the sum can be over 100 per cent.
A widely used scale comes from the Chur botanist Josias Braun-Blanquet.
In this scale, level 3 means a cover of 25 to 50 per cent.
The symbol “r” stands for very rare, single individuals.
Estimated values differ from person to person.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you look **vertically from above** at a meadow. The **percentage cover** of a species states what **share of the area** its leaves and stems cover. It is usually given as a percentage. If clover covers a quarter of the area, it has a cover of 25 per cent. Because plants **overlap in layers**, for example grasses under bushes and trees, the **sum** of all species can be **over 100 per cent**.

The botanist **Josias Braun-Blanquet** was born in **Chur** in 1884. He developed a method for describing plant communities. It includes a scale for **cover and abundance**. The levels are: **r** for very rare, only single individuals, **+** for a few plants, **1** for under 5 per cent, **2** for 5 to 25 per cent, **3** for **25 to 50 per cent**, **4** for 50 to 75 per cent and **5** for over 75 per cent. This scale is still used in many countries today.

Percentage cover is usually **estimated** by eye. That is quick. A known weakness, however, is that **different people estimate differently**. One person sees 30 per cent, another 45 per cent. That is why experts practise estimating and compare their results. For precise studies, measuring methods are used in addition.

In a **point survey**, for example, you lay a frame with 100 fixed points over the area. At each point you note which species is hit. If a species is hit at 35 points, its cover is **35 per cent**. In forests you measure the **canopy closure**, that is, how densely the tree crowns cover the sky. For this you photograph vertically **upwards** with a **fisheye lens**. A computer then calculates the share of the sky that is covered by leaves.

gewusst: Braun-Blanquet later lived in Montpellier in France and founded a well-known research station there.
His method is still often simply called the “Braun-Blanquet method”.

teile.einleitung: The pea is a small, round, green vegetable that grows in a pod. It tastes sweetish and has even played an important role in science and in a fairy tale.
wichtigste: Peas grow in an elongated green pod.
Fresh peas are green, dried ones can also be yellow.
The pea is the seed of the pea plant.
In Switzerland, peas that are eaten with the pod are called Kefen (mangetout).
Gregor Mendel used peas to discover rules of heredity.
Peas are often bought frozen.

abschnitte.text: The pea plant is a climbing plant with white or violet flowers. From the flowers grow elongated green **pods**. Inside them, the small round **peas** lie in a row. Each pea is really a **seed**. If you put it in the ground, a new plant grows from it. The pea belongs to the **legumes**, like beans and lentils.

Fresh peas are **green** and taste sweetish. Dried peas can also be **yellow**, and are used, for example, to cook pea soup. Many peas are **frozen** straight after harvesting. That way they stay fresh and green for a long time. In Switzerland you also find **Kefen**, or mangetout. These are flat pea pods with a tender shell that is eaten whole.

The monk **Gregor Mendel** carried out famous experiments with peas in the 19th century. In the monastery garden in Brno he crossed many pea plants with different features, for example yellow and green peas or round and wrinkled ones. He counted exactly which features appeared in the offspring. In this way he found rules for how features are **inherited**. Today they are called **Mendel's laws**.

In the fairy tale **“The Princess and the Pea”** by **Hans Christian Andersen**, a queen places a single pea under many mattresses. Only a real princess, she believes, will feel the little pea through them. In the morning the girl complains that she slept badly. This shows that she is a real princess.

gewusst: Peas are among the oldest crop plants of humans.
Pea plants improve the soil, because bacteria on their roots fix nitrogen from the air.

teile.einleitung: The boreal zone is a huge belt of coniferous forest in the north of the Earth. This forest is also called taiga. It is the largest continuous forest in the world.
wichtigste: The boreal coniferous forest is also called taiga, using a Russian word.
It lies in North America, Europe and Asia.
Russia has the largest share of it.
Typical trees are spruces, pines, larches and birches.
The winters are long and cold, and the growing season lasts only a few months.
The moose is a typical animal of the taiga.

abschnitte.text: The **boreal zone** stretches as a broad belt across the northern hemisphere, through **North America**, **Europe** and **Asia**. The word “boreal” means northern. The Russian name **taiga** stands for the huge coniferous forests of the north, especially in Siberia. **Russia** has the largest share, because a large part of its area is covered with this forest. In the southern hemisphere there is no boreal zone, because there is hardly any land at the matching latitudes.

The winters are long and very cold, the summers short and often quite warm. Plants can therefore grow only **a few months** a year. In the cold, soil organisms and fungi work very slowly. Fallen needles therefore hardly decompose, and a thick layer of needles and **raw humus** builds up on the ground. The soils are often acid and low in nutrients.

The taiga is shaped by **conifers** such as spruces, pines and larches. They tolerate long, cold winters and short summers. The narrow **cone shape** and the flexible, downward-sloping branches let the snow slide off, so the branches break less often. Alongside grow birches, poplars and willows. The **birch**, with its white bark, is very frost-hardy and grows fast on open ground, for example after forest fires.

The **moose** is the largest deer in the world and typical of the northern coniferous forest. It eats twigs, buds and water plants and copes well with cold. In the taiga there also live brown bears, wolves, lynxes and many birds. Some birds migrate south in autumn, others stay all winter.

**Forest fires** are part of the natural cycle in the taiga. After a fire, birches and poplars grow first, later conifers again. In the soils and bogs of the boreal zone a great deal of **carbon** is stored. That is why this forest is also important for the climate of the whole Earth.

gewusst: The larch is a conifer that drops its needles in autumn.
The boreal zone is the largest forest area on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The oak is a mighty broad-leaved tree that can live for many hundreds of years. You recognise it by its lobed leaves and by the acorns that fall to the ground in autumn. Since ancient times it has been regarded as a symbol of strength and endurance.
wichtigste: The fruits of the oak are called acorns.
Oaks can live for many hundreds of years.
The edge of an oak leaf has rounded lobes.
Wild boar, squirrels and jays like to eat acorns.
In Switzerland the pedunculate oak and the sessile oak are the most common.
Oak wood is very hard and is used for furniture, floors and wine barrels.
Particularly many different species of insects live on an oak.

abschnitte.text: Oaks can grow more than 30 metres tall and have a thick trunk with deeply furrowed **bark**. Their leaves have an edge with rounded **lobes**, by which they are easy to recognise. The crown of old oaks is broad and gnarled, with thick, curved branches. In autumn the leaves turn brown, and on young oaks they often stay on the tree until winter.

The fruits of the oak are called **acorns** and sit in a small cup. In the **pedunculate oak** they hang on a long stalk, while in the **sessile oak** they sit almost without a stalk on the twig. Acorns are an important food for wild boar, deer, squirrels and mice. In the past, farmers drove their pigs into the oak wood to feed.

Hardly any tree in Europe offers a home to as many animals as the oak. Hundreds of species of insects live on it, including the large **stag beetle**. In autumn the **jay** hides acorns in the ground as a winter store. The acorns it forgets sprout and grow into new oaks. In this way the bird helps to plant new oak forests.

Oaks grow slowly but live to a great age. Many hundreds of years are nothing unusual, and some oaks in Europe are even more than 1,000 years old. You can work out how old a tree is by counting the **annual rings** in the wood. Because they are so strong and long-lived, oaks were regarded as sacred trees by the Celts and the Germanic peoples.

Oak wood is hard, heavy and lasts a long time, even when it gets wet. In the past it was used to build ships, bridges and half-timbered houses. Today it is used for parquet flooring, furniture and **wine barrels**, which give the wine a special flavour. The bark contains a lot of tannin, which used to be used for tanning leather.

In Switzerland mainly pedunculate and sessile oaks grow. They are found chiefly in lower, warm areas, for example on the Central Plateau, at the southern foot of the Jura and in Ticino. Because oaks cope with heat and drought better than beeches or spruces, foresters are planting them more often again because of **climate change**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fruits of the oak, which sit in a small cup.
The outer, rough layer of a tree's covering.
Rings in the wood, each of which shows one year of growth.
A bitter substance that can be used to turn animal hides into leather.

gewusst: In autumn a jay can hide several thousand acorns.
A sprig of oak is shown on German one, two and five cent coins.
Raw acorns are inedible for humans because of the many tannins.

teile.einleitung: The CRISPR/Cas method is often called the gene scissors. With it you can change the genetic material of living things at a precisely chosen place. The system originally comes from bacteria, which use it to defend themselves against viruses.
wichtigste: In bacteria, CRISPR/Cas serves to defend against viruses (bacteriophages).
A guide RNA leads the enzyme Cas9 to the right place in the genetic material.
Cas9 cuts through both DNA strands there.
The most widely used Cas9 comes from the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes.
Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 2020.
The European Court of Justice decided in 2018 that genome-edited plants count as genetically modified.

abschnitte.text: Bacteria too are attacked by viruses. These viruses are called **bacteriophages**. Many bacteria store small pieces of the virus DNA in their own genetic material, like in a photo album of their enemies. These places are called **CRISPR**. Translated, this means **clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats**. If the same virus attacks again, the bacterium recognises it and cuts up its DNA.

The enzyme **Cas9** is the actual scissors. A **guide RNA** leads it to the right place. It fits exactly to a short section of the DNA like a key. There **Cas9 cuts through both DNA strands**. Most often the Cas9 from the bacterium **Streptococcus pyogenes** is used. Researchers can adapt the guide RNA almost at will and so target almost any place in the genetic material.

After the cut, the cell tries to repair the DNA. A common repair route is **non-homologous end joining** (NHEJ). In it, the cell glues the ends together again. Often small insertions or losses of building blocks arise. As a result, a gene no longer works, it is **switched off**. If you add a suitable DNA template, you can also build in something new in a targeted way.

The Frenchwoman **Emmanuelle Charpentier** and the American **Jennifer Doudna** showed in 2012 that CRISPR/Cas9 can be used as a tool. For this they received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020**. Today the method is used in many labs around the world. In medicine, for example, researchers are studying how it can be used to treat hereditary diseases. In agriculture, the aim is to make plants more resistant.

In classical **mutation breeding**, random changes arise in the genetic material. With CRISPR/Cas, by contrast, changes can be made **in a targeted way at a particular place**. The **European Court of Justice** decided in **2018** that plants changed in this way count as **genetically modified organisms**. In Switzerland, since a popular vote in 2005 a moratorium has applied to growing genetically modified plants, which has been extended several times. Supporters hope for better varieties, critics warn of risks and demand strict rules.

gewusst: The first strange repeats in bacterial genetic material were discovered in the 1980s, long before their function was known.
It was the first time that a Nobel Prize in the natural sciences went to a team of only two women.

teile.einleitung: The endosymbiotic theory explains where two important building blocks of our cells come from: mitochondria and plastids. According to this theory, they were once free-living bacteria that were taken in by other cells and not digested.
wichtigste: Mitochondria and plastids descend from bacteria that were taken in.
Mitochondria go back to alphaproteobacteria, chloroplasts to cyanobacteria.
Konstantin Mereschkowski already interpreted chloroplasts as former symbionts in 1905.
Lynn Margulis helped the theory to break through from 1967.
Plastids and mitochondria have their own ring-shaped DNA, like bacteria.
Many genes of the former bacteria now lie in the cell nucleus.

abschnitte.text: An **endosymbiont** is a living thing that lives inside another and works together with it. According to the theory, early cells took in bacteria without digesting them. Both partners had advantages: the bacteria lived protected, and the host cell received energy. In time, such bacteria became the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. Later, cyanobacteria were also taken in by the ancestors of algae and plants. From these arose the **plastids**, which include the chloroplasts.

The Russian biologist **Konstantin Mereschkowski** already suspected in 1905 that chloroplasts had originally been independent organisms. His idea was hardly noticed for a long time. Only the American biologist **Lynn Margulis** made the theory known, from 1967. She published a widely noticed paper on the origin of cells with a nucleus through symbiosis. Today the endosymbiotic theory is largely accepted in biology.

Several findings support the theory. Plastids and mitochondria have their own, mostly **ring-shaped DNA** without typical histones, just like bacteria. They are surrounded by two membranes and divide in a way similar to bacteria. Comparisons of genetic material show that the closest relatives of mitochondria are found among the **alphaproteobacteria**. In the **glaucophytes**, a group of algae, the plastids even still have a thin layer of murein between the membranes, as bacteria do.

Chloroplasts and mitochondria can no longer live freely today. In the course of evolution, most of their genes were moved into the **cell nucleus**. Many of their proteins are therefore made in the cytoplasm and then transported in. The former guest has thus become a fixed part of the cell.

Sometimes it was not a bacterium but a whole **eukaryotic alga** together with its plastid that was taken in. This is called **secondary endosymbiosis**. Extra membranes were added in the process, so that such plastids have three or four coverings, for example in diatoms. In some algae, such as the cryptophytes, a tiny remnant of the former cell nucleus even lies between the membranes. This nuclear remnant is called a **nucleomorph**.

gewusst: In every one of your body cells there are mitochondria that descend from ancient bacteria.
Plastids with four enclosing membranes are like a cell in a cell in a cell.

teile.einleitung: Carl Linnaeus, in German Carl von Linné, was a Swedish naturalist. He brought order into the huge diversity of plants and animals. His way of naming living things with two Latin words is still used all over the world today.
wichtigste: Carl Linnaeus was born in Sweden in 1707.
He first studied medicine.
He was a professor at Uppsala University.
His work “Systema Naturae” appeared in 1735.
His work “Species Plantarum” of 1753 is regarded as the starting point of today’s botanical names.
He was raised to the nobility and was therefore called “von Linné”.
The abbreviation “L.” after plant names stands for Linnaeus.

abschnitte.text: Carl Linnaeus was born in southern Sweden in **1707**. Even as a child he was interested in plants. He studied **medicine**, for in those days the study of plants was part of the training of doctors, because many remedies came from plants. Later he became **professor at Uppsala University**. There he taught many students and sent some of them on research journeys all over the world.

In **1735** Linnaeus first published his work **“Systema Naturae”**. In it he arranged **plants, animals and minerals** into groups. The first edition was only a thin booklet, and later editions became thicker and thicker. Linnaeus divided living things into levels, for example class, order, genus and species. Biology still uses this idea of a ranking today.

In his work **“Species Plantarum”** of **1753**, Linnaeus gave each plant species a name of **two words**. The first word names the genus, the second the species. The daisy, for example, is called **Bellis perennis**. This work is regarded as the **starting point of today’s botanical names**. If Linnaeus gave a name, the abbreviation **“L.”** stands after it, so Bellis perennis L.

For his services, Linnaeus was **raised to the nobility** by the Swedish king. From then on he was called **Carl von Linné**. He was famous even in his lifetime and died in Uppsala in 1778. He also gave humans a scientific name: **Homo sapiens**, the wise human. Many of his names for plants and animals are still valid today.

gewusst: A small flower of the north, the twinflower, is called Linnaea borealis in his honour.
As a young man, Linnaeus travelled through Lapland in the north of Sweden and described many plants there.

teile.einleitung: A field copse is a small island of trees and shrubs in the middle of meadows and fields. Such copses offer many animals food, shelter and hiding places.
wichtigste: A field copse is a small stand of trees and shrubs in open country.
It is much smaller than a wood.
A hedge, by contrast, is long and narrow.
Typical shrubs are blackthorn, hazel, elder and spindle.
Field copses slow the wind and so protect the fields.
To keep them dense, copses are coppiced from time to time.

abschnitte.text: A **field copse** is a small group of trees and shrubs in **farmland**. It is much smaller than a wood and often roundish or irregular in shape. A **hedge**, on the other hand, is long and narrow and runs like a ribbon through the landscape. Both are important habitats, because in open country there is otherwise little cover.

The **blackthorn**, also called sloe, blooms white in spring, even before it has leaves. The **elder** bears white clusters of flowers and, in late summer, black berries, which you should only eat cooked. The **spindle** has bright pink fruits that remind you of a priest's cap. They are poisonous. The **hazel** shrub provides nuts that squirrels and dormice like to eat.

In thorny shrubs many birds nest well protected. The **red-backed shrike** impales insects and other prey on thorns. This is how it builds up a small store. Hedgehogs, weasels, butterflies and wild bees also find shelter here. Field copses also link habitats with each other, so that animals can move from one place to another.

Field copses and hedges **slow the wind**. As a result the soil dries out less and is blown away less. In addition, the copses are home to beneficial insects that eat pests in the fields. In Switzerland, hedges and field copses are supported as valuable areas for biodiversity.

If shrubs are never cut, they become bare and thin at the bottom. That is why they are **coppiced** every few years. This means they are cut off just above the ground. Afterwards they sprout again strongly and densely. Only one part is looked after at a time, so that the animals do not lose their habitat all at once.

gewusst: The red-backed shrike is called “Neuntöter” (nine-killer) in German, because people used to believe that it killed nine animals before eating one.
The fruits of the blackthorn, the sloes, taste a little milder only after the first frost.

teile.einleitung: Fair trade aims to make sure that farmers in poorer countries get a fair price for products such as bananas, coffee or cocoa. In Switzerland it is particularly well known.
wichtigste: The first Fairtrade label was called Max Havelaar and was founded in 1988 in the Netherlands.
In Switzerland the Max Havelaar Foundation has been active since 1992.
The Fairtrade minimum price applies even if the world market price falls lower.
World shops sell only fair trade products.
The banana women of Frauenfeld are regarded as pioneers in Switzerland.
For bananas, the Fairtrade share in Switzerland is particularly high.

abschnitte.text: Many raw materials such as coffee, cocoa or bananas come from poorer countries. The people who grow them often earn very little. **Fair trade** wants to change that. An important tool is the **Fairtrade minimum price**. It forms a **price floor**, even if the world market price falls lower. It is meant to cover the costs of production. If the market price is higher, the higher market price applies.

The first Fairtrade quality label was created in **1988 in the Netherlands**. It is called **Max Havelaar**, after a character in a novel who denounces the exploitation in the Dutch East Indies. In Switzerland the **Max Havelaar Foundation** has been active since **1992**. Its label is well known here to this day. Products with the label must meet certain rules on prices and working conditions.

From the 1970s onwards, people in Switzerland were already working for fair trade. The **banana women** of **Frauenfeld** drew attention to the poor pay on banana plantations with campaigns. They are regarded as pioneers. **World shops** also arose from the 1970s. They sell only products from fair trade and are often run by volunteers. Today, a very large share of the **bananas** sold in Switzerland are fairly traded.

Most of the **cocoa** harvested worldwide comes from **Ivory Coast and Ghana** in West Africa. Together they supply well over half. There, low incomes and **child labour** are big problems. Fair trade is meant to help here. Municipalities can take part too: anyone who deliberately promotes fair trade can receive the title **Fair Trade Town**. In Switzerland several municipalities carry this title.

gewusst: Switzerland is among the world leaders for fairly traded bananas.
The Max Havelaar label is named after the hero of a 19th-century novel.

teile.einleitung: The chanterelle is a yellow edible mushroom from the forest. In Switzerland it is known as the Eierschwamm or Eierschwämmli, meaning egg sponge. It is very popular with many people.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the chanterelle is mostly called Eierschwamm.
It is egg-yolk yellow and has a fruity smell of apricots.
Under the cap it has thick, forked ridges.
Older mushrooms have a cap like a funnel.
It lives together with forest trees and can hardly be cultivated.
It is good fried or cooked.

abschnitte.text: The chanterelle is called **Cantharellus cibarius** in science. In Switzerland it is mostly called **Eierschwamm** or Eierschwämmli. The name comes from its **egg-yolk yellow colour**. Fresh chanterelles have a delicate, fruity scent that reminds many people of **apricots**.

Under the cap, the chanterelle has no thin gills but thick, forked **ridges**. They run far down the stem. Young mushrooms have a domed cap. In older mushrooms the middle becomes deep, and the cap looks like a **funnel**. There are similar mushrooms, so you should always have mushrooms you have picked checked.

The chanterelle lives together with the roots of trees such as **spruces, beeches and oaks**. The fungus helps the tree to take up water and nutrients. The tree gives the fungus sugar. Such a partnership is called **mycorrhiza**. Because the fungus needs living trees, it can hardly be grown in a garden. It is almost only collected **wild in the forest**.

Wild mushrooms should be **heated thoroughly**. Chanterelles are usually **fried** in a pan, for example with onions and cream. In many Swiss municipalities there is a **mushroom inspection**. There, experts check free of charge whether the mushrooms you have picked are edible.

gewusst: A fresh Eierschwamm can smell like apricots.
Because it needs living trees as partners, there are hardly any farmed chanterelles.

teile.einleitung: Some plants and animals spread strongly in a new area and push out native species. The enemy release hypothesis, in English “release from enemies”, tries to explain why this happens.
wichtigste: Invasive species often benefit from the absence of their natural enemies in the new area.
Above all, specialised predators and disease-causing organisms stay behind in the homeland.
The EICA hypothesis adds: without enemies, plants put more energy into growth.
Classical biological pest control is based directly on this idea.
In Australia, the cactus moth pushed back invasive prickly pears from the 1920s.
In time, native enemies often adapt to the new species.

abschnitte.text: In its homeland, every species is limited by **predators, parasites and disease-causing organisms**. If it reaches a new area, these enemies often stay behind. The species can then multiply more strongly than native competitors. This is how it becomes an **invasive species**. **Specialists**, which depend on only one host species, are especially important. They are rarely brought in as well. General plant-eaters in the new area, so-called generalists, can however certainly attack the species.

An extension is the **EICA hypothesis**. The abbreviation stands for “Evolution of Increased Competitive Ability”. It was formulated in 1995 by Blossey and Nötzold. The idea: without enemies, costly defence is not worthwhile. The plant saves these costs and puts the energy into **growth** instead.

Researchers compare how strongly a species is attacked by enemies in its **homeland** and in the **new area**. They count parasites, disease-causing organisms and predators. If the attack is clearly lower in the new area, that supports the hypothesis. There is also a limitation, though: the longer a species lives in the new area, the more **native enemies** learn to use it. The advantage then often decreases.

In **classical biological pest control**, specialised natural enemies are brought in from the area of origin. This restores the missing pressure from enemies. A famous example is the **cactus moth** from South America. Its caterpillars eat prickly pears from the inside and, from the 1920s, freed huge areas in Australia from the cacti. In Britain, a **psyllid** was released in 2010 against Japanese knotweed, after long tests.

gewusst: Before a natural enemy is released, it is tested for years to make sure it does not attack native plants.
Japanese knotweed is also regarded as an invasive plant in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Eutrophication means the over-fertilisation of waters. If too many nutrients get into a lake, algae grow in huge numbers, and this can seriously harm the lake.
wichtigste: In most Swiss lakes, phosphorus limits the growth of algae.
A clear lake poor in nutrients is called oligotrophic.
The breakdown of dead algae uses up a lot of oxygen at the bottom of the lake.
If the oxygen runs out, the lake is said to turn over.
Since 1986, phosphates in textile detergents have been banned in Switzerland.
Today a large part of the nutrients comes from agriculture.

abschnitte.text: Algae need nutrients such as **phosphorus** and nitrogen. In most Swiss lakes, **phosphorus** is the nutrient in shortest supply. It therefore limits the growth of algae. If more phosphorus gets into the water, more **algae** grow at once. A lake poor in nutrients is called **oligotrophic**. “Oligo” means little, and “troph” refers to nourishment. Such lakes are clear and rich in oxygen.

Many algae make the water **cloudy**, so the **visibility depth** decreases. When the algae die, they sink to the bottom. **Bacteria** break them down there and use up a lot of **oxygen** as they do so. Oxygen is then often lacking at the bottom of the lake. In the worst case the lake becomes hostile to life: fish die, and foul-smelling gases form. The lake is then said to **turn over**.

abschnitte.titel: The rescue of the Swiss lakes
abschnitte.text: In the 20th century, many Swiss lakes were heavily over-fertilised. The federal government and the cantons acted. **Sewage treatment plants** were built to clean the wastewater. Since **1986**, **phosphates in textile detergents** have been banned in Switzerland. Together these greatly improved the water quality. Today a large part of the nutrients comes from **agriculture**: fertiliser and liquid manure can be washed out of the fields into streams and lakes.

Clean lakes also have a downside for fishing. **Whitefish** (Felchen) feed on **plankton**, which grows more sparsely when there are fewer nutrients. That is why whitefish catches have fallen in many places since the lakes were cleaned up. Experts are looking for a balance here between clean water and enough fish.

gewusst: In some Swiss lakes, air is pumped into the depths so that there is enough oxygen at the bottom.
The clarity of a lake is often measured with a white disc that is lowered on a string.

teile.einleitung: Without humans, the Swiss Central Plateau would be mostly covered by beech forest. Beech forests are shady and tall and are home to many special animals and plants.
wichtigste: On the Central Plateau, mainly beech forest would grow naturally.
The beech tolerates waterlogging and long floods badly.
Since 2021, beech forests at the Bettlachstock and in Ticino have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage.
A beech forest with tall, smooth trunks is called a hall forest.
In the northern Alps the beech climbs to about 1500 metres.
The black woodpecker likes to hack its holes in old beeches.

abschnitte.text: Climate and soils on the **Central Plateau** suit the beech very well. It is so competitive there that it would push out most other tree species. Without humans, the Central Plateau would therefore be mostly covered by **beech forest**. But the beech needs well aerated soils. It tolerates **waterlogging** and long floods badly. In wet hollows and river floodplains, alders or willows therefore grow. In the northern Alps it climbs to about **1500 metres**. Higher up, the winters become too long and late frosts too frequent.

A beech forest with tall, smooth trunks and hardly any undergrowth is called a **hall forest**. The trunks stand like pillars in a big hall, and the canopy forms the ceiling. Little grows on the ground because of the shade in summer. In spring, before the leaves come out, many flowers such as wood anemones bloom there.

On warm, dry **limestone slopes of the Jura**, the beech forest is lighter than usual. **Wild orchids** grow there, for example the white helleborine and other protected species. These forests are often called orchid beech forests. They are among the most species-rich forest types in Switzerland.

The thick, smooth trunks of old beeches are well suited for large cavities. The **black woodpecker**, the largest woodpecker in Europe, hacks its nest holes especially often in beeches. Abandoned black woodpecker holes are later used by **stock doves**, bats and owls. That is why old beeches are important for many animals.

In 2021, **UNESCO** added beech forests at the **Bettlachstock** in the canton of Solothurn and in **Ticino** to the World Heritage site “Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of Europe”. They are regarded as especially close to nature. But climate change is hitting the beech. In the very dry **summer of 2018**, many beeches in northern Switzerland suffered from a lack of water. Their leaves turned brown in midsummer and partly fell off.

gewusst: The World Heritage site “Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of Europe” is spread over many countries of Europe.
Beeches can live for several hundred years.

t9q3pah.t: Botanical Garden of the University of Bern

teile.einleitung: In the middle of the city of Bern, right on the Aare, lies the Botanical Garden of the university. There you can discover plants from all over the world free of charge, from mountain flowers to palms.
wichtigste: The garden belongs to the University of Bern.
It lies on the slope above the Aare in the Altenberg district.
The entrance is next to the Lorraine Bridge.
According to the garden, around 5500 plant species grow there.
Admission is free.
There is an alpinum and show houses, for example a palm house.

abschnitte.text: The **Botanical Garden of Bern** lies on the sunny slope above the **Aare** in the Altenberg district. The entrance is at the Altenbergrain, right next to the **Lorraine Bridge**. From Bern station it is easy to reach on foot. The garden belongs to the **University of Bern**.

abschnitte.titel: Plants from all over the world
abschnitte.text: According to the garden, **around 5500** different plant species grow there. These include native species as well as plants from distant countries. **Admission is free**, both for the garden and for the show houses. That is why it is a popular place to relax and learn in the middle of the city.

In the **alpinum** grow plants of the Alps and other mountain ranges. An alpinum is a rock garden modelled on the stony soils in the mountains. This way you can admire mountain plants without climbing into the mountains. For Bern this fits well, because the Alps are not far.

In the **show houses** a warm climate prevails even in winter. There grow, among others, **palms**, ferns and **succulents**, that is, plants that store water in thick leaves or stems. In the **palm house** you feel almost as if in the tropics. This way you get to know plants that would not survive outdoors in Switzerland.

A university garden shows not only plants. It collects them for **teaching** and **research**. Students learn to identify plants here, researchers study them. Botanical gardens also help to preserve **rare and threatened species**, for example by propagating plants and keeping seeds.

gewusst: Worldwide there are thousands of botanical gardens, many of them belonging to universities.
In the Botanical Garden of Bern you can stroll in the warmth among tropical plants in winter.

teile.einleitung: If you dig a deep hole in the ground, you see different layers one above another. Each layer has its own colour and its own properties. Such layers are called **soil horizons**.
wichtigste: A soil horizon is a layer of the soil with similar properties.
The O horizon is the litter layer of leaves, needles and plant remains.
The A horizon is the humus-rich topsoil, also called mould.
The B horizon is the subsoil.
The C horizon is the parent rock.
Most soil organisms live in the topsoil.

abschnitte.titel: At the very top: O horizon
abschnitte.text: At the very top in a forest lies the **litter layer** of dead plant parts. It consists of **leaves**, **needles** and twigs. It is called the **O horizon**, the O standing for **organic**. Here soil organisms begin to break down the plant remains. Underneath begins the mineral soil.

The **A horizon** is the **topsoil**. It is usually **dark**, because it contains a lot of **humus**. In the garden it is also called **topsoil** or mould. In building work it is removed, stored and later reused. In the topsoil there is a lot of food, air and roots. That is why **most soil organisms** live here. On a field it is called the **Ap horizon**, the small p standing for ploughed.

Below the topsoil follows the **B horizon**, the **subsoil**. It contains less humus and is paler. In it you often find **weathered minerals**, which give it a brownish or reddish colour. At the very bottom lies the **C horizon**. This is the hardly altered **parent rock**. From it the upper horizons have arisen through **weathering**.

The sequence of all horizons is called the **soil profile**. Experts dig a pit for this and look at the wall. From colour, **texture** and **humus content** they recognise the individual layers. This way they can determine which soil type it is and how fertile it is. Not every soil has all horizons, and their thickness varies greatly.

gewusst: Before a soil with distinct horizons forms, thousands of years often pass.
In the Alps, soils at high altitude are often only a few centimetres thick.

teile.einleitung: C4 plants have a special trick in photosynthesis: they first collect carbon dioxide in one layer of cells and then release it in another. In this way they work especially well in heat and drought. Well-known examples are maize and sugar cane.
wichtigste: The first product of CO2 fixation is oxaloacetate, a molecule with four carbon atoms.
The enzyme PEP carboxylase fixes the carbon in the mesophyll cells.
It takes up the carbon as hydrogen carbonate.
The Calvin cycle takes place in the bundle sheath cells.
Typical is the Kranz anatomy of the leaves.
Maize and sugar cane are C4 plants.

abschnitte.text: In most plants, photosynthesis first produces a molecule with three carbon atoms. They are called **C3 plants**. In **C4 plants** the first product is **oxaloacetate**, a molecule with **four** carbon atoms. That is where the name comes from. Researchers described this pathway precisely in sugar cane in the 1960s. It is also called the **Hatch-Slack pathway** after two of them.

abschnitte.titel: Two layers of cells work together
abschnitte.text: In the outer **mesophyll cells**, the enzyme **PEP carboxylase** binds the carbon. It takes it up as **hydrogen carbonate**, that is, as a dissolved form of CO2. The resulting molecule is carried into the inner **bundle sheath cells**. There the CO2 is split off again. Only here does the **Calvin cycle** take place, in which sugar is made.

abschnitte.titel: A ring around the vascular bundles
abschnitte.text: In the cross section of a C4 leaf you see a ring of large bundle sheath cells around each **vascular bundle**. Around it lies a second ring of mesophyll cells. This leaf structure is called **Kranz anatomy**. It ensures that the two steps are separated in space. The mesophyll cells act like a pump for CO2.

The enzyme **Rubisco** in the Calvin cycle works badly when there is little CO2. Then it often binds oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, and energy is lost. C4 plants **enrich CO2 at the Rubisco**. That is why in heat they can keep their **stomata** more closed and lose less water. This is a great advantage in **heat and drought**.

The best-known C4 plant in Switzerland is **maize**, which grows in many fields. In the tropics, **sugar cane**, from which sugar is obtained, is an important C4 plant. Millet and many grasses of warm regions also belong to it. Only a small part of all plant species uses the C4 pathway. Wheat, rice and potatoes, by contrast, are C3 plants.

gewusst: The C4 pathway arose in evolution not just once, but many times independently.
Researchers are trying to breed rice with C4 properties to obtain more harvest with less water.

teile.einleitung: All living things need energy to grow, to move and to stay warm. In an ecosystem, this energy flows from the sun via the plants to the animals, and at every level a large part of it is lost.
wichtigste: The energy of almost all ecosystems comes from the sun.
Plants store only a few per cent of sunlight as chemical energy.
Only about 10 per cent of the energy passes from one level of the food chain to the next.
Most of it is lost as heat through respiration and movement.
Materials are recycled in a cycle, but energy is not.
Warm-blooded animals need more food than reptiles of the same weight.

abschnitte.text: Almost all ecosystems live on the energy of the **sun**. Plants capture the light and convert it into **chemical energy** during **photosynthesis**. This energy is then stored in sugar, fat and protein. However, plants use only **a few per cent** of the light that falls on them. The rest is reflected, passes through or is turned into heat.

The levels of a food chain are called **trophic levels**: plants, plant-eaters, meat-eaters. According to the **ten per cent rule**, only about a tenth of the energy is built into the body mass of the next level. Most of it is used up beforehand for **respiration, movement and body warmth** and goes to the surroundings as heat. That is why there are far fewer foxes than mice and far fewer mice than plants.

What is contained in **droppings, fallen leaves and dead animals** is used by the **decomposers**. These are bacteria, fungi and soil animals that break down dead material. Substances such as carbon or nitrogen thus return to the cycle. The energy does not: in the end it too has been given off as heat. That is why we speak of **energy flow**. The energy flows in only one direction and has to be constantly resupplied by the sun.

An animal needs most of the energy from its food for itself. If humans eat plants directly, this loss is avoided. That is why a field can feed more people if food for people grows on it instead of **animal feed**. There are also differences among animals: **mammals and birds** keep their body temperature constant. To do this they use a lot of energy, which **reptiles** save.

gewusst: A snake can often manage for weeks without a meal, but a mouse of the same weight cannot.
The energy in oil and coal also comes originally from sunlight that plants stored millions of years ago.
