teile.einleitung: A fertile soil lets plants grow well and lastingly. This ability is called **soil fertility**. It depends on nutrients, water, air, the soil structure and the soil life.
wichtigste: Soil fertility is the lasting ability of a soil to allow plant growth.
NPK stands for the three main nutrients nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Legumes such as clover fix nitrogen from the air with nodule bacteria.
Green manure protects against erosion and loss of nutrients.
Heavy machines on wet soil lead to compaction.
Most arable crops thrive best at a slightly acid to neutral pH.

abschnitte.text: Plants need mainly three **main nutrients**. On fertiliser sacks this is written as **NPK**: **N** for nitrogen (nitrogenium), **P** for **phosphorus** and **K** for **potassium**. The **pH value** of the soil is also important. At a **slightly acid to neutral** pH, most nutrients are well available. In strongly acid or basic soils, individual nutrients are taken up poorly.

**Legumes** such as clover, peas or beans increase fertility. In their **root nodules** live bacteria, the **rhizobia**. They fix **nitrogen from the air**, which later also benefits the following plants. A **green manure** is sown between two main crops. It covers the soil, holds nutrients fast and later supplies **organic matter**.

The **soil life** is decisive for fertility. **Earthworms** mix the soil and form **humus**. The naturalist **Charles Darwin** wrote in his last book about their great importance. He showed that over the years they move whole layers of soil. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil.

If you drive **heavy machines** over **wet** soil, it is pressed together. The **coarse pores** are lost. Water drains away less well, and roots get less **air**. Such **compaction** often lasts for many years. That is why farmers take care to drive on the soil only in dry weather.

In the **Amazon region** there is a dark, very fertile soil: the **terra preta**, in English “black earth”. It arose in earlier settlements through **charcoal**, bones, pottery shards and organic waste. Even today it is much more fertile than the surrounding tropical soils. Researchers study it in order to learn from it for agriculture.

gewusst: Under a meadow, hundreds of earthworms can live per square metre.
Darwin’s book on earthworms appeared in 1881 and was a great success in its day.

teile.einleitung: Earth's orbit is the path the Earth follows on its journey around the sun. It takes about a year for one full circuit. In doing so it races through space at an unimaginable speed, without us feeling anything of it.
wichtigste: The Earth takes about a year, more precisely about 365 days and 6 hours, for one circuit of the sun.
Earth's orbit is an ellipse that looks almost like a circle.
On average the Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the sun.
On its orbit the Earth travels at around 30 kilometres per second.
The gravity of the sun keeps the Earth on its orbit.
The seasons are caused by the tilted axis of the Earth and not by the distance from the sun.

abschnitte.text: Earth's orbit is the path on which the Earth circles the sun. Such a path is also called an **orbit**. The Earth is constantly falling towards the sun, but at the same time it moves sideways so fast that it never falls in. The sun's **gravity** acts like an invisible band. All the planets of our solar system move in a similar way.

Earth's orbit is not a perfect circle but a slightly stretched **ellipse**. At the beginning of January the Earth is closest to the sun, about 147 million kilometres. At the beginning of July it is farthest away, about 152 million kilometres. The average distance of around 150 million kilometres is called an **astronomical unit** by astronomers. Sunlight takes a good eight minutes to cover this distance.

On one circuit the Earth covers almost a billion kilometres. To do so it travels at around 30 kilometres per second, which is over 100,000 kilometres per hour. That is much faster than any rocket. We notice nothing of it because everything on Earth moves along with it, including the air. It is similar to being in a smoothly moving train.

One circuit takes about 365 days and just under 6 hours. Our calendar year, however, has only 365 days. To stop the calendar drifting, there is a **leap year** every four years with an extra day, 29 February. This way the start of spring and Christmas always stay in the same season.

Many people think it is warm in summer because the Earth is closer to the sun. That is not true, because in January it is actually closest to it. The seasons arise because the **Earth's axis** is tilted by about 23 degrees. In summer the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the sun, the sun's rays arrive at a steeper angle and the days are longer.

For a long time people believed that the sun revolved around the Earth. In 1543 **Nicolaus Copernicus** published his work in which the Earth circles the sun. Johannes Kepler found out at the beginning of the 17th century that the paths of the planets are ellipses. Isaac Newton later explained with gravity why this is so.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path on which one heavenly body circles another.
A shape like a slightly flattened circle.
The average distance between the Earth and the sun, around 150 million kilometres.
A year with 366 days, added to keep the calendar in step.

gewusst: In one hour of school lessons, the Earth has already covered over 100,000 kilometres on its orbit.
In January, when it is winter here, the Earth is closest to the sun.

teile.einleitung: Niche differentiation means that different species divide up the resources in a habitat among themselves. This way they have to compete less strongly for food and space. It happens through evolution over many generations.
wichtigste: Niche differentiation is the evolutionary sharing out of resources between species.
The realised niche is the range that a species actually uses when competitors are present.
G. Evelyn Hutchinson described the niche in 1957 as an n-dimensional hypervolume.
Character displacement can be seen, for example, in Darwin's finches.
Birds of prey hunt by day, owls by night: this is niche differentiation in time.
Species with a very broad niche are called generalists.

abschnitte.text: An **ecological niche** is not a place but the role of a species: what it eats, and where and when it lives. **G. Evelyn Hutchinson** described it in 1957 as an **n-dimensional hypervolume**. Each environmental factor is an axis of its own. The **fundamental niche** includes all the conditions under which a species could live. With competitors, it usually uses only a smaller part, the **realised niche**.

Several **warbler species** in North America search for insects on the same conifers. A study from the 1950s showed that the species prefer to hunt in **different parts** of the trees, for example at the top or close to the trunk. This way they get in each other's way less. This is **niche differentiation in space**.

**Birds of prey** hunt mice by day, **owls** by night. Both use similar prey, but at different times. This is called **niche differentiation in time**. Species such as the red fox use many food sources and habitats. They are called **generalists**. **Specialists**, by contrast, depend on only a few resources.

**Joseph Connell** studied two **species of barnacle** on the rocky coast of Scotland. The species **Chthamalus** could also live lower down. There, however, it is pushed out by the stronger species **Balanus**. In the upper tidal zone Chthamalus survives, because it can cope better with drying out. This shows how competition makes the realised niche smaller.

Sometimes competing species differ more strongly where they **live together** than where they occur separately. This is called **character displacement**. In **Darwin's finches**, the beaks of two species are more different on islands they share. This way they eat seeds of different sizes.

gewusst: Owls and birds of prey simply share the mice between day and night.
In ecology, a niche is not a place but a way of life.

teile.einleitung: Some giant trees in the rainforest stand on mighty walls of wood that stick out from the trunk like boards. These buttress roots help the trees not to fall over.
wichtigste: Buttress roots are flat, board-like roots at the base of the trunk.
They give tall trees support like buttresses.
They are especially common in the tropical rainforest.
Many rainforest trees root shallowly, because the nutrients lie at the top of the soil.
The kapok tree has mighty buttress roots.
Mangroves, by contrast, stand on stilt roots.

abschnitte.text: **Buttress roots** are vertical, flat outgrowths on the lower trunk that merge into the roots. They look like **boards** set on edge. Usually they grow outwards from the trunk **in a star shape** towards several sides. In large trees they can be taller than a person.

Tall trees with a heavy crown need good support. Buttress roots act like the **buttresses** of a church. Because they point in several directions, they support the tree against wind and forces from different sides. This way it does not tip over so easily.

Buttress roots are especially common in the **tropical rainforest**. There the nutrients from decomposed leaves lie almost only in a thin, **topmost layer of soil**. That is why the roots spread out flat instead of growing deep into the ground. Without deep roots, the tall trees need other help to stand, and that is exactly what buttress roots provide.

A well-known example is the **kapok tree**. It is among the tallest trees of the tropics and has large buttress roots. In its fruits there are fluffy **fibres**. They used to be used for filling cushions and life jackets, because they are light and repel water.

Not all tropical trees have buttress roots. **Mangroves** grow on tropical coasts in the zone of ebb and flood. They stand on **stilt roots**, which grow in arches from the trunk into the soft mud and hold the tree fast. At high tide these roots stand partly in seawater.

gewusst: Between the buttress roots of large trees, niches arise as big as small rooms.
Buttress roots can stick out several metres from the trunk.

teile.einleitung: With a green roof, plants grow on a roof. Such green roofs not only look beautiful. They hold back rainwater, cool the surroundings and offer animals and plants a habitat.
wichtigste: An extensive green roof has a thin substrate layer and needs little care.
An intensive green roof is a roof garden, even with shrubs.
On extensive green roofs, stonecrop often grows.
Green roofs hold back water in heavy rain.
A root barrier protects the roof membrane from roots.
In Basel, unused flat roofs must be greened.

abschnitte.text: There are two kinds. An **extensive green roof** has only a **thin substrate layer** of a few centimetres. Undemanding plants grow there that need **little care**. An **intensive green roof** is a real **roof garden** with a thick layer of soil, lawn, perennials and even **shrubs** or small trees. It is heavier, needs a stronger roof and has to be tended and watered.

On a roof it is often hot, dry and windy. That is why robust plants are chosen for extensive green roofs. Especially common is **stonecrop** (genus Sedum). It stores water in its thick leaves and so survives long dry spells. In addition there are mosses, grasses and wild flowers. Many insects such as wild bees find food there.

A green roof consists of several layers. At the very bottom lies the **roof membrane**, which keeps the house watertight. Above it comes a **root barrier**, so that roots do not damage the membrane. Next follow a layer that drains and stores water, a filter fleece and the **substrate** in which the plants grow. The plant cover protects the roof sealing from **UV radiation** and strong **heat**. As a result it can last longer.

In **heavy rain**, a green roof soaks up a lot of water and releases it slowly. In this way the sewer system is relieved. Part of the water evaporates, and this **cools** the surroundings. That helps against heat in the city in summer. A **solar installation** on the same roof also benefits: solar modules work better when it is cooler around them.

The city of **Basel** is known for its green roofs. In the canton of Basel-Stadt, the law requires that new and renovated **unused flat roofs** be greened. As a result Basel has especially many green roofs in relation to its area. Other Swiss cities today also promote green roofs.

gewusst: Some green roofs in Switzerland are over 100 years old, for example on a waterworks in Wollishofen in Zurich.
Rare orchids have been found on green roofs that have hardly any room left on the ground.

teile.einleitung: Ethnobotany studies how people of different cultures use and understand plants. Important medicines have also come from this traditional knowledge.
wichtigste: Ethnobotany combines botany and ethnology, the study of cultures.
Richard Evans Schultes is regarded as the “father of ethnobotany”.
Biopiracy means using traditional knowledge without consent and a fair share.
The Nagoya Protocol regulates a fair balance, and Switzerland has ratified it too.
From the arrow poison curare came agents for anaesthesia.
From the Madagascar periwinkle, medicines against leukaemia were obtained.

abschnitte.text: **Ethnobotany** combines **botany**, the study of plants, with **ethnology**, the study of cultures. It documents what people use plants for: as remedies, as food, for fibres or for rituals. Much of this is passed on only by word of mouth and is in danger of being lost. The American biologist **Richard Evans Schultes** is regarded as the “father of ethnobotany”. He lived for years among indigenous peoples in the Amazon region and described thousands of useful and medicinal plants.

Indigenous peoples of South America used the arrow poison **curare**. It paralyses the muscles because it blocks the signals from the nerve to the muscle. Its active substance **tubocurarine** was later used in anaesthesia. From **Indian snakeroot** comes **reserpine**, one of the first modern remedies for high blood pressure. From the jaborandi shrub, **pilocarpine** is obtained, which helps in eye drops against glaucoma. In the **Madagascar periwinkle**, **vincristine** and vinblastine were found, which are used against leukaemias.

In the Alpine region, too, there is old plant knowledge. **Arnica**, also called mountain tobacco, is used in folk medicine for **bruises and contusions**. It contains anti-inflammatory substances. It is used only **externally**, because taken internally it can be poisonous.

Companies have in some cases patented active substances based on indigenous knowledge without involving the communities of origin. This is criticised as **biopiracy**. The **Nagoya Protocol** is meant to change that. It belongs to the international **Convention on Biological Diversity** and regulates access to genetic resources and a **fair sharing** of the benefits. **Switzerland** has ratified it too.

gewusst: An arrow poison from the rainforest helped to make modern operations safer.
Many of today's medicines go back to plants that people had known as remedies for a long time.

teile.einleitung: The European yew is an evergreen conifer that grows very slowly and can live to a great age. Almost all parts of it are highly poisonous.
wichtigste: Almost all parts of the yew are very poisonous, especially the needles and seeds.
The yew forms no cones; its seed sits in a red cup.
It grows very slowly and can live to a great age.
Even a few twigs can kill a horse.
The yew also grows in deep shade.
In the past, longbows were made from yew wood.

abschnitte.text: The yew is a **conifer** with soft, dark green needles. Unlike spruce or fir, it forms **no cones**. Its seed sits singly in a **red, fleshy cup** that looks like a berry. The yew grows **very slowly**, but can live to a great age. It needs little light and even thrives in the **deep shade** under large trees.

Almost all parts of the yew are **very poisonous**, especially the **needles** and the **seeds**. You must not eat any of it. Only the red flesh around the seed is not poisonous, but the seed inside it is. For **horses**, yew twigs are especially dangerous. Even a few twigs can kill a horse. That is why yews are not planted near horse pastures.

The wood of the yew is very **tough and flexible**. Even in the **Stone Age**, people made **bows** from it. Later, in the Middle Ages, yew wood was also in great demand for bows. Because so many yews were felled, the tree became rare in many areas.

Yews are easy to **trim** and stay green all year round. That is why they are often planted as a **hedge** in gardens, parks and cemeteries. They can even be shaped into figures. Anyone with children or animals should, however, keep in mind that they are poisonous.

gewusst: Some yews in Europe are well over a thousand years old.
Blackbirds eat the red cups of the yew without coming to harm, because they pass the seed out undigested.

teile.einleitung: Carl Schröter was an important botanist who taught at ETH Zurich for decades. He studied the plant world of the Alps, meadows and moors of Switzerland and campaigned for nature conservation.
wichtigste: Carl Schröter was born in 1855 in Esslingen am Neckar.
He taught botany at ETH Zurich for decades.
His great work is called “Das Pflanzenleben der Alpen” (The Plant Life of the Alps).
The terms autecology and synecology go back to him.
He was instrumental in founding the Swiss National Park in 1914.
With Jakob Früh he wrote “Die Moore der Schweiz” (The Moors of Switzerland) in 1904.

abschnitte.text: Carl Schröter was born in **1855** in **Esslingen am Neckar** in Germany. He came to Switzerland as a child and studied natural sciences in Zurich. After that he taught **botany at ETH Zurich** for decades. Many students got to know the plants of Switzerland with him on excursions. He was known for passing on his knowledge in a lively and understandable way.

abschnitte.titel: The Plant Life of the Alps
abschnitte.text: Schröter’s best-known work is called **“Das Pflanzenleben der Alpen”**. In it he described how plants in the mountains cope with cold, wind and short summers. For mountain hikers he published the handy **“Taschenflora des Alpen-Wanderers”** (Pocket Flora of the Alpine Hiker), an identification book with pictures. Together with the geographer **Jakob Früh** he wrote the standard work **“Die Moore der Schweiz”** in **1904**.

Together with **Friedrich Gottlieb Stebler**, Schröter studied the **meadows and fodder plants** of Switzerland. This was very important for farming, because good fodder is the basis for milk and cheese. The two described which grasses and herbs grow in which meadows. In addition, the terms **autecology** and **synecology** go back to Schröter. Autecology studies a single species and its environment, synecology whole communities of living things.

Schröter also campaigned for **nature conservation**. He was instrumental in founding the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine, which came into being in **1914**. There, nature was to be allowed to develop without human intervention. The park also became important for research. Schröter died in Zurich in 1939.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park is regarded as the oldest national park in the Alps.
Biology students still learn the terms autecology and synecology, which Schröter coined.

teile.einleitung: Glued laminated timber, GLT for short, consists of many glued boards. This produces wooden beams that are longer, stronger and more uniform than any tree trunk.
wichtigste: Glued laminated timber consists of at least three layers of boards glued with the grain parallel.
Otto Hetzer had glued curved beams patented in 1906.
Flaws such as knots are spread over many laminations.
In GL24h, 24 stands for the bending strength, h for homogeneous.
Finger joints connect boards into long laminations.
Cross-laminated timber, by contrast, has layers glued crosswise.

abschnitte.text: For **glued laminated timber**, dried boards, the **laminations**, are glued on top of each other. All layers have the **same grain direction**, which is called parallel to the grain. At least three layers are needed. So that the laminations are long enough, the boards are connected with **finger joints**: the ends are milled out like a comb, glued and pressed. This produces long laminations without great loss of strength.

The master carpenter **Otto Hetzer** from Weimar had a patent granted in 1906 for glued, curved wooden beams made of layers of boards. They are regarded as the forerunner of today’s glued laminated timber. For a long time it was therefore called the **“Hetzer method”**.

A beam of solid wood can have knots or cracks that weaken it. In glued laminated timber such flaws are **spread over many laminations** and bridged by the other boards. In addition, weak spots can be cut out before gluing. That is why GLT is **more uniform** in strength than solid wood.

The strength class shows how much load the wood can bear. **GL** stands for glued laminated timber. The number **24** gives the characteristic **bending strength** of 24 newtons per square millimetre. Higher numbers such as GL28 or GL32 mean wood that can bear more. The **h** means homogeneous, all laminations have the same class. A **c** stands for combined from laminations of different classes.

Glued laminated timber can be made in **great lengths** and cross-sections and even **curved**. This way wooden trusses span sports halls, riding halls and bridges without supports in the middle. To be distinguished from it is **cross-laminated timber** (CLT). Its layers of boards are glued **crosswise**. It is suited to flat walls and floors, while GLT is used mainly for beams and columns.

gewusst: A beam of glued laminated timber can be much longer than any tree its boards come from.
With glued laminated timber and cross-laminated timber, even tall buildings of wood are built today.

thjoqmh.t: Drought and heat in Europe in 2018

teile.einleitung: In the summer of 2018 it was very hot and very dry in large parts of Europe. Rivers carried little water, forests suffered and there were many fires. Switzerland clearly felt the effects too.
wichtigste: In 2018 there was a long spell of heat and drought in central Europe.
The Swiss Army flew water to mountain pastures by helicopter.
In the High Rhine near Schaffhausen, many grayling died because the water was too warm.
Around 1 August, many cantons banned fireworks and open fires.
On the Rhine, ships could sail only partly loaded because of low water.
In Sweden, forests burned even north of the Arctic Circle.

abschnitte.text: From spring to autumn 2018, much less rain than usual fell in many parts of central Europe. At the same time it was often very hot. Such a long dry spell is called a **drought**. Looking back, 2018 was the **beginning of a dry phase lasting several years**, because 2019 and 2020 were also dry in parts of central Europe.

On many mountain pastures, springs and pools dried up. The animals did not have enough to drink. So the **Swiss Army** flew water by **Super Puma helicopters** to pastures that cannot be reached by vehicle. Farmers in the lowlands also had less grass and hay for their livestock.

In the **High Rhine near Schaffhausen**, the water sometimes became warmer than 27 °C in August. That was too much for **grayling**, which need cool, oxygen-rich water. Many fish died, as already happened in the hot summer of 2003. In autumn the water level at **Kaub** on the Middle Rhine fell to a record low. Cargo ships could take on only part of their load.

Because of the great **risk of forest fires**, many cantons and municipalities banned fireworks and open fires. Many **1 August bonfires** were cancelled too. In **Sweden**, numerous forests burned, some even north of the Arctic Circle. The country asked other European countries for firefighting aircraft.

In northern Switzerland, for example around Schaffhausen and in the Jura, many **beeches** had brown leaves already in summer. Weakened **spruces** produced less resin. The **European spruce bark beetle** benefited from this. In the years afterwards, many infested trees therefore had to be felled.

gewusst: In the summer of 2018, army helicopters brought water for cows up to the mountain pastures.
Many municipalities celebrated 1 August 2018 without fireworks.

teile.einleitung: The European larch is a conifer of the Alps with one special feature: it loses all its needles in autumn. Before that, whole mountainsides turn golden yellow.
wichtigste: The larch is the only native conifer that sheds its needles in autumn.
Before they fall, the needles turn golden yellow.
In spring, fresh, light green needles grow back.
The needles are soft and grow in tufts of about 20 to 40.
In Switzerland the larch grows mainly in the Alps, for example in Valais and the Engadine.
Larch wood is rich in resin and stands up well to wind and weather.

abschnitte.text: Most conifers stay green in winter. The **larch** is different: it **sheds all its needles in autumn**. Before that, the needles turn **golden yellow**. In autumn, whole mountainsides therefore glow yellow. In **spring**, new, delicate **light green** needles sprout.

The needles of the larch are thin and **soft**, and do not prick. On the short shoots they grow in **tufts**, each with about 20 to 40 needles. On the long shoots they stand singly. The **cones** are small and egg-shaped, only about 2 to 4 centimetres in size. They often stay hanging on the tree for years.

The larch likes to grow **high in the mountains**. In Switzerland it is especially common in **Valais** and the **Engadine**. It grows up to the **tree line**. It needs a lot of light and tolerates great cold. Because it carries no needles in winter, it loses hardly any water in the cold season.

**Larch wood** contains a lot of **resin** and is very resistant. It stands up well to **wind and weather** and lasts a long time outdoors. That is why it is often used to build balconies, façades, fences and fountains. Many old wooden houses in the mountains are also built of larch wood.

gewusst: The larch is the only conifer in Switzerland that is bare in winter.
Old larch wood on house façades turns almost black in the sun over the years.

teile.einleitung: Bryology is the science of mosses. Mosses are small, but very diverse, and grow almost everywhere, from the forest floor to rocks in the high mountains.
wichtigste: Bryology distinguishes mosses proper, liverworts and hornworts.
Around 16,000 moss species are described worldwide.
Johann Hedwig is regarded as the father of bryology.
His work of 1801 is the starting point for the names of mosses proper.
In Switzerland, Swissbryophytes collects knowledge about mosses.
Dried mosses swell up again in water.

abschnitte.text: **Bryology** distinguishes three large groups. **Mosses proper** mostly have a leafy stem. **Liverworts** are either leafy or form a flat thallus. **Hornworts** bear horn-shaped spore capsules. These keep growing from a zone at their base that can divide, and ripen from the tip.

Worldwide **around 16,000 moss species** are known. After the flowering plants, mosses are thus among the most species-rich groups of land plants. They have no true roots and take up water over their whole surface. Many can dry out completely and revive when it rains.

The **father of bryology** is regarded to be **Johann Hedwig**. He described many mosses very precisely. His work “Species Muscorum Frondosorum” appeared in **1801**. It is regarded as the starting point of botanical naming for most mosses. Older names therefore officially do not count.

Mosses are often kept dried in a **herbarium**. Even after years they can be identified well, because they are **poikilohydric**: in water they swell up again and show their little leaves and cells under the microscope almost as if fresh. An important model of plant genetics is the moss **Physcomitrium patens**, formerly Physcomitrella patens. In it, genes can be altered especially precisely, and its genome was the first of a moss to be decoded.

In Switzerland, **Swissbryophytes** collects records of finds and knowledge about the country’s mosses. This national data and information centre is based at the **University of Zurich**. A special species is the **luminous moss** (Schistostega pennata). Its protonema has lens-shaped cells that focus the weak light in cave entrances and rock crevices. That is why it shimmers golden green.

gewusst: The luminous moss does not glow itself, it reflects the incoming light back like cats’ eyes.
Peat mosses can store many times their own weight in water.

teile.einleitung: The skylark is a small, brown-streaked bird of open country. It is famous for its long song, which it delivers high in the air.
wichtigste: The skylark is somewhat bigger than a house sparrow.
Its plumage is brown-streaked, and on its head it can raise a small crest.
It sings in flight high above the fields.
It builds its nest on the ground.
It eats insects, spiders and seeds.
On the Swiss Plateau, its numbers have fallen sharply.

abschnitte.text: The **skylark** is somewhat bigger than a **house sparrow**. Its plumage is **brown-streaked** and so well camouflaged. On its head it can raise a small **crest**. On the ground you hardly see it when it keeps still. Males and females look very similar.

The skylark is known for its **song flight**. The male climbs high into the air, fluttering, and sings without a pause. Often you hear the song without spotting the bird in the sky. With the singing he shows that this area is taken. The song can last several minutes.

The skylark builds its **nest on the ground**, well hidden among low plants in meadows and fields. It eats **insects, spiders and seeds**. The young are fed mainly with insects. For breeding it needs places where the plants are neither too dense nor too tall.

On the **Swiss Plateau**, the numbers of skylarks have **fallen sharply** in recent decades. In intensively farmed land the crops often stand very dense. In addition, mowing is frequent, so that many nests are destroyed. Insects are also lacking as food. The skylark is therefore regarded as endangered in Switzerland.

A **skylark plot** is a small spot in a grain field that is deliberately left out when sowing. There the skylark can land and look for food. Flower-rich fallow strips and flower meadows also help it. With such measures, farmers support the rare bird.

gewusst: The skylark often sings even before sunrise.
A skylark plot is only about as big as a small room and still helps.

teile.einleitung: A flower fallow, in German Buntbrache, is a piece of arable land where nothing is harvested for several years. Instead, native wild herbs are sown, which bloom colourfully and give many animals food and shelter.
wichtigste: A flower fallow is sown on arable land with native wild herbs.
It stays for several years and is not harvested.
In a flower fallow there is neither fertilising nor spraying.
Grey partridge, brown hare and many insects find cover and food there.
In Switzerland, flower fallows are among the biodiversity promotion areas.
Farmers receive direct payments from the Confederation for them.

abschnitte.titel: A blooming strip in the field
abschnitte.text: A **flower fallow** lies in the middle of arable land, often as a strip at the edge of a field. There the farmer sows a mixture of **native wild herbs**. In summer, for example, cornflower, corn poppy, mullein and the sky-blue **chicory** bloom. The area stays for several years and is not harvested. This creates a dense, colourful jumble of plants.

In a flower fallow there is **no fertilising** and **no plant protection products** are sprayed. Fertiliser would mainly favour vigorous grasses, and the delicate wild herbs would have no room left. Sprays would harm insects and herbs. Without either, the fallow stays a quiet place for plants and animals. Only if unwanted weeds take over may one intervene in a targeted way, for example by mowing a part.

The **grey partridge** is a gamebird that nests on the ground. It lives in open arable land and has almost vanished in Switzerland. Flower fallows offer it cover, nesting places and insects as food for the chicks. That is why they are deliberately laid out, for example in the Klettgau in the canton of Schaffhausen. The **brown hare** also likes to hide in the dense plant cover and raises its young there.

In autumn the plants of a flower fallow are not cleared away. In the **hollow stems** many insects and their larvae overwinter, for example wild bees. The dried seed heads are food for birds such as goldfinches in winter. For hares and partridges the fallow remains a hiding place when the other fields are bare. A flower fallow is therefore valuable all year round.

abschnitte.titel: Where the name comes from and who pays
abschnitte.text: The word **Brache**, fallow, originally means arable land that rests for a time. In the earlier **three-field system**, part of the fields was left unplanted each year so that the soil could recover. Today, flower fallows in Switzerland are a kind of **biodiversity promotion area**. Because farmers give up a harvest, they receive **direct payments** from the Confederation for it. So it is worth it for them to create room for nature.

gewusst: From the roasted root of chicory, which often grows in flower fallows, chicory coffee used to be made.
Flower fallows as a special promotion area exist mainly in Switzerland, and the term is hardly known in other countries.

teile.einleitung: Decomposers are nature’s recyclers. They break down dead plants and animals and turn them back into substances that plants can use. Without them, nature would be smothered in waste.
wichtigste: Decomposers break down dead material such as leaves, wood and dead animals.
The most important decomposers are bacteria and fungi.
Fungi form an underground network of fine threads, the mycelium.
When material is broken down, nutrient-rich humus arises.
Decomposers return minerals to the soil.
The earthworm pulls leaves into the soil and helps with decomposition.

abschnitte.text: In nature there are **producers**, which are plants that make nutrients. **Consumers** are animals that eat plants or other animals. And there are the **decomposers**. In German the word, Destruenten, comes from the Latin word for destroy. They break down dead plants, dead animals and dung. Without decomposers, **dead plants and animals would pile up** in the forest, metre after metre.

The most important decomposers are **bacteria and fungi**. They are often so small that you cannot see them. Fungi form a network of fine threads under the ground and in wood, the **mycelium**. The mycelium runs through leaves and wood and breaks them down. What we collect as a mushroom in the forest is only the fruiting body. The largest part of the fungus lies hidden in the soil.

Many soil animals help too. The **earthworm** pulls leaves into the soil and eats them together with soil. Woodlice, millipedes and springtails chop leaves into small pieces. In this way bacteria and fungi have more surface to attack. In the end **nutrient-rich humus** arises, the dark, fertile upper layer of the soil.

When breaking down material, decomposers return **minerals** such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to the soil. Plants take up these substances again with their roots and grow. Animals eat the plants, and at some point plants and animals die. Then it is the decomposers’ turn again. In this way a **cycle of matter** arises in which nothing is lost.

In a **compost heap**, countless tiny organisms are at work. When breaking down material they give off **heat**, which is why the heap becomes warm inside, sometimes over 60 degrees. Decomposers are also at work when food spoils. An apple spoils more slowly in the **fridge**, because the **cold slows bacteria and fungi**. In warmth, by contrast, they work faster.

gewusst: In a handful of garden soil live more tiny organisms than there are people on Earth.
A honey fungus in the USA, with its huge mycelium, is among the largest living things in the world.

teile.einleitung: The pressure flow hypothesis explains how plants transport sugar from the leaves to other parts of the plant. The transport takes place in the phloem, a conducting tissue made of sieve tubes. It is driven by a difference in pressure.
wichtigste: Ernst Münch put forward the pressure flow hypothesis in 1930.
The transport of sugar takes place in the phloem.
At the source, sugar is loaded, water flows in by osmosis and the pressure rises.
At the sink, sugar is unloaded, water leaves and the pressure falls.
The water comes from the neighbouring xylem.
In the phloem, transport upwards and downwards is possible.
With the sucking mouthparts of an aphid, you can obtain pure phloem sap.

abschnitte.text: Leaves make sugar during photosynthesis. But roots, fruits and tubers need sugar too. A place where sugar enters the conducting tissue is called a **source**. A place that uses up or stores sugar is called a **sink**. A **growing potato tuber** is a typical sink. The sugar flows in the **phloem** from the source to the sink.

The German botanist **Ernst Münch** put forward the **pressure flow hypothesis** in **1930**. His idea: at the source, a lot of **sugar** is loaded into the sieve tubes. This lowers the **water potential**, and water **flows in by osmosis**. Osmosis means that water moves to where there are more dissolved substances. As a result, a **high pressure** builds up. This water comes from the **neighbouring xylem**, the plant's water pipes.

At the sink, the **sugar is unloaded**, that is, taken out of the sieve tubes. Then **water leaves**, and the **pressure falls**. This creates a difference in pressure between the source and the sink. It pushes the sap through the sieve tubes, a bit like water through a garden hose. The plant needs **metabolic energy** mainly for the **active loading** of the sugar at the source.

In the **xylem**, water almost always flows upwards from the roots. In the **phloem**, on the other hand, **transport upwards and downwards** is possible. All that matters is where the source and the sink happen to be. In spring, for example, storage organs can deliver sugar to the young leaves. Later, the leaves deliver sugar to fruits and roots.

To test the hypothesis, you need pure **phloem sap**. That is difficult, because sieve tubes close up quickly when they are cut. Researchers therefore use **aphids**. An aphid pushes its fine sucking mouthpart right into a sieve tube. Then the **mouthpart** is cut away from the animal. Because of the pressure in the sieve tube, sap keeps flowing out of the stump, and it can be collected.

gewusst: The pressure in sieve tubes can be several times higher than in a car tyre.
The sweet liquid that aphids excrete is called honeydew. Ants like to collect it.

teile.einleitung: Ash dieback is a tree disease that has threatened ash trees in Europe for several decades. It is caused by an introduced fungus, which is also killing many trees in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Ash dieback is caused by a fungus.
The fungus is called the false white stalked cup fungus (Falsches Weisses Stängelbecherchen) and comes from East Asia.
In Switzerland the disease was first detected in 2008.
The fungus spreads through the air with spores.
Wilting leaves and dying shoots are typical.
Some ash trees are largely resistant and give grounds for hope.

abschnitte.text: Ash dieback is caused by a **fungus**. In German it is called **Falsches Weisses Stängelbecherchen** (false white stalked cup fungus), and in science **Hymenoscyphus fraxineus**. It comes from **East Asia**. There it lives on native ash species without doing much damage. The **European ash**, by contrast, is hardly protected against it.

The disease was noticed in **Poland in the 1990s**. From there it spread westwards. In **2008** it was discovered in **north-western Switzerland** and soon reached the whole country. The fungus survives the winter in the **leaf stalks**, which fall to the ground in autumn. In summer, tiny white fruiting bodies, only a few millimetres in size, grow on them. They release **spores**, which the wind carries far. If they land on ash leaves, a new infection begins.

Infected ash trees have **wilting leaves**. The twigs die back from the tip, and the crown becomes thin. Damage often also occurs at the **base of the trunk**. Many infected trees die after a few years. Sick trees along roads and paths can fall over and therefore sometimes have to be felled.

For the Swiss forest the consequences are great. After the beech, the **ash** is the **second most common broad-leaved tree** in Switzerland. Its loss changes many forests, especially in damp places. There is hope, though: a small share of ash trees show hardly any signs of disease. Experts are trying to preserve and propagate these **resistant** trees.

gewusst: The fungus that kills so many trees is smaller than a fingernail.
In its home in East Asia, the same fungus does hardly any harm.

teile.einleitung: The beech is the most common broadleaved tree in the Swiss forest. With its smooth, grey bark and the small three-edged fruits, the beechnuts, it is easy to recognise. Because it is so widespread in central Europe, it is often called the “mother of the forest”.
wichtigste: The beech that grows here is called the European beech in full.
It is the most common broadleaved tree in the Swiss forest.
Its bark is strikingly smooth and silver-grey.
The fruits of the beech are called beechnuts.
A beech can grow about 30 to 40 metres tall.
Beeches tolerate a lot of shade and can therefore grow up under other trees.
Beech wood is hard and is used for furniture, toys and as firewood.

abschnitte.text: The European beech has a smooth, grey bark that hardly cracks even in old trees. Its **leaves** are egg-shaped, have a slightly wavy margin and are finely hairy at the edge. In autumn they turn golden yellow to copper brown. It has its name Rotbuche, red beech, not from the leaves but from its slightly reddish wood. A free-standing beech forms a broad, round crown.

The fruits of the beech are called **beechnuts**. They are small, three-edged nuts that sit in pairs in a spiny husk. In autumn the husk springs open, and the beechnuts fall to the ground. Squirrels, mice, wild boar and birds such as the chaffinch like to eat them. In some years beeches bear especially many fruits, which is called a **mast year**.

The European beech grows in large parts of Europe, from southern Scandinavia to Italy. In Switzerland it is common mainly on the Central Plateau and in the Jura. In the mountains it grows up to about 1500 metres. It likes a damp, mild climate and tolerates long drought and severe late frosts badly. Where it is happy, it forms dense **beech forests**.

Young beeches can grow slowly for many years in the deep shade under large trees. This is called **shade tolerance**. When an old tree falls, they use the gap and grow quickly upwards. In summer the dense canopy lets only little light onto the ground. That is why many spring flowers such as the wood anemone bloom before the beech has come into leaf.

Beech wood is hard, heavy and easy to work. It is made into furniture, stairs, wooden spoons, building blocks and parquet. As **firewood** it is very popular, because it burns long and hot. Beechnuts are edible, but should be eaten raw only in small amounts, because they can cause stomach ache. Roasted they taste nutty, and in the past cooking oil was pressed from them.

Foresters today watch the beech closely. In hot, dry summers such as 2018, many beeches on the Swiss Central Plateau got brown leaves or died. In very dry places **oaks** might thrive better in future. In higher and damper areas, however, the beech will probably remain important.

begriffe.erklaerung: The small, three-edged nut fruits of the beech.
A tree with flat leaves that it usually drops in autumn.
A year in which trees bear especially many fruits.
The ability of a plant to grow even with little light.

gewusst: The German word Buchstabe, letter, probably comes from the fact that the Germanic peoples carved signs into staves of beech wood.
The hornbeam, despite its name, is not a beech at all, but is related to the birch.
A large beech can evaporate hundreds of litres of water on a summer day.

teile.einleitung: In the soil there is much more carbon than you would think. It comes mainly from dead plants and soil organisms and is very important for the climate and the fertility of fields.
wichtigste: Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and all plants together.
Most soil carbon is in the humus.
Humus consists of around 58 percent carbon.
Bogs cover only about 3 percent of the land area, but store a great deal of carbon.
Warmth makes soil organisms break down humus faster, which produces CO2.
In Switzerland bogs have been protected since the Rothenthurm Initiative of 1987.

abschnitte.text: In photosynthesis, plants take up **carbon dioxide** (CO2) from the air and build their body from it. When leaves, roots and animals die, their carbon gets into the soil. In the top metre of all soils alone lie around 1500 billion tonnes of **organic carbon**. That is more than in the atmosphere and in all plants together. Soils are thus the largest carbon store on land.

The carbon in the soil is mainly in the **humus**, the dark, decomposed mass of plant remains. Humus consists of around 58 percent carbon. That is why you can estimate the humus content by multiplying the carbon content by about **1.72**. A soil with 2.5 percent carbon therefore has about 4.3 percent humus. Humus makes the soil loose, stores water and holds nutrients fast.

In wet, oxygen-poor **bogs**, dead plants are hardly broken down. They are laid down as **peat**, layer upon layer over millennia. Although bogs cover only about 3 percent of the land area, they store about twice as much carbon as the biomass of all forests. If a bog is drained, oxygen gets into the peat. Microorganisms then break it down, CO2 escapes and the soil sinks. In the **Grosses Moos** in the Seeland region the soil has sunk by more than a metre since the Jura water corrections.

At higher temperatures soil organisms breathe faster and break down humus more quickly. In doing so they release CO2. If this breakdown increases more than the supply from plants, the soil loses carbon and becomes a **CO2 source**. Conversely, you can help soils to store more carbon, for example through catch crops, hedges or little tillage. At the climate conference in Paris in 2015, France launched the initiative **“4 per 1000”**: if the carbon in soils grew by 0.4 percent each year, this could offset a large part of the annual rise in CO2.

abschnitte.titel: Protection in Switzerland and terra preta
abschnitte.text: In 1987 the Swiss people accepted the **Rothenthurm Initiative**. The trigger was a planned military training ground in a raised bog. Since then the Federal Constitution has protected bogs and bog landscapes of special beauty and national importance. A model for more carbon in the soil comes from the Amazon region: the **terra preta**, a dark, very fertile soil. It arose because people brought in charcoal, ash and waste over centuries. Today **biochar** is being researched on this model.

gewusst: Terra preta means “black earth” in Portuguese and is fertile to this day.
In the Grosses Moos some fields today lie more than a metre lower than before, because the peat has disappeared.

teile.einleitung: Dill is a popular kitchen herb with fine, thread-like leaves and a fresh taste. In German it is also called Gurkenkraut, gherkin herb. It goes especially well with fish, cucumbers and potatoes.
wichtigste: Dill has very fine leaves that look like threads.
Another German name for dill is Gurkenkraut.
Dill blooms yellow.
Besides the leaves, the seeds are also used as a spice.
A dill plant lives only one year.
In Scandinavia, dill is especially popular in the kitchen.

abschnitte.text: Dill is a plant with **very fine leaves like threads**. It grows to about half a metre to one metre tall. In summer it forms large umbels with small **yellow** flowers. That is why dill belongs to the **umbellifers**, like parsley, fennel and carrot. Dill is **annual**: the plant grows, blooms and dies within **one year**.

Dill is also called **Gurkenkraut**, gherkin herb, because it is often used for pickling cucumbers. Pickled gherkins get their typical taste from it. For pickling, the flower umbels or the **seeds** are often used. The seeds taste stronger than the leaves, a little like caraway. They are also used for bread.

Fresh dill goes especially well **with fish such as salmon**, with potatoes, quark and salads. In **Scandinavia**, for example in Sweden and Finland, dill is very popular. There it is eaten, for example, with crayfish, fish and new potatoes. Fresh dill is best added to the food **only at the end**. With long cooking it loses its fine aroma.

Dill can be sown in spring directly in the bed or in a pot. It likes sun and loose soil. Because it has long roots, it is hard to transplant. Its flowers attract many insects. The caterpillars of the swallowtail, a large butterfly, also like to eat dill.

gewusst: Dill was already used in ancient Egypt as a spice and medicinal plant.
If you let dill bloom in the garden, you often find new little plants the next year that have grown by themselves from the seeds.

teile.einleitung: Cyanobacteria are tiny living things that carry out photosynthesis, just like plants. In the past they were called “blue-green algae”. They are among the oldest living things on Earth and helped to shape the air we breathe.
wichtigste: Cyanobacteria are bacteria, that is, prokaryotes without a cell nucleus.
They carry out oxygen-producing photosynthesis.
About 2.4 billion years ago they led to the Great Oxidation Event.
Mats of cyanobacteria build layered limestone structures, the stromatolites.
Some make poisons such as microcystin, which damages the liver.
The Burgundy blood alga turns Swiss lakes such as Lake Zurich reddish.
“Spirulina” comes from the genus Arthrospira.

abschnitte.text: Cyanobacteria used to be called **blue-green algae**, because they often look blue-green and live in water. But they are not true algae. Their cells have **no cell nucleus**, which is why they belong to the **prokaryotes**, like all bacteria. True algae have a cell nucleus. The colour comes from the green chlorophyll and a blue pigment.

Cyanobacteria carry out **oxygen-producing photosynthesis**: from light, water and carbon dioxide they make sugar and release oxygen. About **2.4 billion years ago**, a lot of oxygen collected in the air for the first time as a result. This time is called the **Great Oxidation Event**, because many living things of that time could not tolerate the oxygen. Later the chloroplasts of plants developed from them, which were originally cyanobacteria.

Some cyanobacteria form dense mats in shallow water. Lime and sand stick in them, and layer by layer a structure grows upwards. These layered limestone structures are called **stromatolites**. Fossilised stromatolites are among the oldest traces of life. In a few places, such as Western Australia, they still grow today.

Many cyanobacteria float in water. With **gas vesicles**, tiny gas-filled bubbles in the cell, they can regulate their **floating depth**. Filamentous species sometimes form **akinetes**: thick-walled **resting cells** that survive unfavourable times such as cold. In Swiss lakes the **Burgundy blood alga** (Planktothrix rubescens) is well known. It can turn the water reddish, for example in **Lake Zurich**.

When cyanobacteria multiply strongly in summer, this is called a **bloom**. Some species then make poisons. The best known is **microcystin**, which damages mainly the **liver**. During such a bloom, people and dogs should not swim. Other cyanobacteria, by contrast, are edible: the genus **Arthrospira** is dried as **spirulina** and sold as a food supplement.

gewusst: A large part of the oxygen on Earth still comes from tiny cyanobacteria in the sea today.
The Burgundy blood alga has its name because it can colour the water red like Burgundy wine.

teile.einleitung: The expansion of the universe means that space is stretching out. As a result, galaxies are on average moving further and further away from each other. This discovery shows that the universe had a beginning, the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago.
wichtigste: The universe is expanding, so galaxies are on average moving further and further apart.
The further away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away from us.
The astronomer Edwin Hubble made this observation known in 1929.
The expansion leads to the assumption that the universe began with the Big Bang.
The Big Bang was about 13.8 billion years ago.
Since 1998 it has been known that the expansion is getting faster and faster.
Researchers suspect a mysterious dark energy as the cause.

abschnitte.text: Expansion means stretching out. You can imagine the universe like a **raisin cake** in the oven. When the dough rises, all the raisins move away from each other, although no raisin itself travels. In just the same way, the **galaxies** move away from each other because the space between them is stretching. There is no centre from which everything moves.

In the 1920s, the American astronomer **Edwin Hubble** studied the light of distant galaxies. He found that almost all galaxies are moving away from us. He also found that the further away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. Back in 1927, the Belgian researcher **Georges Lemaître** had predicted an expanding universe from calculations. Today people speak of the Hubble-Lemaître law.

How do you measure whether a galaxy is moving away? The light of galaxies that are moving away is stretched and therefore appears redder. This is called **redshift**. You hear something similar with an ambulance: when it drives away, the siren sounds lower. From the strength of the redshift, astronomers can calculate the speed.

If everything is moving away from everything else, everything must once have been much closer together. If you calculate backwards, you arrive at an extremely hot and dense beginning, the **Big Bang**. It happened about 13.8 billion years ago. Since then the universe has been expanding and cooling. From gas, stars, galaxies and planets such as the Earth gradually formed.

In 1998, researchers discovered something surprising with the help of distant exploding stars. The expansion is not slowing down but getting **faster** and faster. For this the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded in 2011. What is driving the universe apart is not yet known exactly. Researchers call this unknown cause **dark energy**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge collection of billions of stars, for example our Milky Way.
The hot, dense beginning of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.
The light of distant galaxies becomes redder because they are moving away from us.
A still unexplored force that speeds up the expansion of the universe.

gewusst: The Andromeda Galaxy is coming towards us despite the expansion, because gravity between nearby galaxies is stronger.
Galaxies, solar systems and also we humans do not expand, because gravity and other forces hold us together.
Because light takes time to travel, we see very distant galaxies as they looked billions of years ago.

teile.einleitung: The common liverwort, in German Brunnenlebermoos, is a flat, green moss that likes to grow in damp places such as fountains, walls and nurseries. For research it is an important model organism.
wichtigste: The scientific name is Marchantia polymorpha.
Its plant body is a flat, forking thallus.
On the upper side, pores lead into air chambers.
Liverworts have cells with oil bodies.
On the underside sit rhizoids and ventral scales.
Its genome was published in 2017.

abschnitte.text: The common liverwort is scientifically called **Marchantia polymorpha**. The species name polymorpha means many-shaped. The genus is named after the French botanist **Nicolas Marchant** of the 17th century, and his son Jean gave it the name. The German name refers to its location at fountains. The moss has no little leaves, but a flat **thallus** that forks again and again. It is therefore called a thalloid liverwort.

On the upper side of the thallus you see small openings, the **air pores**. They lead into **air chambers** with many cells full of chloroplasts, where photosynthesis takes place. Unlike the stomata of higher plants, air pores cannot close. Liverworts also have cells with **oil bodies**. These are droplets with essential oils, surrounded by a membrane. They probably protect against feeding enemies and do not occur in mosses proper.

On the underside sit fine hairs, the **rhizoids**. There are two types. **Smooth rhizoids** grow into the ground and anchor the thallus. **Pegged rhizoids** have wall pegs projecting inwards and conduct water along the underside. In addition there are rows of thin **ventral scales**. Together they help to hold water on the thallus.

Marchantia is an important **model organism** of plant research. It grows fast and is easy to keep in the lab. Since the publication of its **genome** in 2017 it has been especially suited to studying the **evolution of land plants**. Mosses and liverworts belong namely to the early lines of land plants. On the thallus it also forms small cups with gemmae, with which it can multiply quickly.

gewusst: In nurseries the common liverwort often grows as a green coating on damp flowerpots.
Raindrops wash the gemmae out of the small cups and so spread them.

teile.einleitung: Eddy covariance is a measuring method from environmental research. It is used to find out how much carbon dioxide, water vapour and heat a forest, a meadow or a field exchanges with the air. To do this, tiny swirls of air are measured.
wichtigste: The method measures the exchange of CO2, water vapour and heat between an ecosystem and the air.
It is based on small swirls of air that carry air up and down.
Typical instruments are an ultrasonic anemometer and a fast gas analyser.
Measurements are taken about 10 to 20 times per second.
The footprint is the area from which the measured fluxes come.
The worldwide network of such stations is called FLUXNET.

abschnitte.text: Above every forest and every meadow, the air moves in many small **eddies**. They carry air upwards and downwards. If the **rising air** is on average poorer in CO2 than the sinking air, the plants are taking up CO2. The method therefore links the **vertical wind** with the **gas concentration**.

A station usually stands on a mast or tower above the plant cover. An **ultrasonic anemometer** measures the wind in three directions. A fast **gas analyser** measures CO2 and water vapour at the same time. Because the eddies are small and quick, measurements are taken about **10 to 20 times per second**.

The result is the **net ecosystem exchange** of CO2. Flows from the air into the ecosystem are usually counted as **negative**. A negative value therefore means that the ecosystem **takes up CO2**, because photosynthesis exceeds respiration. The station measures air from a certain area, the **footprint**. It changes with wind direction, wind strength and measuring height.

On windless nights a calm layer of air forms near the ground. Then there is **too little turbulence**, and CO2 collects at the bottom. The station then underestimates the exchange. That is why researchers have to check such night-time values and often correct them.

In the **FLUXNET** network, data from many stations are brought together. There are stations in forests, meadows and fields on every continent. This makes it possible to compare how ecosystems react to weather and climate. There are also such measuring stations in Switzerland, for example run by ETH Zurich.

gewusst: The instruments measure the wind up to 20 times in a single second.
A minus in the CO2 exchange is good news: it means the plants are taking up CO2.

teile.einleitung: The evolution of plants tells how today's plant world developed from tiny algae in the sea over hundreds of millions of years. Step by step, plants conquered the land, grew into tall trees and finally invented seeds and flowers. Without this development there would be no forests, no flowers and hardly any oxygen in the air.
wichtigste: Land plants descend from green algae.
According to the endosymbiotic theory, chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria.
In the Ordovician, the first plants settled on the land.
The woody substance lignin in the cell walls made great height possible.
In the Carboniferous, tree-sized clubmosses and horsetails formed extensive swamp forests.
Pollen and the pollen tube made the fertilisation of seed plants independent of water.
In the Cretaceous, the angiosperms, that is, the flowering plants, spread widely.

abschnitte.text: Life began in the sea with simple single-celled organisms. Some bacteria, the **cyanobacteria**, were able to carry out photosynthesis and produce oxygen very early on. According to the **endosymbiotic theory**, such cyanobacteria were taken in by larger cells and lived on inside them. They became the chloroplasts, the green power stations of plant cells. This is how the first algae arose.

Land plants developed from **green algae** that lived in fresh water. In the **Ordovician**, about 470 million years ago, the first simple plants grew on the land. They probably resembled today's mosses and were only a few centimetres tall. On land they had to protect themselves from drying out, for example with a waxy protective layer and tiny pores for breathing, the **stomata**.

An important advance was **vascular bundles**, fine tubes that carry water and nutrients through the plant. Added to this was the woody substance **lignin**, which makes cell walls strong and stiff. Only with this could plants grow large and upright. In the Devonian, about 380 million years ago, the first forests on Earth arose in this way.

abschnitte.titel: The swamp forests of the Carboniferous
abschnitte.text: In the **Carboniferous**, about 359 to 299 million years ago, huge swamp forests grew. In them stood tree-sized clubmosses and horsetails as well as tree ferns that grew up to 30 metres tall. When they died, they sank into the swamp and over time became **hard coal**. The name Carboniferous comes from the Latin word for coal.

Mosses and ferns need water so that their sperm can swim to the egg cells. The **seed plants** solved this problem with pollen, which is carried by the wind. A **pollen tube** grows directly to the egg cell and brings the sperm cell there. In addition, the seed protects the embryo and contains a food store. The first successful seed plants were **gymnosperms** such as conifers and the ginkgo.

In the **Cretaceous**, that is, at the time of the late dinosaurs, the **angiosperms** spread widely. In them the seeds lie well protected in an ovary, from which a fruit later develops. Many attract insects with colourful flowers, and the insects carry the pollen on. Today the vast majority of plant species are flowering plants, from the daisy to the oak.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over very many generations.
The idea that chloroplasts used to be independent bacteria that lived on inside a cell.
A woody substance that makes plant cell walls hard and stable.
Flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed in an ovary.
Seed plants such as conifers whose seeds lie open.

gewusst: The ginkgo tree is regarded as a living fossil, because its relatives already lived at the time of the dinosaurs.
The hard coal that people burn today is to a large extent plant material from the Carboniferous.
A large part of the oxygen in the air was produced by algae and plants over the course of Earth's history.

teile.einleitung: The sweet chestnut is a tree with edible fruits in a prickly case. In Ticino there are whole chestnut forests. In winter, many Swiss towns smell of hot roasted chestnuts.
wichtigste: The sweet chestnut is also called the edible chestnut.
Roasted sweet chestnuts are called Marroni in Switzerland.
The fruits sit in a green case with many spines.
A case usually holds one to three chestnuts.
Especially many sweet chestnuts grow in Ticino.
In the southern valleys the tree used to be called the bread tree.

abschnitte.text: The sweet chestnut is called **Castanea sativa** in science. Because its fruits can be eaten, it is also called the **edible chestnut**. The fruits grow in a **green case with many sharp spines**. It is better to handle them with gloves. A case usually holds **one to three** chestnuts. The horse chestnut looks similar, but its fruits are not edible.

The chestnuts ripen in **October**. Then the prickly cases fall from the tree and burst open. The shiny brown fruits are picked up from the ground. In a **selva**, a carefully tended chestnut grove, grass grows under the trees. That makes it easy to gather the chestnuts.

In **Ticino**, sweet chestnuts grow in large forests on sunny slopes, and also in southern valleys of the Grisons. In the past, people there ate chestnuts almost every day. They were as filling as bread, which is why the tree was called the **bread tree**. The chestnuts were dried so that they lasted all winter.

Roasted sweet chestnuts are called **Marroni** in Switzerland. In winter you buy them hot from the **chestnut stall**. Before roasting, they are scored, otherwise steam builds up inside and the shell can **burst** with a bang. For the dessert **vermicelles**, sweet chestnut purée is pressed through a press. It then looks like thin noodles.

gewusst: Without a cut, a chestnut can burst with a bang when roasted.
The word vermicelles means “little worms”, because of the thin strands of purée.

teile.einleitung: When a soil becomes more and more acid, this is called soil acidification. It can happen naturally, but is greatly accelerated by air pollutants and harms mainly forest soils.
wichtigste: Sulphur and nitrogen compounds from the air acidify soils.
In Switzerland much ammonia comes from livestock farming.
In strongly acid soils, poisonous aluminium dissolves.
Lime buffers acid, so soils on limestone acidify more slowly.
In acidification, calcium and magnesium are washed out.
With liming you can neutralise acid.

abschnitte.text: How acid a soil is, is measured with the **pH value**. The lower the value, the more acid. Part of the acidification is natural: roots and microorganisms give off **carbon dioxide**. In the soil water it forms **carbonic acid**, which slowly dissolves lime. This process, however, takes a very long time.

It goes much faster through air pollutants. **Sulphur dioxide**, **nitrogen oxides** and **ammonia** from traffic, industry and agriculture get into the soil with rain or as dust. There they form acids. In Switzerland ammonia comes mainly from the liquid manure and dung of **livestock farming**. When it is converted into nitrate in the soil, acid is released. This affects forest soils especially.

Soils can absorb acid for a time, which is called **buffering**. Strongest is the **carbonate buffer**: as long as lime is present, the pH stays above about 6. That is why soils on **limestone** in the Jura acidify less quickly than soils on **granite**, which contains hardly any lime. Once the lime is used up, weaker buffers take over at lower pH values.

Acid displaces important nutrients such as **calcium**, **magnesium** and potassium from the soil particles. They are washed out with the seepage water and are missing for the plants. If the pH falls sharply, **aluminium ions** dissolve out of the clay minerals. They are poisonous and damage the fine roots of trees. Weakened trees are more susceptible to drought and storms.

The most important thing is to emit fewer pollutants. Since filters and low-sulphur fuels were introduced, the sulphur in the air has fallen sharply. Nitrogen and ammonia, on the other hand, remain a problem. In the short term **liming** helps: you spread calcium carbonate, which neutralises acid and raises the pH again.

gewusst: Many forest soils in Switzerland have pH values below 5 and thus count as acid.
Acid rain was a big topic in the 1980s in the “forest dieback” debate.

teile.einleitung: A healthy soil is loose and full of cavities. If it is pressed together, this is called soil compaction. This harms plants, animals and the water balance.
wichtigste: In compaction, the pores in the soil become smaller.
Heavy machines are a main cause in agriculture.
Wet soil is especially easily compacted.
On compacted soil, water stays in puddles.
There the roots lack air and space.
Wide tyres with low air pressure spare the soil.

abschnitte.text: Soil consists not only of solid particles, but also of many **pores**, the cavities for air and water. In **soil compaction** the particles are pressed together. The pores become smaller or disappear entirely. You can imagine it like a sponge that you press hard.

In agriculture, **heavy machines** are a main cause. Tractors and harvesters often weigh many tonnes. If they often drive over the same spot, they press the soil together. This is especially dangerous when the soil is **wet**, because then it is soft and easily pressed. Building sites, cattle pastures and many walkers also compact soils.

In compacted soil, rainwater can hardly drain away. It stays in **puddles** or runs off over the surface and washes soil away as it does so. Roots need oxygen and cavities to grow, but both are missing. Earthworms and other soil animals also find habitat harder to come by. The harvest can become smaller as a result.

Compaction in the **subsoil** is especially bad. There it is hardly ploughed, and few living things loosen the soil. Such compaction can last for decades and can hardly be reversed. That is why prevention is much more important than repair.

You should not drive on wet fields with heavy machines. **Wide tyres with low air pressure** spread the weight over a larger area, so the soil is pressed less. Fixed tramlines ensure that you do not drive everywhere. In everyday life you can see compaction well on a **desire path**: the ground is hard, and hardly a plant grows there.

gewusst: A large combine harvester can weigh more than 20 tonnes with a full grain tank.
Plants with deep, strong roots can loosen compacted layers somewhat over time.

teile.einleitung: Brown earth is one of the most common soils in central Europe and on the Swiss Central Plateau. It gets its name from its brown colour in the subsoil.
wichtigste: Brown earths are very common on the Swiss Central Plateau.
The brown colour comes from iron oxides.
The process is called brunification.
The typical horizon sequence is Ah, Bv, C.
Brown earth arises under deciduous and mixed forest in a temperate, humid climate.
It is well suited to agriculture.

abschnitte.text: **Brown earths** are widespread in central Europe. On the **Swiss Central Plateau** too they are among the most common soil types. They form in a **temperate, humid climate**, where there is enough rain and moderate temperatures. By nature **deciduous and mixed forests** grow there, whose litter is broken down well and supplies mild humus.

In **weathering**, minerals containing iron in the rock are decomposed. In the process **iron oxides** form, similar to rust. They colour the subsoil brown. This process is called **brunification**. The brown earth is named after it.

Typical is the horizon sequence **Ah, Bv, C**. At the top lies the humus-rich topsoil **Ah**, the h standing for humus. Below follows the browned subsoil **Bv**. The small **v** means weathered and distinguishes it from other B horizons. At the bottom lies the parent rock **C**.

Brown earths are mostly **loose**, well aerated and quite **rich in nutrients**. Earthworms and other soil organisms feel at home in them. That is why they are often used as **fields** and meadows. On brown earths on the Central Plateau, for example, cereals, potatoes and maize grow. It is important to protect them from compaction and erosion.

gewusst: The letters of the horizons are a kind of secret script of soil science that experts read worldwide.
Without humans, most brown earths on the Central Plateau would be covered by beech forest.

teile.einleitung: Exponential growth means that a population grows by the same percentage in every period of time. As a result the increase gets bigger and bigger, and in the end the number of animals rises at breakneck speed.
wichtigste: In exponential growth, the relative growth rate stays constant.
The absolute increase gets bigger with every generation.
The equation is dN/dt = r · N, the solution N(t) = N0 · e to the power (r · t).
The growth rate r is the birth rate minus the death rate.
The doubling time is ln 2 divided by r.
On a logarithmic scale, exponential growth becomes a straight line.

abschnitte.text: In **exponential growth**, a population always grows by the same **percentage** per unit of time. So it is the **relative growth rate** that stays constant. The absolute increase, by contrast, gets bigger and bigger. An example: 1,000 animals grow by 10 per cent every year. After one year there are 1,000 · 1.1 = 1,100, after two years 1,100 · 1.1 = **1,210**. In the second year 110 animals are added instead of 100, because the population is already bigger.

Mathematically this is described by the equation **dN/dt = r · N**. The increase is therefore proportional to the current size **N**. The solution is **N(t) = N0 · e to the power (r · t)**. The growth rate **r** is the difference between the **birth rate** and the **death rate**, if you leave out immigration and emigration. With a birth rate of 0.5 and a death rate of 0.3, this gives r = 0.2 per year.

The **doubling time** is the time in which the population doubles. It is **ln 2 divided by r**. With r = 0.07 per year, that is 0.693 divided by 0.07, so about **10 years**. If you plot the **logarithm** of the population size against time, you get a **straight line**: ln N = ln N0 + r · t. Its slope is r.

Exponential growth occurs only when **food and space** are practically unlimited and density does not yet play a role. This applies, for example, to the **recolonisation** of a habitat. A well-known example is the **European rabbit** in Australia. In 1859 a settler in Victoria released a few rabbits. Without suitable enemies, they spread within decades over large parts of the continent. At some point, though, lack of food or diseases always slow the growth.

gewusst: If you fold a sheet of paper in half again and again, its thickness also grows exponentially.
With 7 per cent growth per year, a quantity doubles in about 10 years.

teile.einleitung: Fennel is a fragrant plant from the Mediterranean region. It is used as a vegetable, as a spice and as a tea.
wichtigste: Fennel originally comes from the Mediterranean region.
It can grow up to about 2 metres tall.
Its leaves are fine and divided into thread-like parts.
With bulb fennel you eat the thickened leaf bases, which form a bulb.
The so-called fennel seeds are, botanically speaking, fruits.
Fennel tea is traditionally drunk for tummy ache and wind.

abschnitte.text: **Fennel** comes from the **Mediterranean region**. It belongs to the **umbellifers**, like carrot, dill and parsley. The plant can grow **up to about 2 metres** tall. In summer it bears small yellow flowers, arranged in umbels like little umbrellas. The whole plant smells spicy, like aniseed.

The leaves of fennel are **fine and divided into thread-like parts**. That is why fennel fronds are often mistaken for **dill**. The two look very similar, but taste different. Fennel fronds can be finely chopped and sprinkled over salads or fish.

With **bulb fennel** you do not eat the root, but the **thickened leaf bases**. They lie tightly on top of each other and form a white bulb. You can eat them raw in a salad, or cook and fry them. The so-called **fennel seeds** are, botanically speaking, **fruits**. They are used as a spice for bread, sausage or baked goods.

**Fennel tea** is traditionally drunk especially often for **tummy ache and wind**. For this, hot water is poured over the crushed fruits. Many children know it as a mild tea. The taste comes from essential oils, above all a substance called **anethole**.

The **swallowtail** is a large butterfly marked in yellow and black. It likes to lay its eggs on fennel, dill and carrot. The caterpillars eat the leaves of these plants. If you leave fennel standing in the garden, with a little luck you can spot the caterpillars with their green, black and orange pattern.

gewusst: Fennel was already known to the ancient Greeks and Romans.
Aniseed, dill and fennel taste similar because they contain related aromatic substances.

teile.einleitung: The dark honey fungus is a fungus that lives on trees in the forest. What we see as a mushroom is only a small part of it: underground it can grow enormous. In the Swiss National Park lives one of the largest known fungi in Europe.
wichtigste: The dark honey fungus is called Armillaria ostoyae in science.
In the Swiss National Park, one honey fungus measures about 800 by 500 metres.
Researchers from the WSL proved this in 2004.
Its age is estimated at around 800 to 2,000 years.
It spreads with cord-like rhizomorphs.
It attacks living trees and can make them die.

abschnitte.text: The real fungus is the **mycelium**, a network of fine threads in the soil and in the wood. The mushroom caps we see in autumn are only its fruiting bodies. The dark honey fungus is called **Armillaria ostoyae** in science. It is related to the honey fungus Armillaria mellea.

The honey fungus forms dark, root-like cords of fungal threads. They are called **rhizomorphs**, and in everyday speech “bootlaces”. With them it grows through the soil from tree to tree. The mycelium can also **glow** faintly green. Wood that it has grown through used to be called “shining wood”.

On living trees, the honey fungus is a **parasite**. It attacks roots and the lower trunk and can kill weakened trees. After that it lives on in the dead wood and breaks it down. It is then a **decomposer**. At the **Ofenpass** it mainly attacks weakened **mountain pines**.

abschnitte.titel: The giant in the National Park
abschnitte.text: Researchers from the **WSL**, the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research, examined many samples in 2004. In the laboratory they let the mycelia meet each other. If they belong to the same individual, they grow together without a boundary. This showed that a single fungus is about **800 metres long and 500 metres wide** and covers around 35 hectares. Its age is estimated at **800 to 2,000 years**.
The largest known honey fungus grows in the **Malheur National Forest** in Oregon in the USA. It covers around **9 square kilometres**. This makes it one of the largest living things on Earth.

gewusst: A single honey fungus can be older than many castles in Switzerland.
Wood with honey fungus mycelium can glow faintly green in the dark.

teile.einleitung: Rain and wind can carry away fertile soil. This removal is called **soil erosion**. Because soil forms again only very slowly, protecting it is especially important.
wichtigste: Soil erosion is the removal of soil by water or wind.
