Above all the fertile topsoil is lost.
A permanent plant cover protects the soil best.
On steep slopes erosion is especially strong.
For one centimetre of soil it takes around a hundred years or more.
Terraces such as in Lavaux hold the soil back on the slope.

abschnitte.text: In **soil erosion**, soil particles are **washed away** or **blown away**. When raindrops pound on bare earth, they loosen small particles. The running water carries them off. The **steeper** a slope is, the faster the water flows and the more soil it sweeps away. On dry, open areas the **wind** can also remove a lot of soil.

Soil arises very slowly through the **weathering** of rock and through **humus formation**. For a single centimetre it takes **around a hundred years or more**. A heavy rain, by contrast, can wash away a lot of soil in a short time. What is lost is above all the fertile **topsoil**. That is why erosion is so harmful for agriculture.

A **permanent plant cover** protects best. Plants hold the soil fast with their **roots** and slow rain and wind. A field is especially at risk when the soil is **uncovered**. That is why after the harvest **catch crops** are often sown or mulch is left lying. On a slope you plough **across the slope**. These furrows slow the water, while furrows running downhill act like small channels.

In **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva lie steep vineyards with many **terraces**. Retaining walls turn the steep slope into several flat steps. This way the soil is not so easily washed away. The terraces were built over centuries. Since 2007 Lavaux has been a **UNESCO World Heritage site**.

In the **USA** a great catastrophe happened in the **1930s**. The prairie had been ploughed up intensively. After long **droughts**, huge **dust storms** blew the dry field soil away. Many farming families lost their livelihood and moved away. This time is called the **“Dust Bowl”**.

gewusst: After the Dust Bowl the USA founded its own service for soil protection.
Saharan dust is sometimes blown as far as Switzerland and colours the sky yellowish and the snow reddish.

teile.einleitung: The soil too “breathes”. Roots, soil animals and countless microorganisms use up oxygen and give off **carbon dioxide**. This release of carbon dioxide from the soil is called **soil respiration**.
wichtigste: Soil respiration is the release of carbon dioxide from the soil into the atmosphere.
The two main sources are plant roots and microorganisms.
Soil air contains more carbon dioxide and less oxygen than the air above it.
With rising temperature, soil respiration increases up to an optimum.
In wet, oxygen-free soils, methane can arise instead.
Soil respiration shows how active the soil life is.

abschnitte.text: Soil respiration has two main sources. The **plant roots** breathe and give off carbon dioxide. This is called **autotrophic respiration**. **Microorganisms** such as bacteria and fungi break down dead plant parts and **humus**. Carbon dioxide arises here too, and this is called **heterotrophic respiration**. Soil animals such as earthworms and woodlice add to it.

Because the soil is constantly breathing, **oxygen is used up** and **carbon dioxide is enriched**. The soil air therefore contains many times as much carbon dioxide as the air above it. Through the pores in the soil, the gases slowly exchange with the air. If the soil is **waterlogged** and oxygen is missing, special microorganisms break down substances differently. This produces, among other things, **methane**, for example in bogs and rice fields.

**Warmth** speeds up the life processes of soil organisms. That is why soil respiration rises with temperature, up to an **optimum**. For this, enough **water** must be present. If the soil is too dry or too cold, it breathes little. In summer, soil respiration here is therefore usually much higher than in winter.

Worldwide, soils release **many times** the fossil emissions of humans each year as carbon dioxide. A large part of it, however, is taken up again by the **photosynthesis** of plants. Researchers fear that **warmer soils** will break down more humus. The additional carbon dioxide could drive **global warming** further.

In **soil biology**, soil respiration is often measured. The more carbon dioxide a soil gives off under the same conditions, the more **active** its microorganisms are. Soil respiration is therefore an important **indicator** of healthy soil life. This way you can compare, for example, how different kinds of management affect the soil.

gewusst: In one gram of fertile soil live millions to billions of bacteria.
The smell of fresh earth after rain comes from a substance called geosmin, which soil bacteria produce.

teile.einleitung: Ectomycorrhiza is a close partnership between fungi and the roots of trees. The fungus wraps the fine root tips like a coat. Many trees in Swiss forests depend on this cooperation.
wichtigste: In ectomycorrhiza, the fungal threads do not penetrate the cells of the root cortex.
The root tips are wrapped in a mantle of hyphae.
The network between the cortex cells is called the Hartig net.
The tree gives the fungus sugar, and the fungus supplies water, nitrogen and phosphate.
Pines, spruces, beeches and oaks typically live with such fungi.
The term mycorrhiza was coined by Albert Bernhard Frank in 1885.

abschnitte.text: The word **mycorrhiza** means “fungus root”. The term was coined by the German botanist **Albert Bernhard Frank** in **1885**. In **ectomycorrhiza** the fungus stays on the outside of the cells. Its threads, the **hyphae**, grow only between the cells of the root cortex. In **arbuscular mycorrhiza**, by contrast, they penetrate into the cells.

Around the fine **root tips**, the fungus forms a dense **mantle of hyphae**. Root hairs are often missing there, because the fungal threads take over their job. Between the cortex cells grows a fine network, the **Hartig net**. It is named after the forest botanist **Theodor Hartig**. Through its large surface, fungus and tree exchange substances.

The tree passes on part of its **products of photosynthesis**, above all **sugar**, to the fungus. In return, the fungus supplies **water, nitrogen and phosphate**. Its fine threads reach far into the soil. This way the tree reaches nutrients that its roots alone could not reach. Both benefit, which is called **symbiosis**.

Typical partners are **pines, spruces, beeches and oaks** as well as birches. **Ash** and **maple** trees, on the other hand, mainly live with arbuscular mycorrhiza. The **fly agaric** is a well-known partner of birches, spruces and pines. **Porcini** and **truffles** also belong to these fungi.

Ectomycorrhizal fungi usually form their fruiting bodies only with a **host tree** that supplies them with sugar. That is why porcini can hardly be cultivated without trees. **Truffles** are grown on plantations with young trees whose roots have been inoculated with the fungus. **Button mushrooms** and **shiitake**, on the other hand, grow on dead material and are easy to cultivate.

gewusst: On root tips, a fungal mantle can take over the job of the root hairs.
Truffles only grow on plantations if young trees are inoculated with the fungus.

teile.einleitung: Domestication means that people have turned wild animals and plants into pets, farm animals and crops over many generations. In the process, the living things changed a great deal. Without domestication there would be neither cows nor wheat.
wichtigste: The dog is considered the oldest domestic animal of humans.
The ancestor of the domestic cat is the African wildcat.
In domesticated cereals, ripe ears no longer fall apart.
The typical features of crop plants are called the domestication syndrome.
The deliberate choice of which ones to breed from is called artificial selection.
In 1868 Charles Darwin wrote a book about variation under domestication.

abschnitte.text: The word **domestication** comes from the Latin domus, meaning house. The **dog** is considered the **oldest domestic animal**. It descends from the wolf and was living with people more than 15,000 years ago. Later, sheep, goats, cattle and pigs followed. The domestic cat descends from the **African wildcat**, a wild cat from Africa and the Near East. Cats probably joined people because mice lived in the food stores.

Around 10,000 years ago, people in the Near East began to grow wheat and barley. In wild cereals, **ripe ears fall apart** by themselves and the grains drop to the ground. In domesticated cereals, the grains stay on the ear, so they can be harvested. All such features together, for example bigger grains and ripening at the same time, are called the **domestication syndrome**. According to what we know today, rice of the subspecies japonica was domesticated in the **Yangtze valley** in China.

People chose again and again the animals and plants they liked best: the calmest animals, the biggest grains, the sweetest fruits. Only these were used for **breeding**. This deliberate choice is called **artificial selection**. Over many generations the living things changed greatly as a result. From a single wild cabbage species, for example, came cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi.

Many crop plants could **hardly survive without humans**. They **no longer spread their seeds by themselves**, because the grains stay firmly on the ear or the seeds are enclosed in the fruit. People have to harvest them and sow them again. Many domestic animals also depend on being cared for by people.

The English naturalist **Charles Darwin** was very interested in domestic animals and crop plants. He even bred pigeons himself. In **1868** he published a book about the variation of animals and plants under domestication. Darwin saw artificial selection as a model for **natural selection** in nature, which he described in his theory of evolution.

gewusst: All dog breeds, from the Chihuahua to the St Bernard, belong to the same species.
Maize descends from an unremarkable wild grass from Mexico called teosinte.

teile.einleitung: Conrad Gessner was a Zurich naturalist, doctor and scholar in the 16th century. He described animals, plants and books as comprehensively as hardly anyone before him. Many call him one of the first modern naturalists.
wichtigste: Conrad Gessner lived from 1516 to 1565 and worked as town physician in Zurich.
His “Historia animalium” is regarded as the foundation stone of modern zoology.
The “Bibliotheca universalis” was a catalogue of learned books.
For ordering plants he held flowers and fruits to be especially important.
In 1555 he climbed Pilatus and described it.
In 1565 he died in Zurich of the plague.
He was pictured on the 50 franc note of the sixth banknote series.

abschnitte.text: Conrad Gessner was born **in Zurich in 1516**. He studied, among other places, in Basel and France and became a doctor. In Zurich he worked as **town physician** and taught at the Higher School. He spoke many languages and was interested in almost everything: animals, plants, stones, languages and books. Such scholars are called **polymaths**.

His most famous work is the multi-volume **“Historia animalium”**, the history of animals. In it he collected everything that was then known about mammals, birds, fish and other animals, with many woodcuts. Gessner checked reports from old books and added his own observations. The work is regarded as the **foundation stone of modern zoology**. Some fabulous creatures still appear in it, but he often marked what was uncertain.

With the **“Bibliotheca universalis”**, Gessner wanted to list all the learned books he could find. He recorded thousands of works in Latin, Greek and Hebrew with author and content. That is why he is also regarded as a **father of bibliography**, the science of book catalogues.

Gessner recognised that **flowers and fruits** are especially important for ordering plants. In 1559, from a specimen in an Augsburg garden, he was one of the first in central Europe to describe the **tulip**. He loved the mountains: **in 1555 he climbed Pilatus** near Lucerne and wrote a separate work about it. In those days few people climbed mountains for pleasure. The plant family of the **Gesneriaceae**, to which the African violet belongs, is named after him.

In 1564 and 1565 the **plague** raged in Zurich. As a doctor, Gessner cared for many sick people and himself died of the epidemic in **1565**. Switzerland later honoured him on the **50 franc note** of the sixth banknote series, which was issued from 1976. To this day, streets and institutions in Zurich recall him.

gewusst: Gessner became only 49 years old and still wrote dozens of books.
The tulip was almost unknown in central Europe in Gessner’s time and came from the Ottoman Empire.

teile.einleitung: Many plants bear not just a single blossom, but many blossoms together on one shoot. Such a group is called an **inflorescence**. Some inflorescences look like a single large blossom.
wichtigste: An inflorescence is a group of blossoms on a common shoot.
In a raceme, stalked blossoms sit on a long axis, as in lily of the valley.
In a spike, the blossoms sit on the axis without a stalk, as in ribwort plantain.
In an umbel, all the flower stalks start from one point.
The flower head of the sunflower is a capitulum made of many small blossoms.
The red “leaves” of the poinsettia are bracts.

abschnitte.text: In a **raceme**, stalked single blossoms sit one after another on an **unbranched** main axis. An example is the **lily of the valley**. In a **spike**, the blossoms sit **without their own stalk** directly on the axis. In **ribwort plantain** the spike is short and cylindrical. A **spadix** is a spike with a thick, fleshy axis. In **lords-and-ladies** it is surrounded by a funnel-shaped bract.

In an **umbel**, all the flower stalks arise at the same place, like the spokes of an umbrella. **Ivy**, for example, forms such an umbel. A **panicle**, by contrast, is a **branched** inflorescence whose branches become shorter towards the top. In **oats** the small spikelets hang loosely on branched, drooping branches.

The **sunflower** is a **composite**. Its large flower head is a **capitulum** made of hundreds of small single blossoms. The **daisy** is built the same way. Every white “petal” at the edge is a small blossom of its own, a **ray floret**. In the yellow middle sit the tiny **disc florets**. Together the capitulum looks like a single blossom.

In the **poinsettia**, large red “petals” shine. In reality these are coloured **bracts**. The actual blossoms are small and yellowish. They sit in the middle in a special inflorescence. The striking bracts attract animals in place of the small blossoms.

gewusst: The seeds of the sunflower are arranged in a spiral. In it you can see two sets of spirals in opposite directions.
The poinsettia originally comes from Mexico.

teile.einleitung: Cellulose is the most important building material of plants. It makes cell walls firm and is found in wood, cotton and paper. No other biopolymer is as common on Earth.
wichtigste: Cellulose is the most common biopolymer on Earth.
It consists of glucose units with β-1,4-glycosidic bonds.
The repeating building unit is the disaccharide cellobiose.
Cotton consists of about 90 per cent cellulose.
Humans cannot digest cellulose, because they lack cellulase.
Cows make use of it with the help of microorganisms in the rumen.

abschnitte.text: Cellulose is a **polysaccharide**, that is, a multiple sugar. It consists of very many **glucose units** joined into long, straight chains. The link is called a **β-1,4-glycosidic bond**. In it, every second glucose is turned over. The repeating building unit of two glucoses is called **cellobiose**. The **amylose** in starch is also built from glucose, but has **α bonds** and forms helices instead of straight chains.

abschnitte.titel: Building material of the cell wall
abschnitte.text: Many straight cellulose molecules lie parallel next to one another. They form firm bundles, the **microfibrils**. These are embedded in the **cell wall** like steel rods in concrete. This gives the plant its strength. Cellulose is made by **synthase complexes in the cell membrane**. These protein complexes spin the chains directly outwards into the cell wall.

The natural fibre **cotton** consists of **about 90 per cent** cellulose. **Wood** also contains a lot of cellulose, plus lignin and other substances. From wood, pulp is obtained, from which **paper** and cardboard are made. Linen from flax and fibres such as viscose also consist of cellulose. Because plants make it in huge amounts every year, cellulose is the **most common biopolymer on Earth**.

Humans **cannot use** cellulose **as a source of energy**. They lack the enzyme **cellulase**, which splits the β bonds. Even so, cellulose in vegetables and wholegrain is important for digestion as **dietary fibre**. **Cows** eat a lot of grass. In their **rumen**, a large forestomach, live **microorganisms** that break down cellulose. The cow benefits from this.

gewusst: Termites too can eat wood only because tiny helpers in their gut break down the cellulose.
Some bacteria make pure cellulose, which is used, for example, for wound dressings.

teile.einleitung: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants that captures sunlight. Without it, plants could not make food, and there would hardly be any oxygen to breathe. It is the reason why meadows and forests look green.
wichtigste: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that captures sunlight.
It sits in tiny parts of plant cells, the chloroplasts.
With the captured light energy, plants carry out photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and throws back green light.
In the middle of each chlorophyll molecule sits a magnesium atom.
In autumn trees break down the chlorophyll, which is why the leaves turn yellow and red.

abschnitte.text: Chlorophyll is a **pigment** that plants, algae and some bacteria make. The name comes from Greek and means roughly “leaf green”. It is found in small cell components, the **chloroplasts**. A single leaf contains millions of such chloroplasts. There are several kinds, the most important being called chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b.

Sunlight consists of many colours, as you see in a rainbow. Chlorophyll swallows mainly the **red** and the **blue** light. The green light is thrown back, which is why leaves look green to our eyes. The light energy it takes up, chlorophyll passes on to other molecules in the cell. In this way light becomes energy that the plant can use.

With the light energy, plants make grape sugar from water and carbon dioxide from the air. This process is called **photosynthesis**. As a waste product, oxygen is formed, which humans and animals need to breathe. The plant uses the sugar as food and as a building material. In this way almost all life on Earth depends directly or indirectly on chlorophyll.

abschnitte.titel: Why leaves turn colourful in autumn
abschnitte.text: In autumn, deciduous trees break down the valuable chlorophyll and store its building blocks in the trunk. Then other pigments come to light that were in the leaf all summer. The yellow and orange **carotenoids** were previously covered by the abundant green. Some trees such as the maple even make new red pigments in autumn. After that the trees drop their leaves.

In 1817 the French chemists Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou gave the pigment the name chlorophyll. The German chemist **Richard Willstätter** studied its structure, among other times during his period at ETH Zurich. For this work he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1915. He found out that a magnesium atom sits in the middle of the molecule.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny green part of the plant cell in which photosynthesis takes place.
A process in which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen from water and carbon dioxide.
Yellow and orange pigments that you also find, for example, in carrots.
A metal that sits in the centre of chlorophyll.

gewusst: Chlorophyll is built chemically very similarly to the red blood pigment haemoglobin, except that there iron sits in the middle instead of magnesium.
Chlorophyll is also used as a green food colouring, for example in sweets.
Under UV light, dissolved chlorophyll glows red.

teile.einleitung: Blossoms shine in yellow, blue, white or red. Their colours are like advertising signs for animals that seek nectar. Bees see the world quite differently from us.
wichtigste: Colourful blossoms attract animals that carry pollen on.
Blossoms whose pollen is carried by the wind are often small and greenish.
Bees hardly see red, but they do see ultraviolet light.
Bees see blue and yellow especially well.
White blossoms shine at dusk and attract moths.
Hummingbirds in America like to visit red blossoms.

abschnitte.text: Many plants need animals that carry their **pollen** from blossom to blossom. With bright **colours** the blossoms stand out from afar. Plants whose pollen is carried by the **wind** do not have to attract animals. Their blossoms are therefore often **small and greenish**, as in grasses or hazel shrubs. The **daisy**, by contrast, has white petals on the outside and a **yellow centre** that attracts insects.

Bees see colours differently from us. **Blue** and **yellow** they see very well and often fly to such blossoms. **Red**, on the other hand, appears almost black to them, so red blossoms hardly catch their attention. In return, bees see **ultraviolet light**, which we cannot see. Many blossoms have UV patterns that show the bees the way to the nectar.

abschnitte.titel: A colour signal in the horse chestnut
abschnitte.text: The blossoms of the **horse chestnut** have a coloured spot. In young blossoms it is **yellow**, and there is a lot of nectar. Later the spot turns **red**. This shows: here there is no more nectar. Bees then prefer to fly to the fresh blossoms with a yellow spot. This way they save time, and the plant steers them to the blossoms that still have to be pollinated.

abschnitte.titel: White for the night, red for birds
abschnitte.text: At dusk **white blossoms** shine best. **Moths** therefore find them easily. In **America** many red blossoms are visited by **hummingbirds**. These small birds see red very well and drink nectar with their long beak. In Europe there are no hummingbirds.

gewusst: The colour of some blossoms, such as hydrangeas, depends on the soil: in acid soil they tend to bloom blue.
Hummingbirds can hover in the air while they drink nectar.

teile.einleitung: Monocotyledons are a large group of flowering plants. Their seedling has only a single seed leaf. They include grasses, cereals, lilies, orchids and even palms.
wichtigste: The seedling of a monocotyledon has only one seed leaf.
The leaf veins mostly run parallel.
The flower parts are mostly arranged in threes.
The vascular bundles in the stem are scattered.
Wheat, maize and rice belong to the true grasses.
With over 25,000 species, orchids are one of the most species-rich plant families.

abschnitte.text: When a seed sprouts, the **seed leaves** appear first. In the **monocotyledons** there is only one. In the dicotyledons, such as the bean or the sunflower, there are two. The leaves of monocotyledons mostly have **parallel veins**, easy to see in grasses and tulips. Net-like veins are typical of dicotyledons.

In many monocotyledons the flower parts are arranged in **threes**. A tulip, for example, has six petals in two circles of three. Stamens and carpels often follow this number too. This makes it possible to recognise many species just from the flower.

In a cross-section of a **maize stem**, the **vascular bundles** lie scattered. There is no **cambium ring**, which in trees forms new wood every year. That is why there is no typical thickening growth. In grasses the first root soon dies. Instead, many equally strong roots grow from the base of the shoot. This creates a **tufted root system**.

The **true grasses** supply humanity's most important staple foods with **wheat, maize and rice**. With over 25,000 species, the **orchids** are one of the most species-rich plant families. They occur mainly in the tropics. In Switzerland, too, around **70 wild orchid species** grow.

The **palms** are also monocotyledons, for example the **date palm**. Its thick trunk forms without cambium. Already near the tip of the shoot it is laid down as thick as it will stay. This is called **primary thickening growth**. After that the trunk grows almost only in height.

gewusst: A palm is more closely related to grasses than to oaks or beeches.
In Switzerland, too, around 70 wild orchid species grow.

teile.einleitung: The false white stalked cup fungus, known in German as Falsches Weisses Stängelbecherchen, is a tiny fungus with a big effect. It causes ash dieback, which is killing many ash trees all over Europe and in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The scientific name is Hymenoscyphus fraxineus.
The fungus comes from East Asia, where it lives on the Manchurian ash.
At first, in 2006, only an asexual form was described, as Chalara fraxinea.
It looks very similar to the harmless native white stalked cup fungus.
Its white little cups grow on fallen leaf stalks of the ash.
It belongs to the sac fungi.

abschnitte.text: The fungus is now called **Hymenoscyphus fraxineus**. At first, in **2006**, however, only an **asexual form** was described, under the name **Chalara fraxinea**. Only later was the form with the little white cups found. The word “false” in the name has a reason: the fungus looks very similar to the harmless native **white stalked cup fungus**. Only **genetic studies** showed that they are two different species.

The false white stalked cup fungus comes from **East Asia**. There it lives on the **Manchurian ash** without causing much damage. In Europe the fungus meets ash trees that have no defence against it. It belongs to the **sac fungi**. Its cup-shaped fruiting bodies are called **apothecia**, and inside them the spores form in small sacs.

In summer, the tiny white cups appear on the **previous year's leaf stalks** of the ash, which lie in the litter on the ground. From there the **spores** are carried by the wind to new leaves. This is how the fungus attacks leaves, shoots and bark. On weakened ash trees, the **honey fungus**, another fungus, often settles at the base of the trunk as well. Such trees can fall over and become a danger on roads and paths.

A small share of ash trees show hardly any damage. Researchers are looking for such **less susceptible** trees. They are to be preserved and used for **breeding**. This way experts hope that there will still be ash trees in our forests in the future.

gewusst: Other introduced tree diseases are Dutch elm disease and chestnut blight.
The true and the false stalked cup fungus can only be told apart reliably with genetic tests.

teile.einleitung: Firewood is wood that you burn to heat or to cook. It is one of the oldest fuels of humankind and is popular in Switzerland to this day.
wichtigste: Firewood is burned in the stove, in the fireplace or on the campfire.
It must dry well before burning.
Fresh wood usually needs one to two years to dry.
A stacked pile of wood is called a Holzbeige in Switzerland.
A split piece is called a log.

abschnitte.text: **Firewood** is burned in the stove, in the **fireplace** or on the campfire. It gives **warmth** and light. In the past almost everyone cooked and heated with wood. Today many houses in Switzerland still heat with wood, for example with logs, chips or pellets. Wood grows back and therefore counts as a renewable fuel.

Freshly felled wood contains a lot of water. **Wet wood** burns badly, gives little warmth and makes a lot of smoke. **Dry wood** burns hot and clean. That is why freshly split firewood is usually left to dry in the air for **one to two years**. It is best kept in an airy place with a roof against rain.

A split piece of firewood is called a **log**. You split it with the **axe** or splitting maul: you strike the piece of wood apart lengthways. A neatly stacked pile is called a **Holzbeige** or Scheiterbeige in Switzerland. This way the wood dries well, and it needs little space.

To produce little smoke, experts recommend **lighting a fire from the top**. At the bottom lie the larger logs, at the top thin kindling and a firelighter. This way the fire burns slowly downwards. In stoves you may burn only clean, untreated wood. Waste, painted wood or cardboard do not belong in, because poisonous substances are produced.

gewusst: The word “Beige” for a wood pile is known mainly in Swiss German.
Dry firewood sounds bright when you knock two logs together.

teile.einleitung: Detritus is a technical word from ecology for dead organic material. It includes fallen leaves, dead animals, dung and the tiniest remains of living things. Detritus is food for many animals and tiny organisms.
wichtigste: Detritus is dead organic material.
The earthworm is a typical detritus feeder in the soil.
In forests, most of the plant production flows into the detritus food chain.
The top soil layer of hardly decomposed leaves is called the litter layer.
In the ocean, flaky detritus drifts down into the depths as marine snow.
Material that gets into a body of water from outside is called allochthonous.

abschnitte.text: The word **detritus** comes from Latin and means something like rubbed-off material. In ecology it means **dead organic material**: leaves, needles, dead roots, dead animals, dung and tiny remains. In the forest this material first lies on the ground and forms the **litter layer**, the top layer of hardly decomposed leaves and needles. Beneath it, it gradually becomes humus.

Two kinds of food chains are distinguished. In one, animals eat living plants, for example a roe deer that eats leaves. In the **detritus food chain**, everything begins with dead material. In **forests**, the **largest part** of the biomass that plants make every year flows into this chain. Most leaves, namely, are not eaten but fall to the ground.

A typical **detritus feeder** is the **earthworm**. It eats leaves and soil and leaves behind fertile dung. **Woodlice** and **millipedes** chop up the leaves and so **increase** the **surface**. After that, **microorganisms** such as bacteria and fungi can break the material down faster. It is teamwork: the animals chop up, the tiny organisms decompose.

In streams too, detritus plays a big role. In autumn a lot of leaves fall from the bank into the water. Material that gets into a body of water **from outside** in this way is called **allochthonous**. Material that arises in the water itself is called autochthonous. Animals such as the **freshwater shrimp** are among the **shredders**: they eat the fallen leaves and break them into small pieces, on which other animals live.

In the ocean, tiny remains of dead plankton, dung and other particles are constantly sinking downwards. These flakes are called **marine snow**, because in the light of diving robots they look like snowflakes. Marine snow is an important food for animals in the dark deep sea, where no plants can grow. A part of it collects on the sea floor.

gewusst: Marine snow often needs several weeks to reach the deep sea floor.
Without detritus feeders, a new thick layer of leaves would pile up in a deciduous forest every year.

teile.einleitung: Chloroplasts are small green components of plant cells. Photosynthesis takes place in them: with light energy they make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. Without chloroplasts there would hardly be any life on Earth.
wichtigste: Chloroplasts are green because of the pigment chlorophyll.
They belong to the plastids.
They use light energy for photosynthesis.
Inside lie flat membrane sacs, the thylakoids.
Like mitochondria, they have their own genetic material.
In land plants they are usually lens-shaped.
When a tomato ripens, they turn into chromoplasts.

abschnitte.text: **Chloroplasts** are small components of the cell, so-called **organelles**. They contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures light. With this **light energy** they build up sugar from water and carbon dioxide. Oxygen is released in the process. This process is called **photosynthesis**. Chloroplasts belong to the group of **plastids**, which also includes other organelles of the plant cell.

In land plants, chloroplasts are usually **lens-shaped**. They are surrounded by two envelope membranes. Inside lie many flat membrane sacs, the **thylakoids**. They are often stacked like rolls of coins, and these stacks are called **grana**. In the thylakoid membranes sits the chlorophyll. The fluid around the thylakoids is called the **stroma**. There the sugar is made in the Calvin cycle.

abschnitte.titel: Where there are many and where none
abschnitte.text: Especially many chloroplasts lie in the **palisade cells**. These long cells stand close under the upper side of the leaf, where a lot of light arrives. A single cell can contain several dozen chloroplasts. **Roots in the soil** normally have no chloroplasts, because no light gets there. They are also missing in white petals.

Like **mitochondria**, chloroplasts have **their own genetic material**. They multiply by dividing, similar to bacteria. Science explains this with the **endosymbiont theory**: a very long time ago, a cell took in a bacterium that could carry out photosynthesis and did not digest it. In time this became the chloroplast. Its closest relatives are the **cyanobacteria**.

Chloroplasts can change. When a **tomato** ripens, the chlorophyll is broken down. At the same time, red pigments form. The chloroplasts become **chromoplasts**, the pigment carriers. That is why the fruit changes from green to red. Something similar happens in peppers and many other fruits.

gewusst: Chloroplasts can move in the cell: in very strong light they turn sideways so that they are not damaged.
The name comes from Greek: “chloros” means green and “plastos” formed.

teile.einleitung: The date palm is a tall palm that grows in warm desert regions. People have eaten its sweet fruits, the dates, for thousands of years. Its leaves and trunk are also very useful.
wichtigste: Date palms like to grow in warm desert regions.
They need water at the roots, for example in an oasis.
The dates hang in large bunches on the palm.
In every date there is an elongated stone.
Dates are often dried so that they keep for a long time.
People weave baskets from the long leaves.

abschnitte.text: Date palms grow in **warm desert regions**, for example in North Africa and on the Arabian Peninsula. They love sun and heat. But they need water at the roots. That is why they often grow in an **oasis**, where groundwater comes close to the surface. A date palm can grow over 20 metres tall.

The dates grow right at the top under the leaves. They hang in **large bunches** that can weigh many kilograms. Ripe dates are brown, soft and very sweet. In every date there is an **elongated stone**. To harvest the fruits, people climb the palm or use a lifting platform.

abschnitte.titel: Dried, they keep for a long time
abschnitte.text: Fresh dates spoil quickly. That is why they are often **dried**. Dried dates keep for a very long time and used to be an important supply for travellers in the desert. Because they contain so much sugar, they give energy quickly. In Switzerland you find dates in the shops mainly in winter.

The date palm supplies not only fruits. From the **long leaves**, people weave **baskets**, mats and hats. The trunk serves as building timber, and ropes are made from the fibres. The palm also gives shade under which other plants can grow.

gewusst: The date palm is among the oldest crop plants of humankind.
Researchers made a date stone about 2,000 years old from Israel germinate again.

teile.einleitung: High above Interlaken, on the Schynige Platte, lies a special garden. Hundreds of wild plants of the Swiss Alps grow there, and you also have a magnificent view of the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
wichtigste: The alpine garden lies above Interlaken in the Bernese Oberland.
It is at just under 2000 metres above sea level.
You reach it by cog railway from Wilderswil.
It shows wild plants of the Swiss Alps.
It is open only in the summer half of the year.
The garden was set up in 1928 and works together with the University of Bern.

abschnitte.text: The **Schynige Platte** lies south-east above **Interlaken** and high above Lake Brienz. The alpine garden is at just under **2000 metres above sea level**. From there the view reaches far into the Bernese Oberland. Especially famous is the view of the trio **Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau**.

To the garden runs the **Schynige Platte Railway** from **Wilderswil**. It is a cog railway with historic carriages and has run since the 19th century. The journey takes a while and leads up through forest and alpine pastures. Because of the snow, the railway and the garden run only in the **summer half of the year**, roughly from the end of May to the end of October.

The garden shows **native wild plants** of the Swiss Alps. They do not grow in beds arranged by colour, but in their natural **communities**, for example on limestone, on acid soil, in bogs or on scree. At this altitude typical plants of the subalpine and alpine zones thrive. Many bloom especially beautifully in June and July.

The garden was set up in **1928** and opened to the public in 1929. It is among the oldest alpine gardens in Switzerland. Scientifically it works closely with the **University of Bern**, with its Institute of Plant Sciences and the Botanical Garden. Since 1932 the university has held alpine botany courses there. The garden thus serves **education** and **research**.

gewusst: The Schynige Platte Railway has been running up the mountain since the 19th century.
The garden shows plants by habitat, so you learn where they really grow in the mountains.

teile.einleitung: Common valerian is a tall plant with small white to pink flowers. Its root has long been known as a calming remedy. And cats love its smell.
wichtigste: Common valerian is called Valeriana officinalis in science.
It is mainly the root that is used as a remedy.
Valerian is considered a mild remedy for calming down and for trouble falling asleep.
Dried roots have a strong smell, a bit like old socks.
Many cats react to the smell with great excitement.
The plant grows in damp places and reaches about 1.5 metres in height.

abschnitte.text: Common valerian is a tall **perennial**. It usually grows to between half a metre and one and a half metres. At the top it carries many small **white to pale pink flowers** in umbrella-like clusters. They have a sweetish scent. The scientific name is **Valeriana officinalis**.
Valerian loves **damp soil**. It is found at the edges of streams and ditches, in damp meadows and in floodplain forests. It is widespread in Switzerland too. Many insects visit its flowers.

The active substances are mainly in the **rootstock** and the **roots**. These are dug up, dried and processed. Valerian is considered a **mild sedative**. It is taken as a tea, drops or tablets for nervousness and trouble falling asleep. As with all remedies, if you have symptoms it is better to ask a professional first.

When the root is dried, **isovaleric acid** is formed, among other things. It has a strong smell reminiscent of sweaty feet. Most people find that unpleasant. Many **cats**, on the other hand, roll about, purr and get very excited. That is why there are cat toys containing valerian.

The genus name **Valeriana** is often derived from the Latin word “valere”, which means “to be healthy”. The word **“officinalis”** shows that the plant was formerly used in pharmacies. Many medicinal plants carry this addition in their name.

gewusst: The smell that people find disgusting drives many cats wild.
The addition “officinalis” in a name shows that a plant was formerly used in pharmacies.

teile.einleitung: The epidermis is the outermost layer of cells of a leaf, a kind of skin of the plant. It protects the inside of the leaf and uses tiny openings to control how much air and water vapour get in and out.
wichtigste: The epidermis covers the upper and lower sides of a leaf.
It usually consists of only a single layer of cells.
Most epidermis cells are transparent, so that light can enter the leaf.
A stoma consists of two guard cells.
Guard cells contain chloroplasts, the other epidermis cells do not.
Water evaporates through the stomata, and this is called transpiration.

abschnitte.text: The **epidermis** is the outer covering layer of the leaf. It lies on the upper and on the lower side. It is usually only **a single layer of cells** thick. Even so, it is strong, because the cells fit together without gaps. It protects the inside of the leaf from injury, drying out and **disease-causing organisms**. It is often also covered with a waxy layer.

Most cells of the epidermis are **colourless and transparent**. They act like a clear window. This lets the light reach the green cells inside the leaf. There **photosynthesis** takes place, in which the plant makes sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.

In the epidermis lie tiny **stomata**. Each consists of **two guard cells** with a gap between them. Under the microscope they look like two beans. Unlike the other epidermis cells, the guard cells contain **chloroplasts**. They can open and close the gap. Water evaporates from the leaf through the openings. This **transpiration** draws new water up from the roots.

In most plants the stomata lie mainly on the underside. In the **water lily** it is the other way round. Its leaves lie with their underside on the water, so the stomata sit **on top**, where there is air. **Leaf hairs** also grow out of the epidermis. The **stinging hairs** of the nettle are such outgrowths. When touched, their tip breaks off and the stinging sap enters the skin.

gewusst: On the underside of a single leaf there can be tens of thousands of stomata.
The tip of a stinging hair breaks off like a fine glass needle.
